He had cried out to God about injustice and chaos, and God answered that the proud Babylonians would come, and fall, on a timetable Habakkuk would not choose; but the righteous would live by his faith, trusting God through the coming disaster. Two questions often arise. First, the Hebrew word (emunah) can mean faithfulness as well as faith. But the faithfulness meant in Habakkuk is the steady trust of a person who relies on God’s word and waits for it, the trust Abraham showed (Genesis 15:6), so Paul is not changing its meaning but showing its heart. Second, the Greek can be read as “the righteous shall live by faith” or “the one who is righteous by faith shall live”. Both are true, and the letter explains both: chapters 1–4 show how a person is righteous by faith, and chapters 5–8 show how the righteous person lives. Live means more than survive: it is the eternal life God gives (5:17–21; 6:23). The same faith that receives a righteousness you did not earn is the faith you go on living by in the dark, when nothing is visible.

Where Christians differ: what is the righteousness of God? Roman Catholic teaching sees it mainly as a righteousness God works into us over time, making us just. Some recent scholars (the New Perspective) see it as God’s covenant faithfulness. Verdict: it includes God’s faithfulness and his righteous character, but at its heart in Romans it is the gift of a righteous standing before God, credited to the believer on the basis of Christ’s work (3:21–26; 4:5–6; 5:17). We are justified by Christ’s righteousness imputed to us, not by our own righteousness imparted. This is the heart of the Reformation, and of the gospel.

In a sentence. In the gospel the righteousness from God is revealed, by faith from first to last, as Scripture says: the righteous will live by faith.

On a Tuesday. The merit system is not a medieval problem the sixteenth century solved. It is the default setting of the human heart, and it reassembles itself in every generation, including in churches that would sign every Reformation confession. So suppose you were asked tonight why God should accept you. Not what you would say in a Bible study, but what actually rises first. If the answer includes “I try”, or “I have been”, or “at least I never”, your account is being kept in your own name. The gospel’s answer to that question contains no information about you at all. And watch what happens to your sense of acceptance after you sin badly. If it drops, and slowly recovers over a few days of doing better, you have discovered what you are living on. An alien righteousness does not fluctuate, because you never generated it and cannot damage it.

For worship. Luther spent years trying to give God a righteousness God would accept. He was looking at the wrong side of the transaction the whole time. The gospel does not tell you how to produce a righteousness for God. It announces a righteousness from God, the spotless obedience of his own Son, put to the account of every sinner who trusts him. The only hand that can take it is the one that has stopped trying to make its own, and the gates it opens do not close.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul immediately establishes why it is necessary. The gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news — and the bad news Paul now delivers is as stark and unsparing as anything in Scripture. God's wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. The problem is not ignorance; it is suppression. Humanity knows God — knows him through creation, through conscience — and actively holds that knowledge down, refusing its implications, fleeing from its demands.

The structure of vv. 18–32 is a three-stage description of idolatry's logic and its consequences. First, the knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20). Then, God is exchanged for idols — images of creatures replacing the uncreated Creator (vv. 21–23). Then, God gives them up — three times that terrible phrase appears (vv. 24, 26, 28) — abandoning them to the sexual and moral dissolution that is both the consequence and the judgment of their idolatry. The wrath of God is not primarily a future event; it is a present reality, operating through the structure of a moral universe that reaps what it sows.

This passage is not a description of the worst of humanity — the serial killers and tyrants. It is a description of normal human culture operating without the restraining grace of God. The Rome to which Paul wrote would have recognised itself in these verses. So would every culture in every age. So would every human heart that is honest enough to look clearly at itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has insisted, against every attempt to soften or allegorize it, that the wrath of God is real, personal, and active. It is not merely the impersonal outworking of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), nor a primitive metaphor for natural consequences. It is the holy, settled, righteous opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed definitively that in both Testaments, divine wrath is personal and purposeful — God's moral revulsion at sin, expressed in active judgment. The gospel is only fully good news when this wrath is fully real: Christ bore the wrath we deserved (3:25), and those who are in Christ are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's description of idol worship in vv. 22–23 — exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures — described the Roman religious world exactly. The pantheon of Rome was populated by humanised gods and deified emperors, all of them creatures rather than Creator. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance. We exchange the glory of God for the image of the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self, the entertained mind. Every idol is a creature thing promoted to Creator status — and Paul's analysis of the consequences (futile thinking, darkened hearts, moral dissolution) maps precisely onto what happens when any created thing is made to bear the weight only God can carry.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven. The first subject Paul takes up after his thesis is the wrath of God, and that is deliberate: the gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news. Before he explains the cure, he shows why we need it. And the word needs rescuing, because most people hear wrath and picture temper. The gods of Rome were famous for it: capricious, easily offended, dangerous chiefly because they were unpredictable. That is not what is described here. God’s wrath is not a mood he is in. It is his settled, personal, holy opposition to everything that ruins what he has made. It has no flare-ups and no bad days. It is not the opposite of his love but the form his love takes when it faces what is destroying its object, which is why a parent who feels nothing on hearing what was done to their child has not achieved serenity. They have stopped loving the child.

Revealed now. The same verb as verse 17, in the present tense. The wrath is being uncovered now, as God gives people over to their sins (vv. 24, 26, 28), and will be revealed fully at the judgment (2:5). And it is revealed from heaven, the language of a throne. Some have proposed that wrath in Paul is not an attitude in God at all, only an impersonal process by which bad actions produce bad results. But consequences do not come from anywhere; they simply happen. This comes from heaven. And the whole letter treats God as personally engaged with sin, ending at a cross that would be needless if the problem were mismanaged consequences. If nobody is angry, nobody needed to die.

Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Ungodliness is sin against God, the vertical failure; unrighteousness is sin against people, the horizontal one. Paul puts them in that order deliberately, because the rest of the chapter argues that the second always grows out of the first. Every item in the long list at the end, the envy, the gossip, the ruthlessness, arrives as a consequence. Society does not have a morality problem first. It has a God problem, of which the morality is the symptom. And notice who is in the sentence: men, humanity, with no subgroup named. Paul is laying out the case against everyone, and the moment the list ends he turns on the reader who has been enjoying it (2:1).

Who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. “Suppress” (katechontōn) means to hold down by force, and it describes an action, not a condition. Think of holding a football under the surface of a swimming pool. Anybody can do it, but it never happens by itself: the ball pushes up the whole time, and the moment your attention wanders it is on the surface again. That is Paul’s picture of unbelief. Not an empty space where knowledge of God never arrived, not innocent ignorance, but a continuous effort to keep something submerged that keeps trying to rise.

Is God angry with me when I sin as a Christian? Not with the wrath of this verse. For those in Christ, that wrath was spent on the cross, and there is now no condemnation (8:1). God still grieves over our sin and disciplines us, but as a Father who corrects the children he loves, for our good (Hebrews 12:5–11). Discipline is not wrath in smaller doses. It is love making sure we share his holiness.

Where Christians differ: is God’s wrath real? Some say a loving God cannot be wrathful, or that wrath is only the natural consequence of sin. Verdict: God’s wrath is personal and real, the reaction of his holiness to evil. Love and wrath are not opposites; a God who did not oppose evil would not be good. And the gospel is God’s answer: Christ bore that wrath (3:25; 5:9).

In a sentence. God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of people who suppress the truth by their wickedness.

On a Tuesday. Think of the moments when the pressure slips. Standing at a graveside, when the explanations you normally find adequate go thin. Holding a newborn. Somewhere so beautiful that the first thing you wanted to do was thank someone. Three in the morning after bad news. In those moments something surfaces, the sense that there is Someone, that you are known, and it is usually pushed back under within the hour. Paul’s claim is that the pushing is the whole story. Nobody is short of evidence. We are all working very hard. And if you reach the end of this chapter feeling vindicated about somebody else, you have read it as Paul anticipated, not as he intended.

For worship. Put verses 17 and 18 side by side. The righteousness of God is revealed; the wrath of God is revealed: two things uncovered in the world at once. And there is one place in history where both were revealed together. At the cross the wrath of God was displayed more terribly than in any judgment ever recorded, and it fell on the only man who had never once held the truth under. God put him forward as the propitiation, the place where wrath is absorbed rather than deflected (3:25), so that those who are his are saved by him from the wrath of God (5:9). The wrath is real, it is personal, it is being revealed, and it has already arrived somewhere. For everyone who trusts him, that somewhere was not you. It was him.

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.

For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. This is general revelation: God shows himself to everyone through creation (Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:17). Calvin called the world a theatre of God’s glory. The knowledge is universal and unavoidable, and notice who does the showing: God has shown it. Creation is not a set of clues God left lying about for those who care to investigate. It is his own voice, at conversational volume, everywhere, all the time.

His invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature. Paul has put a deliberate contradiction in the sentence: the unseeable is clearly seen. He means it the way you mean it when you say you can see someone is exhausted. You are not seeing tiredness; you are seeing a face, and reading it. Nobody has watched a hand write a letter and observed a mind, yet only a lunatic would say the mind is unevidenced. The world works like handwriting. And Paul is precise about how much it says. Two things: God’s eternal power (he must be powerful to make all this) and his divine nature (he is God, of an altogether different order from what he has made). It does not say that God is merciful, that he has a Son, that there is forgiveness for what you did. Creation is enough light to know you are answerable. It is not enough light to be saved.

So they are without excuse. Anapologētos: having no defence to offer, a courtroom word. Enough to condemn, not enough to save. Paul is not claiming that nobody is ever honestly confused, or that everyone secretly believes and is lying. He is saying that when the case is heard, no one will stand up and say the evidence was insufficient. The claim is about what will be sayable on the last day.

What it does not mean. This is not a licence for contempt. Paul is not authorising you to treat the sceptic at your table as a liar, and if this passage has ever made you feel superior in an argument you have taken a truth about the human race and used it as a weapon against one member of it. The suppression he describes is yours too: it is the reason you can know God is real and still live for stretches of a week as though he were not.

A question every reader asks: what about those who never heard? If creation reveals enough to condemn but not enough to save, what of people who never hear the gospel? Paul answers the parts he answers. People are not judged for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are judged for suppressing the light they did have, in creation and in conscience (2:12–16). God is perfectly just, and no one will be condemned unfairly (Genesis 18:25). If you carry a real grief about a particular person, this verse does not settle their case. It settles that God is not unjust in having a case at all. But that light cannot save, because no one responds to it rightly (3:10–12); salvation comes only through faith in Christ, and faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (10:13–17). That is why Paul was a missionary, and why the church must send the gospel to every nation.

Where Christians differ: can people be saved without hearing of Christ? Inclusivists hold that some who never hear the gospel may be saved by Christ’s work if they respond in faith to the light of creation, appealing to God’s justice and to believers outside Israel such as Melchizedek and Job. Verdict: Scripture gives no warrant for that hope. General revelation leaves people without excuse (v. 20), not with a way of salvation; there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12); and Paul’s own logic assumes that people cannot call on one they have not heard of (10:14–15). God is free to work as he wills, and he can bring the gospel to anyone; but the church’s task is clear: go and tell.

What about infants, and people who cannot understand? Paul is speaking of those who are able to perceive and suppress what God shows them. Infants who die, and people who were never able to understand, are in a different position. Scripture gives real hope here (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions say that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). They are not saved by innocence, but by the same Saviour as everyone else.

In a sentence. What may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain: since the creation of the world his invisible qualities, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen in what he has made, so they have no excuse.

On a Tuesday. Take the last thing that genuinely stopped you: a night sky with no streetlights, a piece of music that went through you before you had decided anything about it, the face of someone you love asleep, the plain fact that there is something rather than nothing. In the moment itself the response was not neutral observation. It was closer to awe, and awe is a response to a someone. That reflex, not the argument afterwards, is what Paul says is the knowledge of God arriving. Then watch what you habitually do with it thirty seconds later.

For worship. The person who says he sees no evidence is standing inside the evidence, saying it. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1), and every sunrise is his signature. The remarkable achievement of the human race is not that we have failed to hear him. It is how good we have become at talking over him. And the God whose power is written across the sky did not leave us with the sky alone. He sent his Son, so that the God who could be known only as Maker could be known as Saviour.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,

For although they knew God. The fall described here is first a fall of worship. Humanity had the knowledge, the evidence and the obligation, and refused two things.

They did not honor him as God. This does not mean they failed to praise loudly. It means they declined to treat him as what he is. To honour God is to give him his proper weight in the actual running of a life. And it is entirely possible to hold a correct opinion about God’s existence and never once let it cost you a decision: to believe in him and arrange your week, your money, your ambitions and your bedtime exactly as you would if he were not there. That is not atheism. It is something the Bible treats as worse, because it knows and does not weigh. Not atheism first, but refusal to give God his due: every sin begins here.

Or give thanks to him. Paul has begun a chapter that ends in murder, malice and ruthlessness, and the first item on the charge sheet is failing to say thank you. That looks like a category error until you see what gratitude is. To thank someone is to admit you have received something you did not produce. And nothing about you was produced by you: not the lungs working without your attention, not the intelligence you use to argue about God, not the century you were born into, nor the fact that you exist at all. Thanklessness is not rudeness. It is a claim about ownership, the quiet insistence that what I have, I hold by right. Nobody has ever genuinely thanked God for something he believed he had earned.

But they became futile in their thinking. Emataiōthēsan: made empty, vain. In the Greek Old Testament this word group is the standard term for idols themselves: the vanities, the empty things, the nothings. So Jeremiah can make the pun that carries the whole indictment: your fathers went after worthlessness, and became worthless (Jeremiah 2:5). You do not merely serve an empty thing. You catch its emptiness. The Psalms give the mechanism: idols have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear, and those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Psalm 115:5–8). Worship is not a transaction you conduct with an object. It is a transformation you undergo. Bow to something blind and deaf, and you will go blind and deaf, which is exactly what Paul reports next.

And their foolish hearts were darkened. The heart, the centre of the person, darkened. And the verb is passive. The lights did not simply fail; they were turned down, by God, in judgment. It is the first tremor of the phrase that will sound three times over the rest of the chapter: God gave them up. And a dark room is the one place where you cannot tell how dark it has become.

Claiming to be wise, they became fools. The claim is not incidental to the foolishness; it is the evidence of it (1 Corinthians 1:20–21; Psalm 14:1). And notice who Paul is describing. Not primitives. He is writing to the capital of a civilisation with law courts, aqueducts, libraries and four hundred years of philosophy behind it, in which serious men carried food to statues. The great irony of proud intellect.

What it does not mean. Paul is not against learning. He is the most educated writer in the New Testament, he quotes pagan poets when it suits him, and nothing here suggests that ignorance is safer than knowledge. The folly he names is not a shortage of information. It is a first-rate mind with its worship pointed at something that cannot bear the weight.

In a sentence. Although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor thanked him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened, and claiming to be wise, they became fools.

On a Tuesday. You cannot usually see your own idol directly. But if we become like what we worship, look at what you are becoming and read backwards. Have you grown more anxious and grasping over the last five years? You may be worshipping something that can be taken from you. Harder, quicker to contempt? Something that requires hardness to keep. Exhausted and unable to rest? Something that never says enough, well done. Your character is sworn testimony about your worship, and unlike your doctrine, it cannot be edited before it is submitted. And give thanks to God today, by name, for three things you did not make.

For worship. Idolatry is a tragedy and not merely an offence. The insult to God is real, but what should frighten a person is the arrangement itself: you will get what you chose. And what you chose has no mouth to speak your name, no ears for anything you say to it in the dark, and nothing to give back, while the God who was set aside is the only one in the transaction who was ever able to love you in return. And we, who are being made like what we behold, are invited to behold the glory of the Lord, and so be changed into his image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18).

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.

And exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images. “Exchanged” is the hinge of the chapter (vv. 23, 25, 26), and it is a commercial word. An exchange is not a loss; it is a transaction, entered into deliberately, in which you hand over one thing and receive another because at the moment of the trade you preferred what you were getting. Nobody exchanges under duress. Paul is not describing people who drifted or were misled. He is describing a swap somebody wanted to make. Idolatry is replacing God with something less.

The terms of the trade. On one side, the glory (doxa) of the immortal God: the weight and blazing splendour of the One who cannot die. On the other, images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things. Not even the creatures themselves: likenesses of them. Copies. So the exchange runs from the living God to a picture of a lizard, and Paul lets the sentence make the argument. Jeremiah put it as bewilderment: has a nation ever changed its gods, even though they are no gods? But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled, O heavens, at this (Jeremiah 2:11–12). Even the sky is invited to stare.

Resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things. A staircase, and it only goes down: man, birds, four-footed beasts, reptiles, each step lower. Greek statues of gods in human form, Egyptian gods with animal heads. And idolatry never levels out. Whatever a person puts in God’s place begins as something reasonably impressive, a career, a cause, a person you admire, a version of yourself you are working towards, and it does not stay there. The thing you serve keeps asking for slightly more and offering slightly less. Nobody sets out to worship a creeping thing. They set out to worship something a good deal higher up, and the staircase does the rest.

The golden calf. Paul writes with Israel’s own story in his ear. The nation had heard the voice of God out of the fire at Sinai, and within weeks had made a calf. The psalm describes it in almost these words: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass (Psalm 106:20). So Paul is not indicting the pagan world from a safe distance. He uses the language of Israel’s worst failure to describe the human race, which is exactly what makes chapter 2 possible. The people with the true revelation did this too, faster and with less excuse.

Today’s idols. Rome made its idols of marble, and ours are not carved, but the definition has not changed: an idol is any created thing given the job that belongs to God. Money, pleasure, power, self, whatever takes God’s place. Created things can carry a great deal; they cannot carry that. A career cannot forgive you. A marriage cannot make you unashamed. A child was never designed to be the meaning of a parent’s life, and a child handed that job will feel its weight long before either of them can name what has gone wrong.

In a sentence. They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images made to look like mortal humans, birds, animals and reptiles.

On a Tuesday. Take something you value and ask what its loss would do to you. If it went tomorrow, the job, the reputation, the health, the person, would you be grieved, or would you be finished? Grief is what you feel when you lose a great gift. The sense that the floor has gone is what you feel when you lose a god. Then ask what you turn to first when you feel small. Not what you believe in; what you reach for. That reflex is worship. And if you do not like the results, this verse is a description of the human race, not a special diagnosis of you. The exchange cannot be reversed by a man deciding to be less idolatrous. It is reversed when the glory that was traded away comes looking for the people who traded it.

For worship. That is the whole of what this letter goes on to announce: God, who said let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). They wanted a god they could look at. In the end God gave them one: not the likeness of a creature, but his own Son with a human face, who could be looked at, and touched, and was.

parallels.desc: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.

Therefore God gave them up. Three times this phrase falls like a gavel (vv. 24, 26, 28). Paredōken is a strong verb: to hand over, to deliver up, what a magistrate does when he consigns a prisoner to the jailer. So this is not God losing interest, and not merely God standing aside; it is a judicial act, a sentence passed. This is the present revelation of God’s wrath (v. 18): not usually fire from heaven, but God letting people have what they want, and its consequences. The worst judgment is to be left to yourself.

In the lusts of their hearts. Note what he hands them over to: the desires of their own hearts. Not something injected from outside. He manufactures no appetite in this passage; he lifts the restraint that held an existing appetite in check, and lets the person have himself. And this is more frightening than fire from heaven, because of how it feels from inside, which is like nothing at all. There is no announcement. If anything the experience is pleasant: the internal argument that once took an hour now takes a minute and then stops happening, and it registers as freedom. You do not feel a hand come off your shoulder. You simply notice, if you notice at all, that you are moving more easily than you used to.

To impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves. The sentence fits the crime. In verse 21 they refused to honour God; here they are given up to dishonouring their own bodies. Withhold from God the weight that is his and you will not keep it for yourself; you will lose your own. Divine judgment in Scripture is never arbitrary: the sentence is the sin, allowed to run its course. And “among themselves” adds the last turn: this is not done to them by an outside power. It is what they do to one another once nothing is holding them back.

Because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie. The Greek has the article English drops: the lie. Not any falsehood, but a particular one, first told in a garden by a creature who suggested that if they took matters into their own hands they would be like God (Genesis 3:5). The lie is that something other than God is God, and every idolatry since has been a variation on it. It is not usually experienced as a theological position. It is experienced as the perfectly reasonable conviction that you are the best judge of what your life is for.

And worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator. Two verbs, which is why idolatry is so hard to spot in a culture where nobody kneels. Worship in the Bible is never only what you revere; it is what you serve, what you organise your hours around, what gets the first call on your energy and the last word in your decisions. Check the diary and the bank statement, which are less polite than the conscience and better informed. This is the essence of idolatry.

Who is blessed forever! Amen. Paul is in the middle of the most damning paragraph he ever wrote, and he cannot get through the words “rather than the Creator” without stopping to bless him. It is a reflex, not a device, and it tells us two things. God’s blessedness is untouched by all this: he is not diminished by being exchanged, and idolatry does not injure God; it destroys the idolater. And the man writing the vice list is a worshipper, not a prosecutor. Anyone who can recite Romans 1 with relish has caught the content and missed the author.

Does God cause sin when he gives people up? No. God never makes anyone sin or tempts anyone to evil (James 1:13). Giving up means that God withdraws the restraints of his common grace and lets people go where their own hearts already want to go. It is a judicial sentence: you have chosen this, so have it. Like a judge who hands a person over to the consequences of a crime, God hands people over to their own desires. It is also a warning: the greatest mercy is that God does not give us all up, but holds us back and calls us home.

Could God have given me up? If you are troubled by the thought, that trouble is itself the sign that he has not. The people of this verse are not distressed by their sin; they enjoy it and defend it. A conscience that still aches, a heart that still wants to come back, is the work of God’s Spirit calling you home. Come back, and you will find that no one who comes to Christ is ever cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. So God gave them over in their hearts’ desires to impurity, degrading their bodies with one another, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshipped and served created things rather than the Creator, who is praised for ever, Amen.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything that used to trouble your conscience and no longer does? Not something you thought through, repented of, or came to see differently: those are fine. Something that simply went quiet. A habit that once cost you a bad evening and now costs you nothing. A way of speaking about your wife or a colleague that would have embarrassed you five years ago. A compromise at work that no longer presents itself as a decision. If you can name one, do not be relieved that the discomfort has gone. The discomfort was the restraint. Being left to your own desires is a judgment, not freedom; ask God not to leave you to yourself.

For worship. Paredōken, gave up, is not confined to this chapter. Paul uses the same verb of God twice more in this letter, and both times the object changes. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses (4:25), and he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (8:32). The word is identical. God handed sinners over to what they had chosen; then God handed his Son over to what they deserved. The second handing over is the answer to the first, and that is why the sentence in this chapter, terrible as it is, has never been the last word about anyone willing to have it lifted.
verseByVerse.note: “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose — his judgment working through their own desires.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.

For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. The second giving up moves from inward corruption to outward expression. This is the passage in Romans that people are most likely to reach already wounded, so let us go slowly and say the true things in the right order. Paul’s analysis is not that sexual disorder causes idolatry; it is that idolatry causes disorder. When the fundamental relationship, creature to Creator, is disordered, every other relationship becomes disordered downstream. And he takes a single illustration because he is arguing that idolatry is an exchange, the creature put where the Creator belongs, and he wants a case where the exchange is visible in the created order itself. He is not ranking sins: the list he is building ends with envy, gossip, boasting and disobedience to parents, under the same verdict.

For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature. “Exchanged” again: the exchange of God for idols is mirrored in exchanging the natural for the unnatural. “Contrary to nature” (para physin) means against the created order of male and female (Genesis 1:27; 2:24). This is the only place in Scripture that explicitly mentions women in same-sex relations.

And the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another. Paul does regard these acts as contrary to how God made men and women, and he grounds that not in the customs of his culture but in the created order, which is why his word is nature and why the passage reaches back past Moses to Genesis. The church has understood him this way for two thousand years, and honesty requires saying so plainly rather than leaving a reader to discover later that the text had been softened for him.

And receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error. “Due penalty” (antimisthia) is a fitting return, a recompense; “error” (planē) is wandering, going astray, and refers back to the exchange of God for idols (vv. 23, 25). Some suggest physical consequences such as disease. But Paul’s own logic points elsewhere: the penalty for exchanging God for idols is to be given over to the disordered desires themselves. The judgment is the condition. The penalty is in the sin, not only after it.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some today argue that Paul had in mind only the forms common in his world, such as men using boys, sex with slaves, temple prostitution, or excessive lust, and that committed, loving partnerships were not in view. Verdict: the text does not bear this out. Paul says the men were consumed with passion for one another, which describes mutual desire, not one party exploiting another, and he says nothing about age, payment or force. He includes women, which the pederasty reading cannot cover. He grounds his teaching in creation (“nature”, “the Creator”), the ground Jesus himself gives for marriage (Matthew 19:4–6), and the rest of Scripture speaks with one voice (Leviticus 18:22; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 1 Timothy 1:10). This is the historic Christian view, and it must be held with compassion.

What it does not mean. Paul is describing the human race, not diagnosing an individual. The sentence is corporate throughout: they, plural, humanity in the dock, tracing what happens to a civilisation that has let go of God. It does not say that a fifteen-year-old who discovers he is attracted to other boys arrived there by personally trading God for an idol, and anyone who uses this verse to tell him so has gone beyond what Paul wrote. Nobody chooses what they find themselves wanting; every person is answerable for what they do with it, and that is true of every desire in this chapter. And temptation is not sin. Our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), which settles it: an unwanted desire, however persistent, is not itself guilt. A Christian who is same-sex attracted and has spent years refusing to act on it is not failing at holiness. He is doing holiness, and a harder version of it than most of his congregation is asked to do.

The burden and the family. What makes this painful is usually not doubt about the ethics. It is loneliness. The church often asks such a brother or sister, in effect, for lifelong celibacy without any of the supports that ever made celibacy bearable: deep friendship, a household to belong to, a place at somebody’s table on ordinary Tuesdays, people who notice when they are ill. If this passage is going to be preached, the church that preaches it is under obligation to be the family it is asking people to do without. And to the parent who was told something by a son or daughter recently and has not slept properly since: you may hold what you believe, and you may keep your child. Nothing in this passage tells you to withdraw your affection, and the Gospels tell you whose houses your Lord sat in.

In a sentence. Because of this, God gave them over to shameful lusts: women exchanged natural sexual relations for unnatural ones, and men likewise abandoned natural relations with women and burned with lust for one another, committing shameful acts with other men and receiving in themselves the penalty they deserved.

On a Tuesday. Paul knows what happens in the mind of a religious reader working through these verses, the small, warm sense of not being one of those, and three sentences later he springs the trap: you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges, because you, the judge, practise the very same things (2:1). Chapter 1 is bait. Anyone who has used these two verses as a weapon has been caught by the trap Paul set, and did not hear it close. God’s design for sexuality is good, and his grace is for every sinner, including you.

For worship. Paul writes to Corinth, lists the sexually immoral, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers and swindlers, and then says: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). Such were. When the first Christians read a list like this one, they read it as a description of the people sitting next to them, including themselves, and the past tense was the whole of their hope, as it is of ours. The blood of Christ has never met a sinner it could not wash.

verseByVerse.quote: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.

And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God. The third giving up, and the repayment in kind is tighter than English can show, because Paul makes a pun and the pun is the sentence. They did not dokimazein, did not think God worth testing, approving, keeping on the books, so God handed them over to a mind that is adokimos: the same word with the negative stuck on the front. They ran the assay on God and marked him rejected; God ran the assay on them and marked them the same. And notice what they refused. Not knowledge of God, which verses 19–20 settled that they had, but to keep him in view, as a live consideration. That is not the atheism of the lecture hall. It is the practical atheism available to anyone, including people who would tick the right box on a survey: God is not denied, he is simply not consulted, and the mind quietly reorganises itself around his absence.

God gave them up to a debased mind. Adokimos belonged to the metal trade: a coin or ingot tested and failed, not currency, whatever it looked like. And that is the right picture, because a debased mind is not a stupid one. The coin has the right face stamped on it and the correct weight in the hand. This mind still reasons, argues, builds bridges, writes laws and wins prizes. What has gone is its ability to reach the right conclusion about anything that matters, which is why the most sophisticated societies in history have been perfectly capable of organising atrocities with excellent paperwork. Intellect was never the safeguard. It will work just as hard for a lie. The chapter has come full circle: it opened with minds made futile (vv. 21–22) and closes with the mind handed over. The organ used to commit the crime is the organ confiscated.

To do what ought not to be done. What is improper, unfitting. The words were the standard vocabulary of the Stoic moralists, the things fitting for a rational creature. Paul deliberately reaches for the ethical language of the best pagan thinkers his readers admired. The charge is not only that these people broke the law of Moses, which they never had, but that they fail the standard their own philosophers set, on their own terms.

In a sentence. And since they did not think it worthwhile to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done.

On a Tuesday. Everyone still keeps a list of things that ought not to be done, including people who will tell you at length that morality is a social construct. Watch what happens when one of those things is done to them: the promise broken, the confidence betrayed, the credit taken. Nobody is a relativist about being wronged. The outrage is instant, and it is the sound of a law being appealed to by a person who has just denied there is one. And keep God in your own thinking: not only believed, but consulted, in the decisions of an ordinary day.

For worship. This verse is not a diagnosis without a cure, and Paul makes the answer unmistakable by reaching for the same root eleven chapters later: be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that by testing (dokimazein) you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect (12:2). The letter that describes a mind failing the assay ends by describing a mind restored to it. It is not reversed by trying harder to think clearly, because you cannot reason your way out of a way of reasoning with the faculty that is compromised. It takes a voice from outside. The mind that would not keep God in view was given a mind that could not see; and the remedy is a new mind, and in this letter that turns out to be one more thing God hands over. We have the mind of Christ (1 Corinthians 2:16).
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them up to a “debased” (adokimon, literally “unfit”) mind.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,

They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. A catalogue of sins, some twenty-one in all, beginning with inward dispositions and moving outward. And the word that governs it deserves its weight. Filled: saturation, not contact, a vessel with no room left in it. And it is passive again. Something poured this in, and the chapter has told us what: a person handed over to himself does not stay level. He fills up. Sin is not a stain that sits where it lands; it is a liquid that finds every space in a container. Paul is cataloguing not unusual criminality but the ordinary human heart without the restraining grace of God.

Full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. Envy and murder side by side, as in Jesus’ teaching, where the inward sin is the seed of the outward crime (Matthew 5:21–22). Anyone can read murder and feel comfortably excluded. Then the sentence carries on into envy, strife and deceit, and the ground gives way. Take the items one at a time and you have an ordinary week in an ordinary office: wanting what a colleague has and being unable to be glad for him; the argument continued for the pleasure of winning it; the small deceit that makes you look better than the facts; the ill-will you would never act on but rather enjoy holding. These are the sins of people who are quite pleasant to have lunch with.

Covetousness. The settled dissatisfaction that another person has what you should have had, and the one sin on the list nobody has ever confessed at a prayer meeting. It is the only one of the Ten Commandments that is invisible from outside. You can keep all the others in public and break this one continuously in a room by yourself, which is why it flourishes in respectable people, and why Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

They are gossips. Psithyristas: whisperers, an imitative word, the sound of a low voice behind a hand. Listed in the same breath as murder, under the same verdict, with no dividing line. Gossip takes a person who is not in the room and makes them smaller, at no cost to the speaker. It produces a warm feeling of closeness between the people talking, while it is actually a transaction conducted with somebody else’s reputation as the currency. It is often accurate, which is its best disguise, and almost always done in a tone of concern, which is the disguise underneath that one.

In a sentence. They are filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed and depravity, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and malice, and they are gossips.

On a Tuesday. Think over the last three conversations you had about somebody who was not present. Ask two questions of each. Would you have said it in the same words if they had walked in halfway through? And what were you hoping the listener would think, about them, or about you? Most gossip is not about the absent person at all. It is a way of arranging myself favourably in someone’s mind, with the absent friend as the material.

For worship. Paul is building a case, and the case is not against Rome. He needs every reader to arrive at chapter 3 unable to plead anything, so that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” lands as a description, not an insult (3:23). The list is long because it has to reach everybody, and the word gossips is in it for the respectable reader who had been nodding along. And the same verse that closes every mouth opens onto the next: justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (3:24). The list is long so that grace can be seen to be longer.

verseByVerse.quote: slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.

Slanderers, haters of God. “Haters of God” is the root of it all, made explicit, and almost nobody would own the phrase. You will find people who doubt God, resent the church, or find the subject tiresome; you will search a long time for someone who says he hates God. So what does it look like from inside? Not a declaration. It shows up as a sense that God is a rival: that his claims and your happiness pull in opposite directions, so that every command reads as something being taken away from you rather than something being kept safe for you.

Insolent, haughty, boastful. Pride in its many forms.

Inventors of evil. The strangest item in the list. Invention is a glory: it is the image of God in a creature who makes things, and here it is conscripted. People apply imagination, effort and genuine ingenuity to finding wrongs nobody had thought of yet. Sin is creative. Every tool the human race has made has been improved for harming people, usually within a generation. And you can watch the faculty early: no child has ever needed lessons in finding the exact sentence that will wound a sibling most efficiently. Cruelty is inventive on its own. It is kindness that has to be taught.

Disobedient to parents. Listed among the serious sins, not because it equals murder, but because the breakdown of the family is the breakdown of the social order that reflects God’s order. A family coming apart is a sign of a society turned from God (2 Timothy 3:2).

Foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless. Four Greek words beginning with the negative a-: without understanding, without faithfulness, without natural affection, without mercy. Paul had every option and did not finish on murder or blasphemy. He finishes on coldness. The final symptom of a world that has let go of God is not that it becomes savage, but that it stops feeling anything about the people in front of it. The word behind “heartless” is family affection with the negative on the front: the love between parent and child that needs no persuading, observable even in animals. The collapse reaches so far down that it takes out the one form of love nobody has to be talked into. And “faithless” is a legal word: a person whose signature means nothing, who says he will be there and is not. The chapter that opened in the heavens, with eternal power visible in everything made, ends in a house: a child who cannot rely on a parent, a promise never meant to be kept, a table where nobody feels much any more. The kitchen is where the damage is finally measured.

What it does not mean. Somebody will reach the word heartless and go cold, because they have felt nothing for months: a mother who looks at her baby and cannot find the love everyone told her would come, a man numb at his father’s funeral, someone so exhausted or depressed that the affection they know is there will not switch on. That is not what Paul is describing. He means a hardness that is chosen, defended and eventually preferred. Numbness that grieves you is not hardness of heart; it is a symptom, and the proof is that you are distressed by it. The people in this verse are not. The enemy of souls is very willing to quote Romans 1 to a tired woman at three in the morning. Do not let him.

In a sentence. They are slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant and boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, heartless and ruthless.

On a Tuesday. When you learn that something you enjoy is out of bounds, watch the reaction that arrives before the one you would say aloud. Is it sorrow at being in the wrong, or a flash of irritation at being interfered with? And when a moral claim you assumed turns out not to apply to you after all, is the feeling relief? Nobody feels relief at being released from the love of someone they actually love. And most of these items would be invisible to your colleagues and obvious to the people who live with you. So ask who the witnesses are: not the people who see you for an hour on a Sunday, but the ones who see you on a Tuesday evening when you are tired.

For worship. Sin destroys love, in families, friendships and whole societies, and Christ restores it. The Son who never once failed his Father, who honoured his mother from the cross, whose word is yes and amen, came into a world of the faithless and heartless so that the love poured out by the Holy Spirit (5:5) could begin again in the kitchen.

verseByVerse.quote: Though they know God's righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.

Though they know God’s righteous decree. Count how often knowledge has appeared in this chapter. What can be known about God is plain to them (v. 19). Although they knew God (v. 21). They did not see fit to keep God in knowledge (v. 28). And now: though they know God’s righteous decree. Four times, and not one of them is a charge of ignorance. The human problem is not a shortage of light but what is done with it, and even at the bottom of the descent, with the mind handed over and the list complete, the knowledge is still there. The conscience knows (2:14–15). Nobody in this chapter ever manages to stop knowing.

That those who practice such things deserve to die. This strikes a modern reader as wildly out of proportion, and the objection deserves an answer. Paul is not proposing a penalty for anyone to carry out; he is stating a worth: these things are of a weight that matches death. And the letter explains why in its plainest sentence: the wages of sin is death (6:23). Wages, not a penalty imposed from outside. If God is the source of life, a settled turning from him has one possible end, and calling it a sentence is God telling the truth about where the road goes.

Does “deserve to die” mean the death penalty? No. Paul is not telling the state to execute people for gossip, disobedience to parents or envy, which appear in the same list. Death here is the sentence God has decreed on sin, death in its full biblical sense, physical death and the second death (5:12; 6:23). Everyone in the list deserves it, which includes every reader. That is the point Paul is driving toward in 3:23, and the reason the gospel of 3:21–26 is needed.

They not only do them but give approval to those who practice them. The climax: not merely doing evil but applauding it, calling evil good (Isaiah 5:20). Why would applause be worse than the act? Three reasons. A man who does wrong and knows it is wrong is at war with himself, and that war is the last thing standing between him and ruin; approval ends the war and dismantles what could have called him back. Approval costs nothing; you can do it from an armchair, endlessly. And approval recruits. Doing wrong damages you; applauding it manufactures more of it in other people, the difference between having an illness and being a carrier. Every society has contained plenty of sin. A society is destroyed when it begins to praise it.

Small approvals. Do not look for this only in loud public endorsement, because that lets almost everyone off. Approval is mostly small and silent. It is the laugh you gave because not laughing would have been awkward, the anecdote passed on because it was entertaining. Most of all it is what our age has industrialised: consuming as recreation behaviour that would appal us in our own street. Watching something for pleasure is a small vote, cast repeatedly, for more of it. Nobody in Rome had to sit in the arena to approve of it. It was enough to have enjoyed the stories.

What it does not mean. Not every silence is approval. There are moments when speaking would be self-righteous, when a thing is not your business, or when the standing to speak has to be earned first. Paul does not require you to register an objection to everything you meet. The line falls where your silence is doing work you would be embarrassed to admit to: where you said nothing not out of wisdom but because you wanted to be liked.

In a sentence. Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things deserve death, they not only keep doing them but approve of those who practise them.

On a Tuesday. Name something you would be ashamed to be caught doing, and that you are perfectly happy to be entertained by other people doing. Then ask what the difference between the two positions actually is. Paul’s answer, at the end of the darkest chapter he wrote, is that there is not much of one, and that the second is the one he chose to finish on.

For worship. Paul does not really finish here. The very next words are: therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges (2:1). The reader who has worked through this catalogue with a growing sense of the state of the world is exactly the person the next sentence is waiting for. The chapter ends with a verdict that everyone in it deserves to die, and the only reason a letter this dark was ever written is that its author knew Someone who had died in their place, and been raised, and was declared Son of God in power. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (6:23).

2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with satisfaction, nodding along at the depravity of the pagan world. Chapter 2 turns without warning on that same reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges." The trap is sprung. The person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not morally superior to the Gentile; he is, Paul argues, in an even more culpable position — because he knows better.

Paul's target in chapter 2 is not the pagan but the moralist — specifically, the Jewish moralist who believes that covenant membership and religious privilege provide a buffer against divine judgment. They do not. God's judgment is impartial: He renders to each according to his works, to Jew and Gentile alike. The Gentile who has only the law of conscience will be judged by that; the Jew who has the law of Moses will be judged by that. In either case, the verdict will be the same: all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rhetorical brilliance of Romans 2:1 is breathtaking. Paul has spent fifteen verses describing the moral ruin of the Gentile world — and now he wheels on the approving reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." The knife Paul had been pointing at the Gentile he now turns on anyone who imagines that moral judgment of others places them above judgment themselves.

The principle Paul establishes is foundational: God's judgment is according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), without partiality (v. 11). These three principles together demolish every form of religious self-satisfaction. "According to truth" means God sees through performance to reality. "According to works" means the whole life is the evidence, not merely the religious moments. "Without partiality" means no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone from accountability before the Judge of all the earth.

Verses 14–15 introduce the remarkable teaching about the conscience as a moral witness — Gentiles who do not have the Torah nonetheless "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." This is Paul's doctrine of moral general revelation: human beings are not morally blank. The conscience, however distorted by sin, retains something of the moral law written at creation. This is why all human beings, without exception, will have no excuse on the day of judgment.

Two things in this section deserve naming here, because they are easily lost between the principles. The first is verse 4, the warmest sentence in the passage and the most often misread: the riches of God’s kindness and forbearance and patience are not evidence that he does not mind. They are “meant to lead you to repentance”. Every day on which judgment does not fall is not indifference; it is an invitation still being held open — and Paul’s charge is that we presume on it, reading the delay as a verdict already returned in our favour. The second is verse 16, which tells us when this happens and who conducts it: “on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus”. The Judge is not a principle but a person with a face, and the material to be weighed is not the record other people can see but the secrets. Which is the most frightening sentence in the chapter, or the most freeing — since for those who are his, the one who will weigh what nobody else knows about them is the one who died for it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 appears to teach salvation by works — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life." Reformed exegesis has understood this as describing the principle of judgment (God will judge the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). The person who truly seeks God from the heart will be given — by grace — the faith that produces the works that evidence genuine conversion. Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is establishing the standard of divine judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in covenant privilege — circumcision, Torah, temple — as a buffer against divine judgment was a live pastoral issue in Paul's day. Many Jews believed that while Gentiles might face judgment, the covenant people were secure by virtue of their membership. Paul demolishes this with surgical precision. Now: The equivalent today is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership, or moral respectability as a substitute for genuine faith and repentance. Paul's word is the same: God is not impressed by religious credentials. He is looking for the transformed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.

Meaning first. Romans 2 turns from the openly wicked pagan world of chapter 1 to the moral, religious person who judges others, and especially to the Jew who has God’s law. Paul shows that they too are guilty. God judges by truth, not by privilege; he judges everyone by their deeds, Jew and Gentile alike, and he knows the secrets of the heart. Having the law, being circumcised, knowing God’s will: none of these saves, if you break the law. True Jewishness, true circumcision, is of the heart, by the Spirit. The point: all are under sin, and no one can be justified by his own record. And the chapter that strips away every human credential ends by pointing to the one praise that only God can give.

Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. This is the sentence chapter 1 was built to deliver, and it is worth admiring the engineering. Paul spent fifteen verses on idolatry, sexual chaos, envy, gossip and the collapse of the family, knowing exactly what a religious reader does with such a passage: he agrees with it, warmly. And the agreement is the trap, because a man who has been nodding for fifteen verses has been establishing in his own mind that he is the sort of person who can tell the difference. Then “therefore” arrives, and the paragraph he has been applauding turns out to be a mirror held at an angle. “No excuse” (anapologētos) is the same word as 1:20. The pagan had no defence; neither has the moralist.

O man. The address changes, too. Chapter 1 was plural: they, them, humanity in the dock, comfortable enough to read. Here it is singular. Paul uses a device his readers knew from the lecture halls, where a speaker rounds on an imaginary objector and argues with him by name. The effect is that nobody can pass this verse along to somebody else. It is addressed to one person, and that person is holding the letter.

For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. The instinctive reply is: I have never done what that man did. Paul means the same fundamental disorder rather than an identical catalogue, living for self rather than for God, and the list of 1:29–31 includes respectable sins: envy, deceit, gossip, pride. By judging, you show you know right from wrong, and so you condemn yourself. And the mechanism operates in all of us every day. We judge other people by their actions and ourselves by our intentions. Another man is short with his child and he is impatient; I am short with mine and I had a difficult day. He did not reply because he is unreliable; I did not reply because I was busy. Same act, filed under two different headings, and the filing is done before any conscious dishonesty, which is why it is so hard to catch.

The log in the eye. Our Lord gave this its permanent image, and the detail everybody forgets is the crucial one. Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and not notice the log in your own (Matthew 7:3–5)? Because the log is in the eye. It is not on the table where it could be pointed out; it is lodged in the very organ you are using to look at him. That is why the man with the worst vision in the room is often the one most confident about what he is seeing, and why the problem cannot be solved by looking harder.

We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things. “Rightly” (kata alētheian): according to truth. God’s judgment, unlike the moralist’s, is based on reality, not appearances, and it has none of the self-exemptions we grant ourselves.

What it does not mean. Paul is not forbidding moral judgment. He has just spent a chapter making moral judgments of unusual severity, and later he will tell churches to deal with sin in their members. Jesus does not end with the log either: first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. The speck is still to come out. What changes is the order, and with it the whole character of the man doing the work: a person who has just removed a log from his own eye handles other people very differently.

So how do I correct someone without being the man in this verse? Start with yourself, honestly and first: what in me is like this? Then go to the person privately, not to others about him (Matthew 18:15). Go gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1), name the specific thing rather than the person’s character, and listen before you conclude. Ask whether you are hoping to win him or to be proved right. And if you find you enjoy it, wait: the pleasure is a sign the log is still there.

In a sentence. So you who judge others have no excuse, for in judging them you condemn yourself, since you do the same things, and we know God’s judgment on those who do such things is based on truth.

On a Tuesday. Take the last thing you genuinely did wrong, an ordinary failure, and write one sentence describing it in the words you would use if your brother-in-law had done exactly the same. Not the words you used at the time; his words. Most of us discover we have two vocabularies for sin and know instinctively which to reach for. And notice which sins produce heat in you out of all proportion to their seriousness. A fury that exceeds the offence is very often a fury at something nearer home.

For worship. Paul is not scoring a point off the respectable reader; he is trying to move a man out of the one position from which the gospel can never be received. Everything this letter is about to offer is for the guilty. Grace has nothing to say to the innocent, and self-approval is a locked door. The verdict “you have no excuse” sounds like the end of the argument. It is the first moment in this letter at which its reader becomes eligible for anything, because Christ came not to call the righteous but sinners (Mark 2:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?

Do you suppose, O man, that you will escape the judgment of God? Paul asks it rather than asserting it, and the form matters. Nobody has ever said that sentence out loud. It is not a belief anyone holds consciously; it is an assumption underneath the beliefs, and Paul drags it into the daylight so the man hears it in his own voice. The man condemns a thing in someone else, does it himself, and expects a different outcome. Ask him why and he could not tell you. There is only a settled sense that his case is somehow different, and that when everything is looked at properly it will be found that he had reasons. The religious person often thinks he is safe.

Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience? “Presume” (kataphroneis) means to despise, look down on, take for granted. Three words for God’s goodness are stacked here. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is his active goodness, not mere tolerance. Forbearance is holding back what could justly be done. Patience (makrothumia) is long-temper, the opposite of a short fuse: the capacity to be provoked for a very long time and not act. So this is not a God who does not notice. He notices, is entitled to act, and does not, yet.

How presumption sounds. It almost never sounds like defiance. It sounds reasonable: it clearly cannot be that serious, or something would have happened by now. I have been doing this for six years and my life has, if anything, improved. God knows what I am like and has evidently made his peace with it. Each is an argument from silence, and each treats a stay of execution as an acquittal. The prisoner whose appeal is pending is not free because the corridor is quiet.

Not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? The hinge of the verse. The word suggests taking someone by the hand and bringing them somewhere. God’s goodness is not a neutral backdrop to your life; it is working on you, with a destination. The purpose of his patience is not to let you off but to give you time to repent (2 Peter 3:9). The mercies you have been enjoying are not evidence that the subject is closed. They are the means by which it is being reopened. His goodness should melt you, not make you comfortable. Sun softens wax and hardens clay, and the sun is not doing two different things.

What does repentance actually involve? Repentance is turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as offensive to him, and grieving over it. It takes hold of God’s mercy in Christ, because repentance without hope only drives a person away. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself to walk with God in new obedience (Westminster 15.2). In practice that means naming the specific sin to God, not a vague apology; putting right what can be put right; removing what feeds it; and starting again the next time you fall, without waiting to feel worthy. It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life.

What it does not mean. Somebody will read “presuming on the riches of his kindness” and conclude that they have used up their allowance, that they are the one person for whom the offer has expired. Read the sentence again. It is not a warning that the kindness is running out; it is a complaint that it is being wasted, and you cannot waste something that has stopped being given. The fact that this frightens you is proof that the kindness is still doing its work. Presumption is a comfortable condition. It does not lie awake.

In a sentence. Do you think, you who judge others while doing the same, that you will escape God’s judgment, or do you show contempt for the riches of his kindness, forbearance and patience, not realising that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?

On a Tuesday. Think of the good things that came to you this year: the recovery, the friendship, the provision, the thing that could have gone badly and did not. Ask what they produced in you. Gratitude, a softening, some movement toward God? Or a quiet increase in confidence that you are basically fine? The same kindness does both; what differs is the person it lands on.

For worship. The kindness in this verse has been running a very long time and has never once been hurried. It waited out the golden calf, the judges, the kings, the prophets who were stoned, and four hundred years of silence. It went on waiting while the men it was aimed at were sharpening the charges against his Son. God is not slow because he is indifferent. He is slow because he intends to bring home everyone he came for, and he has always been willing to be mistaken for absent while he waits. His patience is not him deciding what to do about you. It is the time he is taking to get you back.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:

But because of your hard and impenitent heart. Hardness (sklērotēs, from which we get sclerosis) is not a mood but a condition, and the honest picture is a callus. A callus is not a decision anybody makes. It forms slowly, in response to repeated friction, and its whole function is to stop you feeling what is happening at that spot. That is why hardness of heart is nearly impossible to diagnose from inside: the symptom of the condition is the loss of the sensation that would have reported it. Chapter 1 described the same thing happening to a conscience; here it is the settled state of a religious man who has been listening to sermons for thirty years.

Impenitent: remorse or repentance? Most of us have never distinguished two things that feel alike. Scripture keeps them apart by giving us two men in the same week. Judas was sorry enough to die of it, and Peter wept bitterly, and only one of them came back. The difference is not the amount of feeling. Remorse is mostly about me: what I have lost, how I look now, what this will cost. Repentance is about God: I agree with him about the thing, and I turn to him. Remorse can be enormously intense and leave a person exactly where it found him (2 Corinthians 7:10).

You are storing up wrath for yourself. The verb is the one behind our word treasury, the same one Jesus used: do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, but lay up treasures in heaven (Matthew 6:19–20). Verse 4 spoke of the riches of God’s kindness; verse 5 says you are banking wrath. So the picture is not of a man drifting toward a bad end but of a man making deposits. Every day of unrepentance is another one. Everyone is building a treasury. The only question is what is being put into it.

On the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. The day of judgment, at Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). It is the third “revealed” in barely twenty verses: the righteousness of God (1:17), the wrath of God (1:18), and now his righteous judgment. Everything presently disputed or hidden is on a schedule to be uncovered. Nothing is being lost; it is being kept.

He will render to each one according to his works. Paul is quoting his Bible (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12), and the psalm puts it in the same breath as something else: to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you will render to a man according to his work. Steadfast love and exact recompense, addressed to the same God. And “each one”: not nations or generations, each. No one will be graded on a curve against the people around him or lost in a crowd, which is unnerving and is also the only arrangement that could be just (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 20:12).
