verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand... — Romans 5:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God.

Meaning first. Romans 5 shows what justification brings. First, its fruits: peace with God, access to his grace, hope of glory, joy even in suffering, the love of God poured into our hearts, and certainty of final salvation, since if God loved us when we were enemies, he will surely save us now we are his friends (vv. 1–11). Then the great comparison of Adam and Christ (vv. 12–21): through one man’s sin, condemnation and death came to all in him; through one man’s obedience, righteousness and life come to all in him. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more. The chapter that begins with a man at peace with God ends with grace seated on a throne, and both are the work of one Man.

Therefore. Start with the first word, because it carries four chapters. This is the hinge of the whole letter. Everything from 1:18 has been a court case: the charge, the evidence, the silencing of every mouth, the verdict, and then the astonishing provision by which the guilty are declared righteous. Chapters 1 to 4 establish the verdict. Chapters 5 to 8 describe what it is like to live inside it. Paul is no longer arguing that you can be justified. He is telling you what is now true of you because you are.

Since we have been justified by faith. A completed fact. Not hoping to be, not trying to be, but have been: the verdict has been pronounced and the court has risen. Everything that follows in this chapter rests on this, and none of it rests on anything else.

We have peace with God. Peace with God is not the same as peace about God. It is not subjective tranquillity or the absence of spiritual anxiety; it is the objective end of hostility between the holy God and the sinful creature. The war is over. Christ made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). And it is worth seeing what the hostility actually consisted of, because it ran in both directions and not in the same way. On our side it was real enmity: alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21). On God’s side it was not temper but settled judicial opposition, his wrath, which chapter 1 said is being revealed from heaven. Both had to be dealt with, and only one of them could be dealt with by persuasion. That is why the word is peace and not ceasefire. A ceasefire is an agreement to stop shooting and can be revoked by either party on an afternoon’s notice. A peace treaty settles the terms, and this one was signed in blood by the offended party.

We have, or let us have? A brief word about a footnote you may find in your Bible, since it can be unsettling to discover that the manuscripts differ here. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read let us have peace. The difference is a single letter in Greek, a long o for a short one, and the two were pronounced identically in Paul’s day, so a scribe taking dictation could easily write one for the other. Nearly all translations read we have, and rightly: the context is a list of what we have, and Paul is drawing a conclusion from the argument he has just finished, not issuing an exhortation. And even on the other reading the peace would still be a fact. It would mean let us enjoy the peace we have, never let us try to obtain it.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. The only way. Peace was not negotiated by us and is not maintained by us. It was made by him, and it stands as long as he stands.

Through him we have also obtained access. The word (prosagōgē) described the office of the official who introduced people at a royal court. Nobody simply walked in to see a king; you were brought in, by someone with the standing to bring you. So the word contains both the privilege and the fact that it is not your own. And notice the tense: we have obtained access, a completed action with permanent effect. The introduction has already been made. You are not applying each morning to see whether today is a day on which you may approach.

Into this grace in which we stand. Grace here is not a mood or a transaction but a place: something you can be standing on, which means it is underneath you and bearing your weight. The verb is again the perfect: we took our stand and we are still standing. And a floor is the sort of thing you stop noticing, which is exactly right. Nobody spends the day generating the floor. The man who has understood this verse does not have to re-establish his position with God every morning, any more than he has to re-lay the floorboards before he can cross the room.

And we rejoice in hope of the glory of God. “Rejoice” (kauchōmetha) is boast, exult: the same word as the boasting that was excluded in 3:27. The boasting of the man who trusted his own record has been shut out, and a right boasting has taken its place, in God’s glory, which we will share (8:18, 30). And this is one of the quiet masterstrokes of the letter. Go back two chapters. The charge sheet against the human race reached its summary in exactly these words: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (3:23). That was the indictment; this is the hope. Paul has taken the precise phrase in which our ruin was stated and made it the description of our future. The thing we lost is the thing we are promised. Not merely forgiveness for having fallen short of it, but the glory itself, restored to the creature it was made for.

Hope is not wishful thinking. In ordinary speech, hope means I would like it but I am not sure: I hope it does not rain. In the New Testament it means confident expectation of something God has promised and not yet delivered. The uncertainty is only about the date, never about the thing. Christian hope is as sure as the one who made the promise, and it is called hope only because we have not yet seen it.

Peace behind, ground beneath, glory ahead. Notice the escalation, which is deliberate: peace (v. 1), then a standing in grace, then hope of glory (v. 2). Justification does not merely settle the past; it opens the future. The present standing and the future destination are both secured by the same grace received by the same faith. Paul piles up three things in two verses and none of them fluctuates: peace behind you, a place to stand beneath you, and glory ahead of you.

If I have peace with God, why do I still feel anxious or guilty? Because feelings report on many things, and the verdict of God is not one of the things they are good at reporting. Your peace with God is a fact about God’s judgment of you, settled in Christ, and it is not reopened by a bad night. Guilt you still feel may be pointing to something real you need to confess, and then the answer is to confess it and believe 1 John 1:9. Or it may be the leftover echo of sins already forgiven, and then the answer is to argue with it from this verse. Anxiety may be temperament, tiredness or illness, none of which alters your standing. Do not try to feel your way into peace. Look at the verdict, and let the feelings follow when they can.

In a sentence. Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand, and we rejoice in the hope of God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it goes to which half of the letter you are actually living in. Which of these two sentences describes your normal week: I am trying to get right with God, or I am right with God? Both are said by sincere Christians and only one of them is true. If the first is your instinct, if the ordinary background hum of your spiritual life is effortful and slightly anxious, a project not yet completed, then you are living in chapters 1 to 4 with a doctrine from chapter 5, and the word to hear is Paul’s first one: therefore. The case is closed. The verdict is in. Pray today not as a man applying for an audience but as one who has been brought in and is still standing there. What remains is not to secure the peace but to live in it.

For worship. The God who had every right to remain at war with us made the peace himself, paid for it himself, and then took us by the hand and brought us into his presence, and has never once asked us to leave. The war is over, the ground is firm, and the glory we threw away in Eden is held out to us again, not as a reward but as an inheritance. All of it is through our Lord Jesus Christ: the peace was his blood, the access is his hand, and the glory is his own, shared.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “let us have peace.”

parallels.desc: the effect of righteousness will be peace

verseByVerse.quote: Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope,

Not only that, but we rejoice in our sufferings. Paul has just spoken of rejoicing in the hope of the glory of God (v. 2); now he speaks of rejoicing in sufferings, and “not only that” suggests the second is as natural to the Christian as the first. Not just in spite of them, but in them. The verb is the same boast, exult. The joy of verse 2 looks at the future; the joy of verse 3 is found in the middle of the present at its worst (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

What it does not mean. Two things need saying at once, before the chain, or this passage will do damage. The first is what Paul does not say. He does not say suffering is good, or that it should be sought, or that a Christian ought to feel positively about a diagnosis. Scripture never calls evil good; the Lord himself wept at a grave he was about to empty. And he does not say rejoice because of your sufferings, as though the thing itself were the cause of the joy. The word is in: joy located inside a situation that remains bad, on account of something else that is true about it. The second is that this is not a formula and not a promise about outcomes. Paul is not saying every sufferer automatically becomes stronger. He knows better, and so does anybody who has watched a man come out of a hard decade smaller and harder than he went in. Suffering by itself does not produce endurance. It produces bitterness at least as often, and the difference is not the quantity of the pain but what the sufferer is holding on to while it lasts. That is why the paragraph ends where it does, at the love of God poured into the heart by the Spirit (v. 5).

Knowing that suffering produces endurance. “Suffering” (thlipsis) is pressure, affliction, the crushing of something under weight. “Endurance” (hypomonē) is not passive resignation. It is the compound that means remaining under: staying put beneath a load rather than crawling out from under it. And it can only be produced one way. There is no exercise that develops it in the abstract; nobody has ever become patient in a comfortable year. That is worth knowing about the Christian life generally: several of the qualities we most want are only manufactured in conditions we would never choose.

And endurance produces character. The Greek word (dokimē) is a metallurgist’s: the quality of metal that has been through the assay and come out proved. It shares its root with the failed test at 1:28, where a mind that would not keep God in view was handed over as metal that did not pass. Here the metal passes. And notice what a proving actually is: it does not create the quality, it demonstrates it, and it demonstrates it to the man himself. Most of us do not know what we believe until something has tried to take it away from us. That is why a Christian who has been through something often has a settledness that no amount of reading produces. He is not cleverer than you. He has been tested, and he has the certificate. Faith that has been through trouble is proven real.

And character produces hope. The surprising link. We would have expected the chain to run the other way, with hope enabling endurance. Paul says hope is the output. And the logic is exactly right once you have lived it. The reason a tested believer hopes is that he has evidence: he has been in the place where he was certain he could not go on, and he went on, and looking back he can see that he was carried. Hope is not optimism about the future; it is a conclusion drawn from the past. The man who has been held before has grounds for expecting to be held again. So the chain runs: suffering, endurance, proven character, hope.

If I cannot feel any joy in this. One more guard, for the reader in the middle of it rather than looking back on it. If you are suffering now and can find no joy in it whatever, you have not failed this passage. Paul is describing a trajectory, not a mood available on demand, and he is writing to people at various points along it. Endurance is mostly indistinguishable from simply not leaving. If today you have not walked away from God, if you are still, in some ragged fashion, holding on, then the first link of this chain is being forged in you at this moment, and it will not feel like anything at all while it happens.

Does this include suffering I brought on myself? Yes, though differently. Peter distinguishes suffering for doing good from suffering for doing wrong (1 Peter 2:20), and the second calls first for repentance, not celebration. But God does not waste even the consequences of our own folly. The man reaping what he sowed, the woman living with the results of a bad decision she cannot undo: once the sin has been confessed and forgiven, the pressure that remains is still pressure, and the same God still works endurance, character and hope through it. Paul’s word covers every kind of affliction a believer carries, including the ones with his own fingerprints on them. Grace is not too proud to work with the wreckage.

Does God send suffering, then? Scripture holds two things together without embarrassment. Suffering is an intruder in God’s world, the fruit of the fall that this very chapter goes on to describe, and God takes no pleasure in it for its own sake (Lamentations 3:33). And nothing reaches a believer that has not passed through his hands, and he works all of it for good (8:28). Joseph could say to his brothers that they meant it for evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20), in the same sentence, about the same event. You do not have to call the thing good. You may call God good in it.

In a sentence. Not only so, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and character produces hope.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that costs nothing and does a great deal. Write down, specifically, the three hardest things you have been through since becoming a Christian. Beside each one, write what you were afraid would happen: that you would lose your faith, that you would not cope, that you would never be happy again. Then write what actually happened. Most people find, doing this honestly, that the thing they feared did not occur and that they cannot now reconstruct how they got through. That inability is the point. It was not resilience; you were carried, and you have already forgotten it. That list is the raw material of hope, and this is exactly how Paul says hope gets made. Keep it, and read it at the start of the next hard thing.

For worship. The God who wastes nothing has taken the worst things in a fallen world and set them to work for his children: the pressure that was meant to crush us becomes the furnace that proves us, and the fire that should have destroyed our faith becomes the evidence that it was real. He did not spare his own Son suffering, and the Son, though he was a son, learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). Every link of this chain he forged first in himself, and he walks the road with us, so that even our affliction becomes a path to glory.

verseByVerse.quote: and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

And hope does not put us to shame. The phrase is not primarily about embarrassment. In the Old Testament, to be put to shame is what happens to a man whose confidence turns out to have been misplaced: the one who trusted an ally that did not come, or a god that could not answer. It is the shame of having backed the wrong thing in public (Psalm 25:3; Isaiah 28:16). Hope in that sense is a risk: every hope is a bet on something, and most of them eventually expose the person who made them. Paul says this one will not. We will not stand on the last day like someone who trusted a false promise. Not because we hope sincerely, but because of what is holding the other end.

Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts. The reason he gives is not the one we would expect. Having just said that hope is produced by tested character, he might have grounded its reliability in the same place: you have come through before, therefore you will come through again. Instead he goes outside the chain entirely and points to something given. The chain of verses 3 and 4 is real, but it is not what makes hope safe. What makes it safe is that God has already done something inside you.

Whose love? Note the direction of the love, since it can be read either way and the difference is everything. This is not first our love for God, welling up. It is his love for us, poured in: the sense of being loved by God arriving in a human heart as an experienced thing rather than an inferred one. Paul is not describing a doctrine you hold; he is describing something that has happened to you. Not only believed, but known.

Poured. The verb (ekkechytai) is extravagant. It is the word for a downpour, for something emptied out without measuring: the word used of the Spirit being poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:17), and of the blood poured out at the cross. Not administered in a therapeutic dose. God is not careful with this. And the tense is perfect: it has been poured, an act completed with results that remain, which means the reservoir was filled before today and is not depleted by a bad week.

Through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. Every believer has the Spirit, given at conversion (8:9), and it is the Spirit who assures us of God’s love, so that we cry Abba, Father (8:15–16). He is the firstfruits of the coming glory, God’s own pledge that the hope will be honoured. This internal witness to the love of God is what sustains the rejoicing of verses 3 and 4 through the darkest seasons of suffering.

What if I have never felt anything of the kind? A great many faithful Christians read a verse like this and conclude that whatever Paul is describing has not happened to them. So three things, carefully. First, this is not describing a particular kind of experience: not a moment, not an emotional register, not the sort of thing that could be arranged at a meeting. It shows up in more ways than one. It is in the man who finds, to his surprise, that he wants to pray. It is in the sudden and inexplicable conviction, halfway through an ordinary Tuesday, that you are not facing your life alone. It is in tears at a line of a hymn you have sung a hundred times. It is in the fact that you mind about your sin at all. None of those announces itself as the love of God being poured out, and all of them are.

Temperament and health are real. Second, some people feel everything strongly and some feel very little, and the difference is largely how they were made and how they slept. There are believers who have loved Christ for forty years with the emotional volume permanently low, and others whose capacity for felt experience has been flattened by depression or exhaustion or grief. Scripture never treats intensity of feeling as the measure of anything, and a man whose illness has taken his feelings has not thereby lost the Spirit who was given to him.

The evidence is not only inward. Third, and most usefully: Paul says the love was poured in through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, and the presence of that Spirit is demonstrable in ways that do not depend on your feelings today. Do you call God Father, and mean it? That is the Spirit (8:15). Do you want holiness, even while failing at it? Is Christ precious to you in a way he was not at nineteen? Those are not achievements. They are symptoms.

Does every Christian have the Spirit, or is he a later blessing for some? Every Christian has him. Paul says plainly that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (8:9), and here he speaks of the Spirit as given to us, all of us, the whole church in Rome. There is no second class of believers who have been given him and a first class who are still waiting. Christians may be filled afresh, strengthened and led more deeply as they grow (Ephesians 5:18), and you should ask for that. But you do not need to seek the Spirit as though you lacked him. You need to believe what he has already been given to do in you.

In a sentence. And hope does not disappoint us, because God has poured out his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, whom he has given us.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is better than asking whether you feel loved. Ask when you last noticed something that would be inexplicable if God were not real and did not care for you. Not a miracle: a comfort that arrived from nowhere at the right moment, a peace you could not account for, a word in Scripture that landed as though addressed to you. Most Christians have a small collection of these and have never counted them, because each one on its own seems too slight to mention. Count them tonight, and thank God for each by name. That is the pouring, and it has been going on longer than you thought.

For worship. The chain from suffering to hope would be a cruel arrangement if it ran on human strength, because the people who most need it are precisely those who have least of it. It does not. Underneath the endurance and the testing and the hope is something poured in from outside, by a Spirit who was given and not earned. The Father loved us, the Son died to make the love righteous, and the Spirit carries it into the heart and empties it out without measuring. That is why the man at the bottom of the pit can still be told that his hope will not let him down: the love holding the other end is the love of God himself.

parallels.desc: in you they trusted and were not put to shame

verseByVerse.quote: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will scarcely die for a righteous person — though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die —

For while we were still weak. Notice that Paul is now doing something he has not done before in this letter: he is offering proof of the love he has just asserted. Verse 5 said God’s love has been poured into our hearts, and a sceptic, or a Christian on a bad night, might reasonably answer that this is exactly what one would expect a religion to claim, and that inward feelings are not evidence of anything. So Paul goes outside us altogether. The proof is not a state of mind. It is a death, in public, at a datable moment, and its evidential force lies entirely in when it happened. And “weak” (asthenōn) is worth resisting the urge to soften. It does not mean we were doing our best in difficult circumstances. It means without strength: the word used of the physically helpless, the invalid who cannot get himself to the water. The picture is not a man who needed assistance. It is a man who could not have contributed to his own rescue if he had wanted to.

At the right time Christ died for the ungodly. “At the right time” (kata kairon): the crucifixion was not an accident of history but an event scheduled in the eternal purpose of God, when the fullness of time had come (Galatians 4:4), falling at the precise moment of human helplessness. And “for the ungodly” means in their place, on their behalf: not for those who had earned divine favour, but for those in active opposition to God. It is the same word as 4:5, where God justifies the ungodly. The timing is repeated with insistence across three verses: while we were still weak, for the ungodly, while we were still sinners. Every one of them is a state we were in at the time. If Christ had died for the repentant, the cross would prove that God responds well to repentance. If he had died for the promising, it would prove God has an eye for potential. He died for people who were at that moment incapable, opposed and guilty, which proves something about God and nothing whatever about us.

For one will scarcely die for a righteous person. Then Paul does something unexpected, and readers often skim it as rhetorical padding. It is not. He is conducting a search: going out into human experience to find the highest instance of love he can, so that he can measure God’s against it. And watch him qualify himself twice as he goes. For a righteous man, the upright, correct, admirable sort, one will scarcely die.

Though perhaps for a good person one would dare even to die. Then he corrects himself: perhaps for a good man, the warm and generous kind, a benefactor you would actually be fond of, someone might dare it. Even that is hedged with perhaps and dare. This is the best the human race can offer, and Paul cannot state it without qualification. And his estimate is right. People do die for others: a mother for her child, a soldier for the man beside him, occasionally a stranger in a river. But notice the invariable condition: there is always something in the object that draws it out. Love, in us, is a response to worth or to belonging. Nobody has ever laid down his life for a man he found contemptible, who had wronged him, and who would not be grateful. That is not cynicism about human beings; it is a fair description of where our ceiling is. Christ died for neither the righteous nor the good. He died for the ungodly.

A different kind of love. This means these verses are doing more than praising God warmly. They establish that divine love is a different kind of thing, not a larger quantity of the same thing. Ours is drawn out; his originates. Ours responds to something; his creates the something it will later delight in. And that is why the question what does God see in me? has no answer: not because the answer is disappointing, but because the question assumes the wrong mechanism. He was not looking for something to see.

Does this mean Christ died for me in particular? Paul writes we and us: he is speaking to believers about what Christ did for them. But look at the description: weak, ungodly. Those are not the names of a select class you might fail to qualify for. They are the names of everyone, and the gospel is offered freely to every one of them. No one who comes to Christ will discover that he was not included. If you are trusting him, you may say with Paul that he loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and if you are not yet, the only qualification for coming is the one you already have: being ungodly.

In a sentence. When we were still powerless, at just the right time Christ died for the ungodly, and very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is not about your feelings toward God but about what you think you are bringing. When you try to believe that God loves you, notice what you instinctively reach for as the reason. Most of us produce something, even if we would never say it out loud: that we have been trying, that we mean well, that we are not as bad as we might be, that at least we care about this. Now take whatever you produced and set it against verse 6. Christ died for the weak and the ungodly: categories that contain not a single reason. Whatever you were holding was not what secured this and cannot be what maintains it. Put it down.

For worship. If God’s love were like ours, it would have been drawn out by something in us, and it could therefore be exhausted by something in us. A love with a reason can lose its reason. But the love demonstrated at a specific hour, for people who were at that hour helpless and hostile, has nothing in us to lose. The Son of God did not wait for us to become good enough to die for. He came down to the ungodly, at the time his Father had appointed, and laid down his life for people who could not lift a finger to help him, and that is the love that holds us still.

parallels.desc: when the fullness of time had come

verseByVerse.quote: but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

But God shows his love for us. The verb (synistēsin) is worth pressing, because it is not the word for announcing something. It means to exhibit, to present, to prove by putting on display, and the tense is present: God goes on demonstrating his love in this. The cross is not a historical fact from which we may infer that God was once well disposed. It is a standing exhibit. Two thousand years later it is still being held up, and it is still the answer to the only question that matters when a man is at the bottom of himself. If you doubt God’s love, look at the cross.

The demonstration he chose. Notice what God chose to demonstrate it with. He could have shown his love by a statement, and he has made many. He could have shown it in provision, and he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matthew 5:45), which proves something, but not this. When he set out to prove that he loved people who hated him, the only thing sufficient was the death of his Son. That tells you something about the size of the claim being made. Nothing smaller would have carried it.

His own love. Then notice whose love is on display. The Greek says God shows his own love, not a love delegated to someone else, and later in the letter Paul makes plain what it cost him: he who did not spare his own Son (8:32). It is not the loving Son appeasing an angry Father; it is the Father showing his love by giving his Son (John 3:16). The demonstration is not that God arranged a rescue at some cost to a third party. The cost fell inside the Trinity. Anybody can be generous with somebody else’s son.

How can it be loving to punish an innocent man in the place of the guilty? This verse answers a question people ask honestly and are rarely answered on. Stated that way it sounds like a miscarriage of justice with a cheerful gloss. But the sentence does not describe a third party being conscripted. The Judge did not find a substitute; he became one. The one who was owed the debt is the one who paid it, in the person of his Son, by agreement within the Godhead before the world began. The Son was not volunteered against his will; he laid down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). That is not injustice. It is the only arrangement in which mercy costs the person extending it, and in which justice is fully satisfied and the guilty fully freed.

In that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Paul will not let go of the timing. While we were still sinners: not when we were sinners, as though describing a former category we have since left, but still, mid-course, in the act. Not after we improved. God’s love is not a response to our goodness; it came first. Whatever there was in your life at its worst, the cross was aimed at precisely that. It was not aimed at the person you have since become, and it is not waiting on the person you hope to be. The greatest love in the universe was given to those who deserved it least.

The two moments to reach for this verse. They are opposite. The first is when you have failed badly and cannot bring yourself to pray. The accusation at that hour always takes the same form: not like this, not after this. And the answer is that the love was demonstrated at a moment when you were doing exactly this, and worse, and had no intention of stopping. Your failure this week is not a new development. It was in the file when the price was set. The second is subtler and catches the respectable. There are believers who have never doubted that God loves them and have quietly concluded that this is reasonable enough: they are, after all, the sort of person who goes to church, gives, prays, means well. That confidence is not resting on this verse. It is resting on an assessment, and an assessment can be revised. Verse 8 takes it away, which feels at first like a loss and is in fact the only route to a peace that does not depend on how the year has gone.

If God loves me like this, why does my life feel as though he does not? Because Paul does not point you to your circumstances as the proof of God’s love; he points you to the cross. Circumstances are mixed in a fallen world, and they shift every week; read on their own, they will tell you God loves you on Monday and has forgotten you by Thursday. The cross does not shift. It is the one fixed point from which everything else is to be interpreted: the God who gave his Son for you while you were his enemy has not stopped caring because your job was lost or the treatment failed. He who did not spare his own Son will, with him, graciously give us all things (8:32). Read your life by the cross, never the cross by your life.

In a sentence. But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is one sentence. Say aloud: God loved me at my worst hour, and nothing I have done since has improved his opinion, and nothing I do next can lower it. Then notice which of the three clauses you want to argue with. Most people trip on the second, not the third: we can accept that our sins do not disqualify us far more readily than we can accept that our progress does not impress him. That resistance is worth locating, because it is the exact place where you are still living on your own reputation. When you doubt God loves you today, do not look inward. Look at the cross.

For worship. God demonstrates his love. Not offers, not promises, not describes: demonstrates, in the way a thing is proved when the evidence is put where everyone can see it. He does not gesture at a sunset, or a harvest, or the ordinary mercies that fall on everyone alike. He points to one afternoon, one man, one hill outside Jerusalem, and a death of the kind reserved for slaves and insurrectionists, and says: that is what I am like. It is the only demonstration he offers. He has never seen the need to provide a second.

verseByVerse.quote: Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood. “By his blood” means by his sacrificial death, the propitiation of 3:25. And Paul now reasons in a form that was standard in Jewish argument, from the heavy to the light, from the harder case to the easier. It works by asking what a thing already established implies about something smaller. If a man has given you his house, he is not going to quibble about the key.

Much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. The whole force lies in getting the two halves the right way round, which is where most of our anxiety goes wrong. Instinctively we assume the hard part is still ahead. The cross is behind us and settled; what remains uncertain is whether we will make it: whether faith will hold, whether the next twenty years will go well enough, whether we will be found acceptable at the end. Paul says we have the difficulty exactly inverted. The hard part was justifying enemies. That is done. What is left is the comparatively minor matter of God keeping his friends safe on the day of wrath, and it is unthinkable that he would fail at the easy end of his own work. Final salvation is certain.

For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son. Notice the word Paul uses for what we were: not the weak, not the unaware, not even the sinners now, but enemies, hostile to God (8:7). He has been escalating for four verses, helpless, ungodly, sinners, enemies, and this last is the strongest and the least flattering. Christianity does not teach that God found us lost and pitied us. It teaches that he found us in arms against him and made peace at his own expense. That is why the word for what happened is reconciled: a word for parties who were at odds and are not any longer. And God took the initiative. It is God who reconciled us to himself through Christ (2 Corinthians 5:18–20). We did not come to the table. He came to us.

Much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. The two halves of the sentence divide the work of Christ in a way worth having, because most Christians know only the first. We were reconciled by his death; we shall be saved by his life. The cross deals with the debt. But Paul does not leave our future resting on a transaction completed by a dead man; it rests on a living one, and what the living Christ is doing now is not idle. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). So the security of your Christian life does not depend on the strength of your grip on Christ. It depends on a man who is alive at this moment and whose present occupation is you. A living Saviour guarantees our salvation.

Assurance and perseverance. These verses are a foundation for the perseverance of the saints. If God loved us as enemies, he will not abandon us as friends. They are the answer to the fear almost every serious Christian carries and rarely says: I might not last. Not that God is unwilling, but that I am unreliable, and I have twenty or forty years still to go, and I know myself. That fear is perfectly reasonable if the finishing depends on you. This argument removes it from your hands entirely: the one who did the hard part when you were his enemy is the one doing the rest now that you are his child.

What it does not mean. This is not an invitation to drift. Paul is not saying perseverance does not matter or that nothing is required of you; he will spend chapter 6 and chapters 12 to 16 on what is. He is saying where the guarantee is located. The Christian is still called to endure, and the reason he can is that the outcome does not hang on the quality of his enduring. A man rowing a boat that is also under tow rows better, not worse.

If I am already saved, what does saved from wrath mean? Scripture speaks of salvation in three tenses. You have been saved from the penalty of sin, at the moment you were justified (Ephesians 2:8). You are being saved from its power, day by day, as the Spirit makes you holy (1 Corinthians 1:18). And you will be saved from its presence and from the wrath to come on the last day (1 Thessalonians 1:10). Paul is speaking here of the third: the final rescue when Christ returns. It has not happened yet, and it is not in doubt, because it was paid for in the first.

But what about the warnings, and people who seem to fall away? The New Testament does warn believers, seriously, against drifting and unbelief (Hebrews 3:12–14), and some who professed faith did leave. John explains them: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Their departure showed that the root was never there, not that God failed to keep someone who was his. The warnings are one of the means by which God keeps his people: a believer who hears them and turns back to Christ is persevering. So if you are frightened that you might be one who falls away, the fear itself, and the turning to Christ that it produces, are signs of life. Those who fall away are not usually worried about it.

In a sentence. Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him, for if while we were God’s enemies we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life.

On a Tuesday. A test, and it is diagnostic of where you have quietly placed the burden. Ask what you think would have to happen for you to end up lost. If an answer comes readily, a sin serious enough, a period of coldness long enough, a falling-away far enough, then notice what that answer assumes: that the decisive factor at the end will be something about you. Now put your answer beside verse 10. The God being described did the impossible thing while you were his enemy. Whatever you have just imagined, it is a smaller obstacle than the one he has already cleared. Take the next hard step of obedience today as a man under tow.

For worship. Twice in two verses: much more. Paul is not offering encouragement here; he is doing arithmetic. The hardest thing has already been done, and it was done at the point of maximum difficulty, on the wrong side of the account, for people who were not asking. The Son who died for his enemies now lives for his friends, and he has never lost one whom the Father gave him (John 6:39). If God loved you as his enemy, how much more will he keep you as his own. Everything after the cross is downhill.

verseByVerse.quote: More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than that, we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

More than that, we also rejoice in God. Follow the three rejoicings, because Paul has been climbing a staircase and this is the top step. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God (v. 2): that is joy about the future. We rejoice in our sufferings (v. 3): joy about the present, even at its worst. And now: we rejoice in God. The first two are joy about what God gives. The third is joy in God himself, and Paul marks the step up with more than that, as though everything before it had been preliminary. This is the climax: not just in God’s gifts, but in God himself. The goal of salvation is not a set of benefits. It is God.

The gifts and the Giver. This is worth stopping over, because it exposes something most of us have never examined. It is entirely possible to be delighted with the benefits of Christianity while having little appetite for God. A man can be genuinely glad about forgiveness, relieved about judgment, grateful for peace, warmly attached to his church, comforted in trouble, and all of it can be love of the gifts. That is not hypocrisy; the gifts are magnificent and were meant to be enjoyed. But it can be tested, and the test is what happens when the gifts are withdrawn.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation. The word Paul finishes the section with is the largest he has used yet. And notice it is not we have achieved it, or even we have entered it, but we have received it: the same passive that has run through the whole letter. Reconciliation is not a settlement negotiated between two aggrieved parties who each move some way. One party was entirely in the wrong and did not want terms; the other party made peace, at his own cost, and then handed the completed reconciliation to the offender as a gift. There was nothing for us to do but take delivery.

Now. The small word is Paul’s drumbeat through the section: we have now been justified by his blood (v. 9), we are now reconciled (v. 10), we have now received reconciliation (v. 11). Three times in three verses. Not at the last day, not when the process is complete, not pending review. Whatever remains outstanding in the Christian life, and chapters 6 to 8 will be honest about how much does, the relationship itself is not among it. That was settled while you were an enemy and delivered before you understood it.

What does rejoicing in God actually look like? It looks like enjoying God for who he is, not only for what he does. In practice it shows in praise that dwells on his attributes, his holiness, faithfulness, wisdom and mercy, and not only on the week’s answers to prayer. It shows in prayer that sometimes asks for nothing and simply stays in his company. It shows in reading Scripture to see him, not only to find instructions. And it shows in a quiet steadiness when the gifts are thin, because the chief good has not gone anywhere. It does not need to be loud. The psalmist put it simply: whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25).

In a sentence. Not only this, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

On a Tuesday. Here is the sharpest question in this chapter. Suppose God were to give you everything you have ever asked him for, the health, the child restored, the marriage healed, the work fruitful, the fear lifted, and then were himself absent. No sense of him, no dealings with him, the benefits without the Benefactor. Would that be enough? If it would, then what you have wanted from Christianity is its results. And if the honest answer is that it would not, that something essential would be missing from a world in which everything went well and God was not there, then you have discovered what verse 11 is about, and it is the surest evidence in the chapter that something real has happened to you. That preference cannot be manufactured. Nobody talks himself into wanting God more than God’s gifts. Today, spend five minutes thanking God for nothing he has given, only for what he is.

For worship. The section that began with peace ends with joy, and the joy is not in the peace. Paul has spent eleven verses listing what the justified man possesses: peace, access, a place to stand, hope, endurance, character, love poured in, rescue from wrath, reconciliation. And then he sets the whole inventory aside for one more sentence, to say that the best of it is not on the list. The gifts were never the point. They were the road to the Giver, and the Giver is the blessed God himself, Father, Son and Spirit, who made us for himself and, through our Lord Jesus Christ, has given us himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Death in Adam, Life in Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The argument that begins in v. 12 is the most theologically ambitious in the entire letter. Paul steps back from the individual experience of justification and places it within a cosmic, historical framework: the story of two men, Adam and Christ, whose representative actions determined the status and destiny of everyone who belongs to them. This is the doctrine of federal headship — the two-Adam theology that is foundational to the Reformed understanding of both sin and salvation.

The parallel is deliberate and asymmetrical. Adam sinned; condemnation and death spread to all. Christ obeyed; righteousness and life are given to all who are in him. But the parallel is asymmetrical because grace exceeds sin in every dimension: "the free gift is not like the trespass" (v. 15). The trespass brought condemnation; the gift brings justification for many trespasses. Adam's one sin brought death; Christ's one act of righteousness brings the free gift of life. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (v. 20). The gospel is not simply the repair of the damage done by Adam; it is a new creation that surpasses Eden.

The phrase "as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 21) is the conclusion to which the whole argument has been driving. Sin had a reign — a dominion, a kingdom of death. Grace now has a counter-reign — a dominion of life and righteousness. The believer has been transferred from one kingdom to the other. Adam is no longer her representative head; Christ is. She bears the condemnation of neither Adam's sin (fully atoned) nor her own (fully forgiven). She stands under the reign of grace, heading toward the eternal life that is the gift of her new federal head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Federal Headship: The Solidarity of Adam and Christ

Romans 5:12–21 is the biblical foundation of the Reformed doctrine of original sin and the imputation of Adam's guilt. Paul teaches that death spread to all because all sinned in Adam — not merely by imitating his example, but by being represented by him. Adam was the covenantal head of humanity; his act was our act in the only sense that matters covenantally. This is why all die, even infants who have not sinned in the way Adam sinned (v. 14). The parallel with Christ is the point: just as we were condemned in Adam by imputation, we are justified in Christ by imputation. The same covenantal logic that makes us sinners in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. You cannot reject one side of the parallel without undermining the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Adam-Christ typology was deeply embedded in Jewish theology of Paul's day — the figure of Adam as the representative of humanity was well established. Paul takes this shared theological framework and uses it to explain both the universality of sin and the universality of the gospel's offer: as Adam's headship was universal (all who are human bear his guilt), so Christ's headship is available to all (all who are in him receive his righteousness). Now: The doctrine of original sin is the one Christian teaching that can be empirically verified by reading any newspaper. Every generation produces fresh evidence that something has gone profoundly wrong with the human race at its root. Romans 5:12–21 names it: Adam. And then offers the only remedy: Christ. The diagnosis and the cure are inseparable.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned — for sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law.

Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man. “One man” is Adam (Genesis 3). Sin entered human history through him, and death entered as its consequence. Paul treats him as a real, historical man, and introduces the Adam and Christ comparison that will dominate the rest of the chapter.

A sentence left unfinished. One structural thing first, because it explains why this passage feels so hard to follow. Paul begins a comparison, just as sin came into the world through one man, and then never finishes it. The matching half, the so also, does not arrive until verse 18, six verses later. He breaks off at verse 13 and spends the intervening verses clearing obstacles out of the way before he will let himself complete the thought. So if you have ever read this paragraph and lost the thread, the fault is not yours. The thread is genuinely interrupted, and knowing that verses 13 to 17 are a parenthesis makes the whole thing legible.

And death through sin. Death is not natural; it is the penalty of sin (Genesis 2:17; Romans 6:23). And what is the death that spread? More than the grave. God had warned Adam that in the day he ate he would surely die. He died at once in his relationship with God, and in his body years later. So death here includes physical death, the spiritual death of being cut off from God (Ephesians 2:1), and, apart from Christ, the eternal death that is the wages of sin (6:23). That is why the answer at the end of the chapter is not only resurrection but eternal life (v. 21).

And so death spread to all men. Notice what Paul actually offers as evidence, because it is not a doctrine but a fact anybody can check. His argument runs on death. Sin entered, death entered with it, and death spread to all, and there the case rests, because there is no exception anywhere in the record. Every civilisation, every temperament, every degree of virtue or vice, every infant. Whatever else is disputed about this passage, the universal reign of death is not in dispute; it is the most thoroughly evidenced proposition in human experience. Paul is pointing at a fact and asking what could possibly account for it.

Because all sinned. “Because” translates eph’ hō, and everything turns on it. Augustine, reading the Latin translation (in quo, in whom), took it as in whom all sinned, that is, in Adam. Most scholars now agree the Greek means because, so the translation in whom cannot be pressed. But the question remains: in what sense did all sin?

Where Christians differ: two readings of “all sinned”. The first says all die because each person sins personally, following Adam’s example. The second says all sinned in Adam, when he sinned as the representative head of the human race. Verdict: the second, for three reasons Paul gives in the passage itself. First, death reigned even over those who did not sin as Adam did (v. 14), including infants, who have committed no personal sins; so their death must come from Adam’s sin. Second, Paul says five times that condemnation and death came through one man’s one trespass (vv. 15–19), not through each person’s many sins. Third, verse 19 says that by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners: a passive construction, in which Adam’s act, not our own, is the ground of our sinner-status. Personal sins follow, and they are real and add to our guilt; but the root is our union with Adam. This is what theologians call original sin: we inherit both Adam’s guilt, counted to us, and his corrupted nature (Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3).

Federal headship. The Reformed tradition, worked out by the Westminster divines, Owen and others, calls this federal headship, from the Latin for covenant. Adam stood as covenant head of the race, and his sin is reckoned to his posterity just as Christ’s obedience is reckoned to believers (Westminster 6.3). Another older view, natural or seminal headship, says we sinned in Adam because all human nature was present in him, so that we were, in some sense, there. Both reject the idea that Adam merely set a bad example, and the federal view best explains both this chapter and the exact symmetry Paul draws between the two men.

Where Christians differ: was Adam a real person? Some Christians, seeking to harmonise Genesis with evolutionary theories of human origins, hold that Adam is a symbol of humanity rather than a real first man. Verdict: Paul’s argument requires a real, historical Adam. He sets one man against one man, one trespass against one act of righteousness, and a real history of death reigning from Adam to Moses (v. 14). If there was no real Adam whose sin brought condemnation, Paul’s parallel with the real Christ whose obedience brings justification falls apart, and so does the comfort, because Christ’s obedience was a real act in history. Paul treats Adam the same way elsewhere (1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Timothy 2:13–14). Jesus too treated Adam and Eve as real (Matthew 19:4–5), and Luke traces Jesus’ genealogy back to Adam (Luke 3:38).

For sin indeed was in the world before the law was given, but sin is not counted where there is no law. “Counted” (ellogeitai) is charged to an account, as in a ledger. Why mention that sin was in the world before the law? Because of what happened during that period: people died. Generations of them, between Adam and Moses, in an era when there was no written law, so their sins were not charged as transgressions of a stated command in the way Adam’s was (see 4:15). If death is the penalty only for individual transgressions formally reckoned, those deaths are unaccounted for. Yet people still died, and death is the penalty of sin. Why? Because Adam’s sin was counted to them. This is Paul’s evidence for the point he has just made: death reigned because all sinned in Adam. And it shows in passing that the law is not the definition of sin, only its written codification: sin was real before Sinai.

Where Christians differ: original sin. Pelagians taught that Adam only set a bad example, and each person sins freely on their own. Verdict: Paul teaches that Adam’s sin was counted to the whole human race, so that all are born guilty and corrupt (vv. 18–19; Psalm 51:5; Ephesians 2:3). Adam was the federal head of humanity, and his fall became ours. This is hard, but it is the background of the gospel: in the same way, Christ’s righteousness is counted to all who are in him.

Is it fair to be condemned for Adam’s sin? This is the question every reader asks, and it is usually felt not as a dispute about imputation but as: I never voted for Adam. Paul does not run from it, and several things help. Representation is how God has always related to humanity: the head acts for those in him, as a nation’s leader can bind the whole nation to war or peace. It is the fabric of ordinary life. A country goes to war on the decision of a government most of its citizens did not choose. Children inherit the language, the nationality, the debts and the reputation their parents handed them. We accept the inherited goods readily and object loudly to the inherited liability. Adam was the best representative humanity could ever have had, placed in a perfect world with every advantage; no one can say they would have done better. Each of us confirms Adam’s choice by our own sins, every day: every human being has stood where Adam stood, with what God has said on one side and his own preference on the other, and has chosen as he chose. That is why Paul can say both that we were made sinners by one man’s disobedience and that all sinned, without contradiction. And most importantly, if we reject the principle of representation, we lose the gospel, because we are saved in exactly the same way: by another man’s obedience counted to us (vv. 18–19). We cannot accept the second Adam and refuse to understand the first. The question is not whether we will be represented, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

Standing alone. Pressed all the way, the objection argues against itself. Suppose you insist on standing alone: no representative, no federal head, judged strictly on your own record and nobody else’s. You would be safe from Adam. You would also be entirely alone with your own file, and this letter has spent three chapters describing what is in it. The principle you would have to abolish in order to escape Adam is the same principle by which a righteousness not your own is credited to you. Both men acted before you were consulted. The difference is that only one of them was acting on your behalf on purpose.

Does original sin mean I am not really responsible for my sins? No. Original sin explains where the disease came from; it does not excuse what you do with it. Scripture always holds people accountable for their own choices (Ezekiel 18:20; Romans 2:6), and nobody sins against his will; we sin because we want to. The doctrine actually deepens responsibility rather than removing it, because it shows that the problem is not a few bad decisions you could put right with effort but a heart turned from God at the root. That is bad news for self-improvement and very good news for the gospel. You need not a better example but a new head and a new heart, and both are offered in Christ.

In a sentence. Just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death came to all people because all sinned, for sin was in the world before the law, though sin is not charged where there is no law...

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it uses the one piece of evidence in the passage that is available to everybody. Ask yourself what you actually believe death is. Almost everyone, asked directly, will say it is natural: the way of things, part of the cycle, biologically ordinary. Then watch what the same person does at a graveside. Nobody stands at a funeral thinking this is how it should be. We grieve as though something has been done wrong, as though a person has been taken rather than merely ceasing. That instinct is not sentimentality. It is the memory of a world where this was not so, and Scripture agrees with your instinct rather than your theory: death is an enemy, the last enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). The next time you stand at a grave, let your grief say what Paul says, and then let your hope say what he goes on to say.

For worship. You were in Adam, and fell with him. But God did not respond to the disaster by abandoning the race that ruined itself. Before the first sin was committed he had already purposed a second Man, and in the fullness of time the eternal Son took our flesh, stood where Adam stood, and did not fall. In Christ you are raised with him. The first man brought death into the world uninvited; the second walked into it willingly, and walked out again. Thank God for the second Adam.
verseByVerse.note: “One man” is Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam, who was a type of the one who was to come.

Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses. The verb is the striking thing. Death did not merely occur; it reigned. Paul uses the word for a king exercising dominion, and he will use it four more times before the chapter closes. Death is not presented here as a biological full stop but as a power with a territory and subjects, ruling a period of history. That is a more accurate description of the thing than the modern one, because death does not only take you at the end. It governs the whole of a life long before it arrives: it sets the limit on every plan, gives every love its ache, and stands behind a great deal of what people do to secure themselves. Everyone lives inside its jurisdiction. Everyone died in that age: infants, and people who never broke a direct command.

Even over those whose sinning was not like the transgression of Adam. The hard clause, which verse 13 laid the groundwork for. Adam had received an explicit command with an explicit penalty, and broke it knowingly. Between him and Moses there was no such published command, and people died anyway. That is Paul’s proof. Their deaths cannot be accounted for by transgressions formally charged against them, because there was no code to charge them under. They still died, because of Adam.

What about infants and those who could never sin knowingly? This brings a great many readers, rightly, to a question that is not academic: the infant, the stillborn, the profoundly disabled, anyone who dies before there is anything to charge. It is usually asked by somebody with a name and a date in mind, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a systematic one. Start with what this verse does say, because it is sobering: it says they die. Scripture does not exempt anybody from the solidarity of ruin, and the theology of this passage is the reason infants are mortal at all. But notice what the verse does not say. It does not say they are condemned. Paul’s subject here is death’s dominion, not the final destiny of individuals, and it is a serious mistake, one that has caused enormous grief, to read a paragraph about the reign of death as though it were a roll of the lost.

The ground of hope. Scripture gives real ground for hope, without giving a formula. David’s child died, and David stopped fasting, washed, worshipped, and said: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Samuel 12:23), words of expectation, not resignation, from a man who elsewhere says he will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. Our Lord took children in his arms and said the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he judges according to the light given (2:12). The Westminster Confession speaks of elect infants dying in infancy as regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3), and many Reformed teachers, among them Charles Spurgeon, Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, have held that all who die in infancy are among them. They are saved not on the ground of an innocence this chapter denies them, but by sovereign mercy, through the same Christ, without the faculties for conscious faith. Scripture does not state that in so many words, and it would be wrong to pretend it does. It is a hope that rests on the character of God, which is the only place a hope was ever safe.

If you are reading this with a grave in mind. Hear the two halves in the right order. Yes, this passage explains why that death happened at all: it is the reign Paul is describing, death is an enemy, and your grief is not a failure of faith but an accurate response to an intruder. And no, this passage is not a verdict on that child. The one who will decide is the one who wept at a friend’s tomb while fully intending to empty it, and who himself became an infant.

Who was a type of the one who was to come. A “type” (typos) is a pattern, a mould, a foreshadowing. That is an extraordinary thing to say about Adam. Everything we have been told of him in this chapter is catastrophe: the trespass, the condemnation, the reign of death. And Paul calls him a preliminary sketch of Christ. Not in his sin, obviously, but in the shape of his significance: one man, one act, and a whole race implicated by it. Adam, head of the old humanity, points to Christ, head of the new. Two men, two heads, two families. Adam is the pattern Christ reverses (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49).

The mechanism kept. This is a striking thing to notice about how God works. He did not respond to the disaster by abolishing the mechanism that produced it. God built representation into the structure of humanity from the first day, and the arrangement that ruined us was the arrangement through which we would be rescued. He kept the mechanism and sent a second Man to stand at the head of it, so that the very thing you would have complained about, had you been consulted in Eden, turns out to be the thing that makes your salvation possible. Adam was never merely a warning. He was a rough draft, and the finished work was already in view.

How do I know which family I am in? Not by birth, church background or how you feel. Everyone begins in Adam; nobody is born into Christ. You come into the second family by being joined to its head through faith: trusting Christ himself, not your record, for acceptance with God. If you are resting on him, you are in him, whatever your past. If you are not sure, do not wait to be sure: come to him now, as you are. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command as Adam did, who was a pattern of the one to come.

On a Tuesday. Death reigns in Adam. Life reigns in Christ. Which family are you in? Notice this week how much of what you do is quietly shaped by death’s reign: the plans you make to feel secure, the fear behind the money, the dread of a diagnosis, the need to leave a mark. Then name each one before Christ, and say plainly that you belong to another King. Death still has its day in your body, but it has lost its throne over your life.

For worship. The God who drew up the pattern in Eden had already drawn the Man it pointed to. Death reigned for thousands of years, over the great and the small, over infants and kings, and in all that time not one grave escaped it. And then One came into its territory who owed it nothing, let it take him, and broke its rule from the inside. The first Adam was a type; the last Adam is the reality, and he is the Lord of life.
verseByVerse.note: A “type” is a pattern or foreshadowing: Adam, head of the old humanity, foreshadows Christ, head of the new.

parallels.desc: the first man Adam, the last Adam

verseByVerse.quote: But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man's sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the free gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many. And the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation, but the free gift following many trespasses brought justification.

But the free gift is not like the trespass. Similar in pattern, but not equal in power. It is worth noticing how deliberately Paul sabotages his own illustration. He has spent three verses building an elegant symmetry, one man, one act, a race implicated, and now, twice in two verses, he stops to say that it does not actually balance. The free gift is not like the trespass; the free gift is not like the result of that one man’s sin. A lesser writer would have polished the parallel and left it. Paul breaks it on purpose, because a tidy symmetry would be a lie: it would suggest that Christ merely undoes Adam, that the gospel is a repair job, that grace restores the balance and we are back where we started. He will not have it. The comparison is real, and the two sides are nothing like the same size. The gift is greater.

For if many died through one man’s trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift abounded for many. “Much more” is the heart of it: grace is stronger than sin. The word for abounded means to overflow, to exceed the container. Paul does not say the gift is equal to the trespass in effect. And this means the gospel is not the restoration of Eden. Adam lost a garden; we are promised a city. Adam had innocence, which is a fragile thing and was lost in an afternoon; the believer has a righteousness that is not his own and therefore cannot be forfeited by him. Adam could fall. The man in Christ cannot finally fall, because he is not standing on his own record. We do not end where Adam began. We end considerably further on, and the difference is not sentiment but the specific gain of having been redeemed rather than merely restored.

The grace of that one man Jesus Christ. Notice that the gift is named twice: the grace of God, and the free gift by the grace of one man. The Father’s grace and the Son’s are one grace. And it comes through a man: the eternal Son had to become one of us to stand at the head of a new humanity, as Adam stood at the head of the old.

For the judgment following one trespass brought condemnation. The first imbalance is in the arithmetic of what each act had to deal with. Adam faced one command and broke it: a single trespass, and condemnation followed.

But the free gift following many trespasses brought justification. Christ faced the accumulated mass of every sin of every person he came to save, a mountain of them, and justification followed. So the judgment worked from one offence to condemnation; the gift works from many offences to acquittal. The arithmetic runs in the direction nobody expects. If it took only one sin to ruin the race, you would assume that a great many sins would be proportionately harder to deal with. It is exactly the reverse: one was enough to condemn, and the countless were not too many to forgive. Grace takes on a whole lifetime of sins.

Can he forgive this much? That answers a fear a great many Christians live with privately. Not can God forgive sin? That is settled. But can he forgive this much of it? The man converted at fifty who cannot stop counting the years. The believer who keeps returning to the same failure and has begun to suspect there must be a limit somewhere. This verse is the answer, and it is a mathematical one. The gift is not calibrated to the size of the debt. It was never a matter of grace being sufficient for a certain quantity of sin and running short beyond that, because grace was never measured against the sin in the first place. It is measured against the worth of the one who gives it.

If I am forgiven, why do I still feel the weight of sins I have confessed? Because memory and conscience are slower than the verdict. God has removed your transgressions as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12); your memory has not, and it is not meant to be the judge. When an old sin returns, do not confess it again as though the first confession failed. Thank God that it was forgiven, and use the memory to humble you and make you gentle with others. Where a wrong you did to someone can still be put right, put it right, because forgiveness from God does not cancel the duty of restitution. And where it cannot, leave it with the Christ who bore it. Feelings of guilt over forgiven sin are not God’s voice; the gospel is.

In a sentence. But the gift is not like the trespass, for if many died through one man’s trespass, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, overflow to many; and the gift is not like the result of one man’s sin, for judgment followed one sin and brought condemnation, but the gift followed many trespasses and brought justification.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is about which of the two men you instinctively think you belong to. Take the last serious failure you had, the one you would not want repeated, and notice how you described it to yourself afterwards. Did you find yourself calculating: how much ground have I lost, how long before things are normal again, how many good weeks does this cost me? That calculation is Adam’s arithmetic, and it is entirely reasonable inside his system, where everything runs on your record. The whole point of these two verses is that you are not in that system. There is no ground to make up, because the ground was never yours, and there is no quantity at which the gift becomes insufficient, because it was never being weighed against you. Confess it, receive the gift, and get up.

For worship. Paul’s refusal to tidy the parallel is itself the good news. If Adam and Christ balanced, the Christian life would be an anxious accounting, losses on one side, gains on the other, and the outcome genuinely in doubt. They do not balance. One man’s trespass brought a verdict; one Man’s obedience brought a gift that exceeded it, and the scales were broken deliberately by the God who put his own Son on one of them. Grace is bigger than all your sins, because it is as big as he is.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.

Because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man. Death the tyrant. And watch what Paul does not write next, because the sentence he was building would have finished itself. Death reigned through one man’s trespass, so the matching clause should be that life will reign through Jesus Christ. That is the tidy version, and it is not what he says.

Much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life. He says that those who receive will themselves reign in life. The parallel breaks again, and it breaks upward: the second half is not about a power replacing a power, but about people replacing a power. Under Adam we were the territory being ruled. Under Christ we are not merely liberated subjects; we are given a throne. Believers become kings, sharing Christ’s rule (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). That is a far larger claim than most Christians have noticed. Whatever else salvation means in this letter, it does not mean being restored to a safe neutrality. It means being handed authority: the destiny Genesis described before anything went wrong, when the creature made in God’s image was told to have dominion, and which has been in ruins ever since. Adam was made to rule and ended as a subject of death. The man in Christ was a subject of death and ends by ruling.

Will reign. The tense does two things at once. Will reign is future. The full thing is not yet, and anybody who looks at his own life and cannot find much evidence of sovereignty is reading his situation correctly. We are not there. But the participle beside it is present: those who are receiving the abundance of grace. So the receiving is now and the reigning is later, which is exactly the shape of the Christian life: a king in exile, whose title is already granted, whose coronation is on a date he does not know.

Receive. Notice the single condition, stated in one word. It is the only verb in the sentence that we perform, and it is the one verb that contributes nothing. Everything else is done by somebody else: the grace is given, the righteousness is a gift, the reign is conferred. And “the free gift of righteousness” means righteousness itself is a gift, credited to us, not a quality we produce. Paul chooses his nouns to make refusal look absurd: not grace but the abundance of grace, not righteousness but the free gift of righteousness.

How do I receive it? By faith, which is the empty hand of the beggar. You receive the gift of righteousness by trusting Christ: believing that what he did is enough, and resting your whole case with God on him rather than on yourself. It is not a feeling you must work up or a prayer with the right words; it is a reliance. You go on receiving it in the same way, every day, by coming back to him as the only ground of your acceptance, especially on the days you have failed.
