They will be there because God was merciful, and mercy cannot be demanded. Think of a judge who pays the fine of one guilty man out of his own pocket. The others have not been wronged; they received justice. The one has received a gift. Grace is not a matter of being fair, and that is the best news there is, because fairness would condemn us all.

In a sentence. What should we say then? Is God unjust? Absolutely not! For he says to Moses that he will have mercy on whoever he chooses to have mercy on, and compassion on whoever he chooses to have compassion on.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to say God is unfair, remember: you do not want fairness. Fairness is judgment. You need mercy, and it is his to give. Here is a test to run on paper. Try writing the rule by which God would be obliged to be merciful to you, the condition that would make mercy something he owes. Then read your rule back and ask honestly whether you meet it. Anything that obliges God to be merciful is a standard, and a standard that lets you in on your performance can also shut you out on your performance. A mercy answerable to nothing but God’s own freedom is the only kind that cannot be revoked when you fail.

For worship. Justice is what the calf deserved. Everything after the calf is mercy. Paul is not defending God against the charge of giving somebody too little. He is answering people who have not yet grasped that the whole story, from the mountain onward, is God giving somebody far too much. Blessed be the LORD, who when asked to show his glory showed his mercy, who is gracious to whom he will be gracious, and whose freedom to have mercy is the only hope of sinners and the sure hope of all who come to him in Christ.

parallels.desc: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious

verseByVerse.quote: So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, "For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

So then it depends not on human will or exertion. The conclusion. “Will” (thelō, desire, choice) and “exertion” (trechō, running, the image of a race): literally, not of him who wills, nor of him who runs. Ask almost anyone how a person gets right with God and the answer will be some version of wanting it enough or trying hard enough. Those are the two: desire and effort. Paul excludes both in one clause, and there is no third thing left that a human being brings. Esau wanted the blessing and ran to hunt game for it (Genesis 27), but did not get it.

But on God, who has mercy. Salvation rests finally on God’s mercy. We do will and run, but only because God has first worked in us both to will and to work (Philippians 2:13). Paul ran hard and said so: I do not run aimlessly (1 Corinthians 9:26). What he denies is that willing and running are the cause. He put both halves in one sentence once: I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own (Philippians 3:12). The pressing on is real, and it is downstream. You do not run in order to be laid hold of. You run because you were.

Relief for the exhausted. There is relief in this that tired people miss. If salvation did depend on will and exertion, the honest follow-up question would be: how much? How much wanting counts as enough, how much effort clears the bar? Nobody could ever answer that, and nobody could ever rest. Verse 16 does not remove your hope. It removes a measurement no one has ever passed.

For the Scripture says to Pharaoh. The other side: hardening. Paul quotes Exodus 9:16. Notice “the Scripture says”: what Scripture says, God says. And put the quotation back where Exodus has it, because much turns on that. Read Exodus 9:15–16 whole: by now God could have put out his hand and struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence, and they would have been cut off from the earth, but for this purpose he raised him up. So the verse is God explaining to Pharaoh why he is still alive. It is spoken to a man who by every reckoning should already be dead, six plagues into a contest he has lost, and it accounts for his continued existence. It belongs with the same chapter’s account of God enduring with much patience (v. 22).

For this very purpose I have raised you up. God brought Pharaoh onto the stage of history, made him king, and kept him standing through the plagues. Pharaoh’s whole career was ordered by God’s purpose: not as approval of his wickedness, but as the stage on which God’s power would be displayed to the nations.

That I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth. God’s purpose was to display his power and glory through Pharaoh’s defeat. It is not a boast; it is a statement of what actually happened, and the evidence can be traced. Forty years later, in Jericho, a Canaanite prostitute told two Israelite spies why she had hidden them: we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you, and our hearts melted (Joshua 2:10–11). The news had crossed a desert and a border and got into a brothel in a doomed city. The Philistines had heard of it too (1 Samuel 4:8). And it saved Rahab. She and her household came out of Jericho alive, and her name stands in the first chapter of Matthew, in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. The display of God’s power against a king who would not yield became the report that reached a woman with no standing at all, and she became an ancestor of the Messiah.

What it does not mean. It does not mean human choices are fake or that we should not repent and believe. The gospel commands everyone to believe (10:9–13). It does not mean willing and running are worthless. It means that when anyone does believe, the credit goes to God’s mercy, not to his own wisdom or effort.

If it does not depend on my will, should I just wait for God to act? No. God’s mercy does not bypass your will; it renews it, so that you willingly come. The gospel calls you to repent and believe now (Acts 17:30; 2 Corinthians 6:2), and Paul will say in the next chapter that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (10:13). If you want Christ, that desire is already the sign of God’s mercy at work. Do not sit waiting for a feeling. Call on him, read his word, go where it is preached, and pray, Lord, have mercy on me. No one who ever came to him was refused.

In a sentence. So it does not depend on human desire or effort, but on God’s mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh that God raised him up for this purpose: to show his power through him and to make his name known throughout the world.

On a Tuesday. Take stock of how you are trying to hold on to God. If your peace rises and falls with how hard you prayed this week, you are measuring the wrong thing. Keep running, because Christ has laid hold of you, but rest your weight on his mercy rather than on your stride. And when you share the gospel, remember Rahab: the news of what God has done travels further than you think, and reaches people you would never have picked.

For worship. Run the two verses together and see what Paul has built. Not of him who wills or runs: Pharaoh willed and ran harder than anyone in the story, and it moved nothing. But of God who has mercy: and the mercy reached the last person in the region anyone would have picked, by way of the hardest heart in it. Blessed be the God who makes his name known through the defeat of tyrants and the rescue of outcasts, and whose mercy, not our running, carries every one of his children home. If you have run to Christ, praise the mercy that made you run.

parallels.desc: for this purpose I have raised you up

verseByVerse.quote: So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”

So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills. The two sides of God’s sovereignty, drawn from the two quotations: mercy (Moses) and hardening (Pharaoh). To harden (sklērynō) is to make stubborn, unresponsive. And notice that the two halves do not rest on the same kind of evidence, and Paul does not pretend they do. He has mercy on whomever he wills summarises God’s own self-declaration at Exodus 33:19. He hardens whomever he wills is Paul’s conclusion from the Pharaoh narrative. Nowhere does God announce himself as the one who hardens in the way he announces himself as the one who is merciful. Scripture is not even-handed between the two, and neither is this chapter; that comes back with force at verses 22–23.

How God hardens. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (Exodus 9:12; 10:20), and God foretold it before any plague (Exodus 4:21). Both are true. The order in the story is worth noticing. Through the first five plagues it is Pharaoh who hardens himself. The first time the account says the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart is at the sixth (9:12), after Pharaoh had done it to himself repeatedly and had promised to let the people go and gone back on it. That does not soften the doctrine, since God announced the hardening in advance. What it shows is the shape of the thing. God does not put evil into a good heart. He hardens by withholding the softening grace that would melt the heart, and by giving sinners over to the sin they already love (1:24, 26, 28). Pharaoh is Romans 1 in a single man. He freely chose his stubbornness and was fully guilty; God judicially confirmed him in it. The Westminster Confession says that God, for sinners already sinful, withholds his grace and gives them over to their own lusts (5.6).

You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?” The second objection. If God decides who is hardened, how can he blame anyone? Again, the objection only arises because Paul really is teaching that God decides. No one asks this of an election based on foreseen faith. And let the objection stand at full height, because there is no point answering a weak version of it. If God’s will cannot be resisted, and if what I am is finally traceable to that will, then blaming me is like blaming a stone for falling. Every honest reader of this chapter has felt it, and Paul writes the sentence for exactly that reader: you will say to me then. He knows this is where his argument leads a thinking person.

Paul declines to solve it. Say it plainly: Paul does not answer this objection with an argument. What follows in verse 20 is not a rebuttal but a question about who is asking. He had other options and did not take them. He could have distinguished what God decrees from what he permits, or pointed out that Pharaoh was never coerced, or argued that freedom and sovereignty are compatible. He uses none of them. So if you came wanting the logic resolved, you will not get it here, and you are not slow for noticing. But declining is not evading. Paul is doing what God did with Job. Job asked for a hearing and had a case, and what he got out of the whirlwind was a long series of questions about the sea, the storehouses of snow, the wild donkey and the ostrich, and not one word on the question he had asked. And Job was satisfied: not because he received the information, but because he received the one speaking. A God whose decisions you could fully audit would be a God the size of your understanding. People want that God right up until they are in trouble, and then they want a bigger one.

The chapter does not stop at the potter. Here is the balance that keeps all this from being a dodge. Paul does eventually give a cause for Israel’s failure, and it is not a decree. It is Israel. They did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works (v. 32). They stumbled over a stone that was there to be seen. And in the next chapter God holds out his hands all day long to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21). Paul refuses to explain the mechanism, and then he places the responsibility exactly where the objector feared it could not be placed. Anyone who quotes verse 20 as though it settled the question of human responsibility has stopped reading eleven verses too early.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God makes people sin against their will or forces innocent people to reject him. No one who wants God is turned away (John 6:37). The hardened are sinners who do what they want.

Has God hardened me? If that question frightens you, look at what the fear itself shows. Pharaoh never once asked it. Hardness does not lie awake wondering whether it is hard; that is the whole trouble with it. Alarm about your own heart is a sign of feeling in it. And the remedy was never introspection. A heart of stone is not repaired by being examined more closely. It is replaced, and God promised to do exactly that: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26). You do not soften your own heart. You ask for the one thing you cannot manufacture, and you ask the God who gives it.

In a sentence. So God has mercy on whom he chooses and hardens whom he chooses. Then someone will ask Paul why God still blames us, if no one can resist what he wills.

On a Tuesday. Do not play with sin, thinking you can repent later. Repeatedly refusing God hardens the heart, and God may give you over to it. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15). And run the test on a real case rather than in the abstract. Take one thing you did this week that you know was wrong: one instance, with a time and a place. Did you experience it as compulsion? Nobody does. It felt like choosing, because it was. Whatever is true about the eternal decree, no one has ever sinned against his own will, and no one has ever stood before God able to say, I wanted you and you turned me away.

For worship. The objection asks how God can still find fault. The answer this chapter finally gives is not that fault is an illusion, but that mercy is not an obligation. And the God who need not have mercy on anyone has had mercy on multitudes, softening hearts of stone, opening blind eyes, and drawing rebels who once hardened themselves against him. Blessed be the Lord who is free and holy and good, who answers our hardest questions not with a formula but with himself, and who gives the new heart we could never make.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it.

verseByVerse.quote: But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, "Why have you made me like this?" Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?

But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Paul does not give a philosophical answer. He rebukes the attitude behind the question. Start with the address, because it carries the argument. O man: the same address Paul used at 2:1 to the reader who was enjoying chapter 1. It is not an insult. It is a reminder of category, and the category is the answer: whatever else you are, you are a creature, having this conversation from inside the made world, not outside it. Then the verb. “Answer back” (antapokrinomai) means to reply against, to contradict, to talk back, arguing with God as if he owed us an account. It is the word for cross-examining, not the word for asking. Job learned the same lesson (Job 38–42; 40:2).

Questions are not forbidden. That distinction is not a technicality, and getting it wrong has done real damage. Paul is not forbidding questions. This chapter is made of questions, and he asked two of the hardest himself, at verse 14 and verse 19. Scripture is full of people who put hard questions to God and were not struck down: Job demanded a hearing; Habakkuk asked how long; Jeremiah said, Righteous are you, O LORD, when I complain to you; yet I would plead my case before you (Jeremiah 12:1). Mary asked how this could be, and was answered. So if this verse has ever been used on you to shut down an honest question, in grief or doubt, it was misused. What Paul rebukes is the posture of summoning God to the stand as a defendant and appointing yourself the bench.

Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?” From Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9. A clay pot has no rights against its potter. We are creatures; God is the Creator. He is not answerable to us. The clay does not dictate to the potter, and the creature does not sit in judgment on the Creator.

Has the potter no right over the clay. “Right” is exousia, authority. The image comes from Jeremiah 18:1–6, and it is worth going there, because the image is often used in the opposite direction from Jeremiah’s. God sends Jeremiah to the potter’s house to watch a man work. The vessel he was making was spoiled in the potter’s hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as seemed good to him (Jeremiah 18:4). The clay is spoiled, and the potter does not sweep it into the yard. He keeps the same lump on the wheel and starts again. And the application God draws is an appeal: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, he will relent of the disaster (Jeremiah 18:7–8). That does not blunt Paul; he cites the potter for the potter’s right, and the right is real. But it tells you what kind of potter has that right. Isaiah 29:16 sits in an oracle that ends with the deaf hearing and the meek obtaining fresh joy; Isaiah 45:9 sits beside the promise of a king raised up to set the exiles free. Every potter passage in the Old Testament is set within a promise of restoration. Not one is about God shrugging.

To make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use. The same lump: all humanity, all alike sinful in Adam (5:12). From it God makes some vessels for honour (salvation) and leaves others for dishonour (judgment). The lump is not innocent clay; it is fallen humanity, already deserving wrath. God wrongs no one by showing mercy to some. And out of the same lump settles something else: not two grades of clay, not a superior material for the honourable vessel. There is no better stuff. The difference between two vessels from one lump lies entirely in the potter’s intention and nowhere in the clay. One caution about pressing the picture further than Paul does: in a household, honourable and dishonourable use means the fine dish and the common pot; the final destinies come in verses 22–23. Elsewhere Paul uses the same image and has a person cleanse himself to become a vessel for honourable use (2 Timothy 2:20–21). The picture is doing a particular job here. It is not a whole system.

Where Christians differ: double predestination. Some say God chooses only to save, and the lost simply choose damnation without any decree. Others (hyper-Calvinists) say God creates people in order to damn them and causes their sin in the same way he causes faith. Verdict: Scripture teaches that God decrees both: he elects some to life, and he passes by the rest and ordains them to wrath for their sin (Westminster 3.3, 3.7). But the two are not symmetrical. God works faith in the elect by his Spirit; he does not work sin in the reprobate. The saved owe everything to grace; the lost owe their condemnation entirely to their own sin. Hold the mystery with humility, as Paul does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is a tyrant who enjoys destruction, or that we should not ask God honest questions. The psalms are full of honest questions. Paul forbids not the question but the accusation: the creature putting the Creator on trial. Nor is this a call to stoicism. Not knowing why is a real grief, and Scripture never tells you to pretend otherwise. You are not required to feel resolved. You are required not to climb onto the bench.

Does this mean we are just pots, without dignity? No. The image is about authority, not worth. Paul is not saying people are mere objects; Scripture says we are made in God’s image and crowned with glory and honour (Psalm 8:5). The point is the relationship: we cannot stand over God and judge him, because he made us and we did not make him. And the potter who has this right is the one who reshapes spoiled clay rather than throwing it away, and whose own Son took human clay in the incarnation. To be clay in such hands is not humiliation. It is the safest place a creature can be.

In a sentence. But who are you, a mere human, to talk back to God? Should a clay pot ask its maker why it was made like this? Doesn’t the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one pot for honourable use and another for common use?

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing in your life you most want an explanation for. Now ask honestly which you want more: the explanation, or the God who has it. Most of us discover we want the explanation, and would take it and go. That is what Paul puts his finger on. The demand to be answered is often, underneath, a wish not to need God, to be given the information so that the relationship becomes optional. Bring him your questions, as the psalmists did, loudly if need be. But bring them as a child to a Father, not as a prosecutor to a defendant.

For worship. The last word belongs to the potter’s hands. Genesis says God formed the first man from the dust of the ground, the potter’s own work, done once, by hand. And there is exactly one occasion in the Gospels when anybody makes clay. Jesus spits on the ground, mixes it, and puts it on the eyes of a man born blind (John 9:6). The potter took up dust a second time. He did it to give a man his sight, and the man had been sitting there since birth while everyone walked past asking whose fault it was. Bow before God’s right to rule. He is the potter, and we are the clay. And the hands that shape us were pierced for us.

parallels.desc: shall the potter be regarded as the clay?

verseByVerse.quote: What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory —
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—

What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power. God has good purposes in permitting evil and judging it. He wants his holy wrath against sin and his power to be seen, as with Pharaoh. And notice the shape of the whole sentence, which is stranger than it looks in English. It begins What if God, and never finishes. There is no second half, no conclusion drawn. Paul asks and lets it hang. At the hardest point in his hardest chapter, having just told a man not to answer back, Paul himself does not assert. He puts a question and leaves it with you. If he will not close this sentence, nobody preaching it should close it harder than he did.

But why would God want his wrath to be seen? A fair question, and Paul answers it in the very next verse. Five reasons, from this passage and the rest of Scripture.

1. Because it is true of him. God’s glory is God made known as he really is. When he showed Moses his glory, he named himself merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love, forgiving iniquity, and also one who will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:6–7). Justice is part of who he is. A God who hid it would be hiding himself. And a God who did nothing about evil would not be good: we would not call a judge good who let a child abuser walk free.

2. Because evil must not have the last word. Pharaoh was enslaving and killing God’s people. The plagues that showed God’s power were also the rescue of the oppressed. The cry of every victim, how long, O Lord? (Revelation 6:10; Psalm 94:3), is answered by God’s wrath. His judgement tells the world that cruelty and injustice will not win.

3. So that his name would reach the nations. God told Pharaoh, I have raised you up, that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth (v. 17; Exodus 9:16). And it was. Forty years later, in Jericho, a Canaanite woman named Rahab said, we have heard how the Lord dried up the Red Sea, and she turned to Israel’s God and was saved (Joshua 2:9–11). The display of God’s power against Pharaoh became mercy for a Gentile. That is the pattern of this chapter.

4. So that mercy is seen as mercy. This is Paul’s own answer: in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy (v. 23). Mercy only means something where judgement is deserved. A jewel shines brightest against dark cloth. Those who are saved see what they were saved from, and so they see the riches of grace: we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind. But God, being rich in mercy … (Ephesians 2:3–4). The one who is forgiven much, loves much (Luke 7:47).

5. Supremely, at the cross. The place where God shows both his wrath and his mercy most fully is Calvary. God put Christ forward as a propitiation, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:25–26). There wrath against sin is fully shown, and fully borne, by the Son, for the vessels of mercy.

What this does not mean. Not that God enjoys destroying: As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Not that his wrath is a loss of temper; it is his settled, holy opposition to evil. And not that God shows his glory out of vanity or insecurity, as a person might. For us, living for our own glory is pride, because we are not the greatest good. For God it is the opposite: he is the greatest good, so making himself known is the best thing he can give his creatures. Notice too that Paul asks this as a question, what if? He gives us enough to trust God, and calls us to humility where we cannot see further (v. 20; 11:33–36).

Has endured with much patience vessels of wrath. In the middle of the sentence sits the phrase that ruins every caricature of this passage. God endured with much patience. Not tolerated briefly, but bore with, at length: the word is makrothumia, long-temper, the same quality this letter said at 2:4 is meant to lead you to repentance. And look at who receives that patience. It is not the vessels of mercy. The patience in this verse is spent on the ones headed for destruction. If the only aim were to display wrath, there would be no reason to wait, and God does not wait a little; he waits long. Peter uses the same word for the same behaviour and tells you what is inside it: the Lord is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Whatever Romans 9 is doing, it is not describing a God in a hurry to condemn.

Prepared for destruction. Notice the grammar. The Greek participle (katērtismena) is passive, and Paul does not say who prepared them. They are ripe for destruction, fitted for it by their own sin. Contrast the next phrase, where Paul says God prepared the vessels of mercy.

In order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy. The ultimate goal. God’s patience with the wicked and his judgment of them show the vessels of mercy what they were saved from, and so make his grace shine brighter. And this is where the two verses become personal. The patience toward the one is the room in which mercy reaches the other. Every Christian who has ever lived was on the wrong side of that sentence for a while. The waiting was not happening around you while you stood safely elsewhere. You were inside it. The delay people demand an explanation for is the delay they were saved during.

Which he has prepared beforehand for glory. Here the verb is active, and God is the subject: he prepared them beforehand (proētoimasen), as in Ephesians 2:10. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish. The difference in grammar is deliberate: God is the author of salvation, but not the author of sin.

Three differences in one sentence. Look at the two halves side by side. Of the vessels of mercy: an active verb, God named as the one who acts, and a prefix meaning beforehand, so the preparing is dated before the vessel existed. Of the vessels of wrath: a passive participle, no agent named, no beforehand. Three differences, all running the same way. Paul had every word he needed to make the halves match, and he was not careless with this chapter. Be careful not to claim more than that: a passive with no stated agent can still have God’s decree behind it, and careful readers in this tradition have said so. But anyone who presents election and reprobation as two identical acts, worked the same way by the same hand, is being more symmetrical than the apostle. The historic Reformed confessions take this path. Election is God’s active, unconditional choice to save. Reprobation is his decision to pass others by, leave them in the sin they have chosen, and condemn them for that sin (Westminster 3.7). God is sovereign over both, but he is the author of faith and never of sin. The lost are condemned for what they did; the saved are saved for what God did.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the cause of sin. It does not mean we can know who the vessels of wrath are, or that anyone who wants to repent is barred. We do not know who is elect; we preach to all. And this is not a God arranging for people to be destroyed so that the scenery looks better. Watch where the weight of the sentence falls: on verse 23, on riches, on glory, on mercy prepared beforehand. Wrath is the thing God is said to endure. Mercy is the thing he is said to prepare.

Could the person I love be a vessel of wrath? You cannot know, and you are not asked to know. The categories are not visible, and the patience described here has not run out, not for the person you have given up on and not for you. Paul himself was once a persecutor who looked for all the world like a vessel of wrath, and God showed him mercy so that he might display his perfect patience as an example (1 Timothy 1:16). As long as it is called today, the enduring in verse 22 is a present tense, and so is the invitation. Your task is not to sort people but to pray for them and to tell them about Christ.

In a sentence. What if God, wanting to show his anger and make his power known, has been very patient with the objects of his wrath, ready for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory to the objects of his mercy, whom he prepared in advance for glory?

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a vessel of mercy, prepared for glory. Live like it, and be patient with sinners, as God was with you. Here is a test that takes about a minute. Work out roughly how long it was between the first thing you did that you knew was wrong and the day you came to Christ. Ten years. Thirty. Fifty. Whatever the number, that interval is much patience, measured from the inside. You are not being asked to accept the doctrine of divine forbearance as a proposition. You have already lived in it, for years, and were not consumed. That is not an argument. It is a receipt. So when someone tries your patience today, remember how long God endured you.

For worship. The darkness of judgment is the background against which the light of grace shines most brightly, and at the cross the two meet in one place: wrath fully shown, fully borne by the Son, so that vessels of mercy could be prepared for glory. The God who endures the rebellious with long patience, and who prepared his people for glory before they existed, is rich beyond telling. Blessed be his name, who did not consume us while we were still his enemies, and who will show the riches of his glory to us for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?
verseByVerse.commentary:
even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?

Even us whom he has called. The vessels of mercy are identified: we, whom God has effectually called (8:30). Election is not abstract. It shows in a real church, made of real people who were called by the gospel and came. And stand back to see what has happened to the sentence, because this is the moment the chapter has been travelling toward. For twenty verses everything has been in the third person: Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Moses, Pharaoh, a potter, a lump, two vessels. Ancient names, old quarrels, other people’s families, all safely at a distance, which is how most readers prefer this chapter. And then, without warning, Paul writes us. It lands like a hand on the shoulder. The vessels of mercy prepared beforehand for glory are not a category. They are the people in the room where this letter is being read aloud.

Called. The verb has been running quietly under the whole passage. Through Isaac shall your offspring be named, in Greek, called (v. 7). Not because of works but because of him who calls (v. 11). Called sons of the living God (v. 26). And in the previous chapter, those whom he predestined he also called (8:30). That thread matters for a practical reason. You cannot observe an eternal decree; there is no window into it, and staring at the place where the window should be has driven serious people to despair. But a call is a thing that happens in time, to a person, at an address. It leaves marks.

Not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles? God’s choice crosses the boundary of race. This brings Paul back to his question about Israel: God’s purpose never was to save every Jew, but to call out a people from Jews and Gentiles alike. The inclusion of the Gentiles is not a contingency plan after Israel’s rejection; it was always in the promise to Abraham, that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Notice too the preposition: called out of the Jews and out of the Gentiles. Out of both. Neither group is summoned wholesale. So the narrowing Paul described inside Israel at verse 6 is now running inside the Gentile world as well. There is no category anyone can join that carries him in. Any Gentile Christian who has been reading this chapter with quiet satisfaction about Israel has just been included in its terms, and Paul will tell him to his face: do not be arrogant toward the branches (11:18).

A church with a seam down the middle. Picture the room this was read in. The letter went to a congregation with a seam down the middle: Jewish believers who had been expelled from Rome under Claudius and had come back (Acts 18:2), and Gentile believers who had kept the church going in their absence. Two groups with real grievances, each with a private account of whom the church really belonged to. Into that room Paul sends a sentence that refuses to award it to either: us, called by him, out of the Jews and out of the Gentiles. The doctrine of election arrives in Romans not as a seminar topic but as the one thing capable of settling an argument about who sits where.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has abandoned the Jews. Paul himself is a Jew who was called. Chapter 11 will show there is still a remnant, and a future for Israel. Nor is it only about nations: Paul has spent his argument on peoples, and he ends it by pointing at a congregation of persons.

How do I know if I have been called? Look not for a voice but for a summons you have answered. God’s effectual call comes through the gospel: you heard the message about Christ, and something in you, against your old inclinations, found it true and came to him (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). If you now trust Christ, want to know him, and find yourself, however unevenly, turning from sin, those are the marks of the call. It may have been sudden or gradual; that does not matter. What matters is that you have come to Christ and are still coming. If you are unsure, do not stare at yourself. Answer the call now, and keep answering it.

In a sentence. Those objects of mercy include us, whom he called, not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Here is a small test, and it is more revealing than it sounds. Read verse 24 again and notice whether you instinctively counted yourself in the word us. Many people read Romans 9 as spectators: weighing its fairness, worrying about people they love, assessing God’s conduct from the gallery. Paul wrote it as a member. If the chapter has felt like a court case you are watching rather than a mercy you are inside, this verse is where the seating was assigned. Then look around your church at the different backgrounds and races, and the people you find hardest to sit beside. Each one was called by the same God. Treat them as fellow members of one family.

For worship. The chapter began with a man weeping because his own people would not come. It ends its argument by naming the people who did. And they turn out to be a mixed, unlikely, quarrelling congregation in the capital of the empire that would shortly kill him: called, out of both halves of a divided world, by the God who has been doing exactly this since Isaac. Praise him for his wide mercy, which reaches across every border, and for his particular call, which reached you by name.

verseByVerse.quote: As indeed he says in Hosea, "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved.'" "And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved.’” “And in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’”

As indeed he says in Hosea. Paul now shows that the Old Testament foretold both the calling of Gentiles (vv. 25–26) and the saving of only a remnant of Israel (vv. 27–29). He quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10. And these sentences have a history, one of the most painful in the prophets. Paul is not quoting an abstract principle. He is quoting the names of a man’s children.

Those who were not my people I will call “my people.” God told Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him, and he did, and she was. They had three children, and God named them. The second was a daughter: Lo-ruhamah, No Mercy, or not loved. The third was a son: Lo-ammi, Not My People (Hosea 1:6, 9). Stay with that a moment. A prophet stood in his doorway at dusk and called his daughter No Mercy and his son Not My People, every evening for years, in front of neighbours who knew exactly what the names were about. The sermon was his family. He had to live inside his own message. So when Paul quotes her who was not beloved I will call beloved, he is quoting a little girl’s name being taken off her. And that is the mechanism of the reversal. God does not hand out replacement names. He cancels the negative on the names already given. The lo comes off. No Mercy becomes Mercy. Not My People becomes My People.

How Paul uses Hosea. Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel, who by their idolatry had become like pagans. Paul applies the words to Gentiles. This is not misuse. Israel had become like the nations, and so the principle is the same: God can make a people out of those who are not a people, by sheer grace. If God can re-people the un-peopled, he can also people the never-peopled. Peter applies the same words to Gentile believers, independently: once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people (1 Peter 2:10). Two apostles, one prophet, the same move.

And in the very place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they will be called “sons of the living God.” God’s grace reaches the very place of rejection and makes outsiders sons. This is adoption. Not somewhere else, not after a relocation or a fresh start in a town where nobody knows. In the same place. At the same address where the disowning was announced, the renaming happens. Most of us would prefer the other arrangement; we would rather God restored us somewhere new, where the story is not known. He tends instead to do it in the room where it happened, in front of the same people. And notice how high the promise climbs. It would have been enough to say my people again. Hosea says sons of the living God: not merely readmitted, but family, and the God whose sons they are is the living one, over against the dead idols they had left him for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the northern tribes have no part in the promise; Hosea’s words are fulfilled in the church made up of Jews and Gentiles. Nor does it mean the old names were cruel mistakes. Israel really had gone after other gods; the names were true when they were given. That is exactly why this passage can bear weight that mere reassurance cannot. God is not saying you were never really that. He is saying you were, and you are not now. A verdict has been reversed, not a misprint corrected.

What did the renaming cost? Everything, and Hosea shows it. God sent him back to buy his wife out of what she had sold herself into, and Scripture records the price, down to the barley (Hosea 3:2). That is the shape of every renaming God does: somebody goes and pays for the one who left. Hosea was rehearsing, in a small way and at his own cost, what it would take. The final price was paid by Christ, who was treated as not God’s Son on the cross, forsaken, so that those who were not God’s people could be called sons of the living God (Galatians 4:4–5). Your new name is free to you because it was not free to him.

In a sentence. As God says in Hosea, he will call those who were not his people his people, and her who was not loved his beloved; and in the very place where they were told they were not his people, there they will be called children of the living God.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that needs a pen rather than a feeling. Write down the sentence you believe is truest about yourself when you are not performing for anyone, the one that surfaces when the house is quiet. Most people find it is a name of some kind, and often it is one of these two: not wanted, or not forgiven. Then put beside it the name God gives everyone in Christ: beloved, my people, a child of the living God. Do not argue that the old name was never true. Agree that it was, and that God has taken the not off it. Then live today under the new name, among the very people who knew the old one.

For worship. The argument of this chapter arrives at a doorway in eighth-century Israel, with a man calling his children names that were true, and a God who came back for all three of them. If mercy can reach that house, the question of whether it can reach Rome or you is already settled. You were once not my people. Now you are called a child of the living God. Blessed be the Father who renames the disowned, and the Son who paid the price of our homecoming.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea spoke of the northern tribes of Israel; Paul applies the words to the Gentiles too.

parallels.desc: I will say to Not My People, “You are my people”

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: "Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”

And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel. “Cries out” (krazei) is the word for a shout, a raised voice, urgent prophetic proclamation. Paul changes his verb: two verses ago it was simply he says in Hosea; two verses later it will be as Isaiah predicted. Here Isaiah cries out. Paul is telling you how the sentence sounded. This is not a prophet reading out a projection. It is a man raising his voice about his own nation. Paul quotes Isaiah 10:22–23, mainly from the Greek translation.

A boy named Remnant. There is a reason Isaiah of all people had to shout this one. He had a son called Shear-jashub, which means a remnant shall return (Isaiah 7:3). God had him take the boy along to meet the king, so that the king had to look at the child and hear the name. That is the second time in four verses that Paul has quoted a prophet whose children were the sermon. Hosea’s were the judgment; Isaiah’s was the hope. But the hope came in a form that cut both ways. A remnant shall return can be read with the stress on either word, and both readings are true. Only a remnant: that is the threat. A remnant shall return: that is the promise. To a man secure in his numbers and his ancestry, the word is only. To a man who has counted the faithful and thinks he has reached the end of them, the word is a remnant: there is one.

Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea. An echo of God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Israel became numerous, as promised. Isaiah is not cancelling that promise. Paul is not saying the multitude promised to Abraham was cancelled and replaced by a handful; he is saying the multitude was never going to arrive by descent. Where that finally goes is chapter 11, and this verse is not his last word on it.

Only a remnant of them will be saved. The remnant (hypoleimma): a small number preserved through judgment. In Isaiah, only a remnant returned from the Assyrian disaster. The principle runs through the Old Testament, from Noah to Elijah’s seven thousand (11:4). So the fact that most Jews have rejected Christ is not a surprise; the prophets foretold it. And read the sentence just before the one Paul quotes, because it defines the remnant: a remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God (Isaiah 10:21). The remnant is not defined by having survived. It is defined by having returned to God.

For the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay. God will do what he has said, decisively. His word of judgment and of salvation will be accomplished. The Greek of this line is genuinely difficult, and the translations pull in different directions; it is honest to say so. The sense is that God will bring his word to completion and will not let it drag. There is mercy even in that. A sentence carried out decisively is not the same as one deferred indefinitely. God does not leave a people suspended for centuries in a judgment that never arrives and never lifts.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the remnant were saved because they were better. Chapter 11 says it is a remnant chosen by grace (11:5). And remnant language is the most easily corrupted in Scripture. It is the natural vocabulary of every small, embattled, self-congratulating group that has decided everyone else has compromised. Look at what Isaiah’s remnant actually is: survivors of a catastrophe, people who came out of a burning country with nothing, whose only distinction is that God kept them. There is not a syllable of achievement in it. The moment remnant becomes a compliment you pay yourself, it has stopped describing you.

Our church is small. Does that mean we are the faithful remnant? Not necessarily, and the question itself can be a trap. Size proves nothing either way. Large churches can be faithful and small ones proud, and the reverse. A small congregation that is preaching Christ faithfully can take comfort from this verse: God has often worked through few, and he is keeping his word. But it must never become a badge, as if being few made you better. The remnant is marked not by smallness but by returning to God, by grace alone. Be faithful, pray for growth, and leave the counting to God.

In a sentence. And Isaiah cries out about Israel that even if the Israelites are as many as the sand on the seashore, only a remnant will be saved, for the Lord will carry out his sentence on the earth with speed and finality.

On a Tuesday. Do not measure God’s faithfulness by numbers. Even when the faithful are few, God is keeping his word. And here is a test sharper than counting heads. Do not ask whether you are among the few. Ask whether you have returned. Plenty of people stay: they never leave the building, never renounce anything, and their name is on a roll somewhere. Staying and returning are not the same act, and only one of them is what Isaiah means. If you have drifted, today is a day to return.

For worship. Isaiah had to shout this over a crowd who did not want to hear it, and then go home to a boy he could not call in for supper without saying the doctrine aloud. Paul, holding the same truth, has already told you what it costs him. And through it all God was keeping a remnant for himself, not one of whom earned his place, and bringing his word to completion without delay. Blessed be the mighty God to whom the remnant returns, who never lets his promise fail for want of numbers, and who in Christ is gathering a people more than the sand of the sea.

parallels.desc: only a remnant will return

verseByVerse.quote: And as Isaiah predicted, "If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”

And as Isaiah predicted. Paul quotes Isaiah 1:9, the final scriptural witness of the section.

If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring. “Lord of hosts” (Sabaōth, from the Hebrew): the Lord of the armies of heaven, all-powerful. And look at the grammar, because it is not the sentence people think they are reading. This is a counterfactual. If the Lord had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom. It is not a lament about how few were kept. It is a statement about what did not happen. That changes the whole chapter. Everything up to here has pressed a question about the people who were passed over. Isaiah asks the other question, the one that is rarely asked: why is there anybody here at all? He is not standing outside the disaster, counting survivors and finding the number disappointing. He is standing in the wreckage, one of the survivors, saying we should not be here.

Offspring. The word is sperma, seed, and it is the hinge of the verse. Not survivors, not remains. A remnant is what is left over when something has been consumed. A seed is what is put into the ground on purpose. One word looks back at a loss; the other looks forward to a harvest. Isaiah is not saying God salvaged a few. He is saying God planted. And that is why Paul ends the argument with this citation rather than the sterner one from Isaiah 10. He has spent the chapter on the freedom of God, and he closes the section on a word that means a future.

We would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah. The cities wiped out completely for their sin (Genesis 19). Israel deserved the same. That any survived at all was God’s mercy alone. And the comparison is far more brutal than a modern reader hears, because we treat Sodom as a byword for somebody else. Read one verse further in Isaiah and you find out whom he is addressing: Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom! Give ear to the teaching of our God, you people of Gomorrah! (Isaiah 1:10). He is calling Jerusalem Sodom, to its face. The temple was operating; the sacrifices were offered; and the prophet addresses the congregation by the name of the city God rained fire on. So the difference between Jerusalem and Sodom, on Isaiah’s own account, was not the behaviour. It was that one had seed left in it and the other did not. Abraham pleaded and could not find ten righteous men in Sodom. Lot was pulled out by the hand. Sodom is what a place looks like when nothing has been kept back: no seed, no next generation, no morning after.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the remnant is a reason for pride. The point is the opposite: without God’s mercy, no one would be left. And this verse can be turned into the cheapest thing in religion, the comparison with people who are worse. Isaiah forecloses it in the next breath by calling his own congregation Sodom. Nobody is being ranked here. Everybody is being reprieved, and the reprieve is the only distinction anyone in the sentence has.

Does this mean the church today is only kept alive by God? Yes, and that is a comfort, not a threat. Every generation of believers exists because the Lord of hosts has left a seed. The church has survived persecution, heresy and its own failures not because it was strong but because Christ said he would build it and the gates of hell would not prevail (Matthew 16:18). When you see churches shrinking or a nation turning from God, do not despair as though the gospel were dying out. God has never let his seed be wiped out, and he will not now. Pray, and keep sowing.

In a sentence. As Isaiah said before, unless the Lord Almighty had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that uses the verse’s own grammar. Take a sheet of paper and finish Isaiah’s sentence about yourself: If the Lord of hosts had not left me ______, I would have been ______. Most people can complete it faster than they expect, and the naming matters. A friend who would not give up on you. A church you nearly walked out of. A conscience that would not settle. An illness that stopped you at the exact moment you were about to do the irreparable thing. What the exercise does is move the accounting. Left to ourselves we audit the deficit: the years wasted, the people not saved, the smallness of what remains. Isaiah audits the reprieve. Both are honest arithmetic; only one of them is the arithmetic of someone who knows what he escaped.

For worship. The section that began with a man swearing that he could not stop grieving ends with a prophet saying we should not be alive. Between those two sentences stand the potter and Pharaoh and the vessels and the hardest questions in the letter. And the last word is not a verdict on the lost. It is a seed in the ground. Without God’s mercy we would all be Sodom. Blessed be the Lord of hosts, who always leaves a seed, who planted his own Son in the ground like a grain of wheat, and from that one seed is raising a harvest no one can number.

parallels.desc: if the LORD of hosts had not left us a few survivors

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–33 — The Stumbling Stone: Israel's Pursuit and Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter ends with a turn from theology to history. The Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, have attained it — by faith. Israel, which pursued the law of righteousness, did not attain it — because they pursued it as if it were by works rather than by faith. They stumbled over the stumbling stone: Christ. The stone God laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) was meant to be the foundation of Israel's hope; it became the obstacle over which they fell.

The irony is complete. The people who had every advantage — every covenant privilege, the law, the promises, the patriarchs — failed to reach what the people with no advantage attained. The reason is not their lack of zeal (Paul will say in 10:2 that they have zeal, but not according to knowledge) but their misdirection: seeking a righteousness of their own rather than the righteousness of God. The stumbling stone is not a surprise or a trap; it is the very cornerstone that God announced. But it requires faith to receive it as such.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Stone and the Two Ways

The stone of Romans 9:33 is used in the New Testament as a central Christological image (cf. 1 Peter 2:6–8, Matthew 21:42–44). Christ is simultaneously the cornerstone (the secure foundation for all who believe) and the stumbling stone (the cause of fall for all who refuse). The same Christ who is salvation to the one who believes is judgment to the one who will not. The gospel is never neutral; it is always either the savour of life or the savour of death (2 Corinthians 2:16). There is no third option.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's pursuit of righteousness by works was not insincere. It was zealous and disciplined. But zeal misdirected is more dangerous than apathy, because it produces a confidence in one's own religious achievement that closes the hand against the gift of grace. Now: The same dynamic plays out in every religious context. The most difficult people to bring to genuine faith are often the most religious — those who have so much invested in their own righteousness that they cannot bring themselves to stand before God empty-handed and receive what only grace can give.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.

What shall we say, then? Paul now turns from God’s sovereignty to human responsibility. Both are true. Election explains why some believe; unbelief explains why others are lost. This section runs to the end of chapter 10.

That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it. A paradox. “Pursue” (diōkō) is a hunting or racing word, to chase something down; “attain” is to overtake it and lay hold of it. The Gentiles were not chasing a right standing with God, yet they caught it. Paul ruled out the runner back at verse 16; here he shows you the race itself, and the result board makes no sense. The people standing at the finish are the ones who never entered. They were not in training, not on the track, but somewhere else entirely, doing the things chapter 1 described. And they are across the line.

That is, a righteousness that is by faith. The righteousness of chapters 3–4: God’s gift of a right standing, received by faith in Christ. The Gentiles did not run a better race. They did not run at all. They were handed the prize at the moment they stopped being the sort of people anyone would have bet on, which is the only way anyone has ever received it.

But that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Israel ran hard after righteousness through the law, and failed to reach it. The irony: the ones who tried hardest missed, because they ran on the wrong track. The athletes who trained for fifteen centuries, who knew the course better than anyone alive, who had the rules and the records of every runner before them, are still out on the track, and the race is over. And look closely at how Paul words it, because the oddity is deliberate. He does not say Israel pursued righteousness and failed to reach righteousness. He says they pursued a law and did not reach that law. The object changes at the end of the sentence. The people who studied it, memorised it, fenced it about with further rules and died rather than break it, did not get to the law. The law had a destination of its own, and they never reached it, because its destination was a person and they were treating it as a syllabus. Paul will say it outright in a few verses: Christ is the end of the law (10:4).

Not a lack of zeal. The diagnosis is never insincerity. Paul says plainly in the next chapter that they have a zeal for God (10:2). He had it himself, more than any of them, and he used it to arrest Christians. And here is the uncomfortable practical edge, which every pastor eventually learns. Misdirected zeal is harder to reach than apathy. The indifferent man has nothing invested. The devout man has forty years invested, and every one of those years argues against the one thing being asked of him. It is often not the person who has never entered a church who finds grace impossible. It is the person who has not missed a Sunday in fifty years, because to receive righteousness as a gift he has to agree that the fifty years bought him nothing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean effort is bad, or that the law was a bad goal. The law itself pointed to Christ (10:4). The problem was the way they pursued it. Paul is not against effort; he ran hard, and he is about to spend four chapters urging obedience in detail. The problem was never that Israel tried. It was what they were trying to produce. A man can sprint with great discipline in a direction that does not lead anywhere, and his discipline is not the fault.

How can I tell if I am pursuing righteousness by works? Ask what you are resting on when you come to God. If your confidence before him rises after a good week and collapses after a bad one, you are probably trusting your performance. If you think God owes you something for your faithfulness, or you look down on less disciplined Christians, the same root is showing. Faith rests on Christ’s righteousness, credited to you, which does not change with your week. That does not make you careless; it frees you to obey out of gratitude rather than fear. The remedy is not to try less but to look away from yourself to Christ every day.

In a sentence. What then shall we conclude? That Gentiles, who were not seeking righteousness, have received it, the righteousness that comes by faith; but Israel, who chased a law that would bring righteousness, did not attain it.

On a Tuesday. Religious effort cannot win God’s approval. Stop running on the wrong track, and receive Christ’s righteousness as a gift. Then test how you actually experience the Christian life. Is it a distance still to be covered, ground you are making up, a verdict still ahead of you? Or is it an address you already live at? Both kinds of Christian work hard, and from outside you cannot tell them apart. But one is running toward acceptance and the other is running from it, and the difference shows the first time you have a really bad week. If never arriving is your settled experience of God, verse 31 is not describing an ancient nation. It is describing your Tuesday.

For worship. The finish line was crossed long before any of us arrived, by the one runner who kept the law perfectly and reached its end, because he is its end. Christ ran the whole course in our place, and his righteousness is handed to the outsiders and the exhausted alike, to all who stop running for it and simply receive it. Blessed be the God who gives the prize to those who never entered, and who welcomes the weary athletes too, the moment they lay down their efforts at the feet of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. The reason. Israel treated the law as a ladder of works to climb up to God, rather than receiving his promise by faith. “As if”: works were never the true way. Even in the Old Testament, people were justified by faith (4:1–8). And notice the first word, because the whole chapter has been building to it. Why? Paul asks for a reason, and the reason he gives is not the potter, not the hidden will of God, not the clay’s lack of standing. It lies squarely in Israel. Twelve verses ago Paul refused to answer the question of fault by argument, and that refusal stands. But it was not his last word. Here, at the end of the same chapter, Paul names a cause for Israel’s fall, and the cause is what Israel did.

They have stumbled over the stumbling stone. The stumbling stone is Christ. A crucified Messiah offended them (1 Corinthians 1:23). He tells them their works cannot save; that is the offence. And the difficulty was not merely that a crucified Messiah was undignified or disappointing. Deuteronomy 21:23 says that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God. So a crucified Messiah was not a lowered expectation; it was a contradiction in terms. The one thing the Christ could not possibly be was accursed. Except that this is exactly what the chapter opened with. At verse 3 Paul wished he could be accursed and cut off for his people, and could not. The stone they tripped over is the one person who could do the thing Paul wanted to do, and did it. What made him unthinkable to them is the whole reason he is any use to anybody.

As it is written. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion) with Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling). The same stone is a foundation for those who trust it and a stumbling block for those who do not. Peter uses the same combination (1 Peter 2:6–8). The splice is the argument. In Isaiah 8 the LORD himself becomes a sanctuary and a stone of offence in the same breath. One stone, sanctuary and obstacle; the difference is not in the masonry but in the approach. Picture what a foundation stone at a doorway does. Come to it as a threshold and it takes your weight and holds you up for the rest of your life. Come at it in the dark, at speed, looking elsewhere, and it takes your feet from under you. The stone has not moved. And notice the word laid: God says I am laying it. It was not rubble in the road, nor a trap set for the unwary. It was placed, deliberately, in Zion, at the front of the building, where nobody could get in without meeting it.

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Believing in him is the way. Not put to shame means never disappointed or disgraced at the judgment. “Whoever” opens the door to anyone, Jew or Gentile. This leads into chapter 10, where everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved. After twenty-eight verses of narrowing, it is the widest sentence in the chapter. Count what is not in it: no lineage, no prior standing, no evidence of having been chosen. It is the one sentence in Romans 9 that a frightened reader can act on directly, and Paul has deliberately put it last. And shame is the word Paul used of himself at the start of the letter: I am not ashamed of the gospel (1:16). He was not making a brave noise. He was stating what this stone does for those who trust it: shame is the very thing it takes away.

Where Christians differ: sovereignty and responsibility. Some think that if God elects, human responsibility vanishes; others think that if humans are responsible, God cannot be fully sovereign. Verdict: Paul holds both in the same chapter without apology. Israel’s unbelief is truly their fault (vv. 30–33; 10:21), and salvation is truly God’s sovereign mercy (vv. 6–24). We cannot fully reconcile them in our minds, but Scripture teaches both, and we must too (Westminster 3.1; Acts 2:23). Sovereign mercy is why anyone is in. Unbelief is why anyone is out. A reader who can only carry one of them will misrepresent Paul whichever one he keeps.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ is a trap. He is offered as a foundation to all. Only those who refuse him stumble over him. And whoever means whoever. It is not a trick sentence with a hidden condition for those who turn out to have been chosen. Paul, who has just written the most uncompromising paragraph on election in the Bible, ends it by throwing the door open and standing back.

If God chooses, can I be sure the invitation is really for me? Yes. The promise says whoever believes, and God does not make offers he does not mean. You are never asked to find out first whether you are elect and then believe; you are asked to believe, and in believing you will discover that you were chosen. Jesus said that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). Election is the reason anyone comes, not a barrier at the door. If you want Christ, nothing in God’s decree stands between you and him. Come, and you will not be put to shame.

In a sentence. Why? Because they sought it by works, not by faith. They tripped over the stumbling stone, as Scripture says: God is placing in Zion a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall, and the one who believes in him will never be put to shame.

On a Tuesday. Everybody has an answer to this test. Name your stone. There is something about Christ that you have to get past rather than merely accept: his exclusive claim, the wrath in chapter 1, the cross itself, or the requirement to arrive with nothing in your hands after a lifetime of being competent. Now notice what this verse says about that stone. It was laid. It is not an unfortunate obstruction on the way to God which you must edge around to reach him. It is the foundation. The thing you are stumbling over is not in front of the door. It is the door. Build on Christ the cornerstone today, and let go of whatever you were carrying to earn your place.

For worship. The chapter that began with a man weeping ends with a stone and an invitation. In between are Pharaoh and the potter and the vessels and every hard question a reader can ask. And Paul’s final word is not a verdict on anybody. It is an offer with no name on it, addressed to whoever will have it. The builders looked at the stone, could not see a use for it, and threw it aside (Psalm 118:22). It is holding up everything. Blessed be Christ, the precious cornerstone laid by God in Zion, who was made a curse that we might never be put to shame, and on whom every one who trusts him stands secure for ever.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

9.text: <sup>1</sup>I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit—<sup>2</sup>that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.<sup>3</sup>For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.<sup>5</sup>To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!<sup>15</sup>For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”<sup>16</sup>So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.<sup>17</sup>For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”<sup>18</sup>So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills.<sup>19</sup>You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is molded say to its molder, “Why have you made me like this?”<sup>21</sup>Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?<sup>22</sup>What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,<sup>23</sup>in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory—<sup>24</sup>even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles?<sup>25</sup>As indeed he says in Hosea, “Those who were not my people I will call ’my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ’beloved.’”<sup>26</sup>“And in the very place where it was said to them, ’You are not my people,’ there they will be called ’sons of the living God.’”<sup>27</sup>And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will be saved,<sup>28</sup>for the Lord will carry out his sentence upon the earth fully and without delay.”<sup>29</sup>And as Isaiah predicted, “If the Lord of hosts had not left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah.”<sup>30</sup>What shall we say, then? That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith;<sup>31</sup>but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law.<sup>32</sup>Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,<sup>33</sup>as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 moves from the theology of election (chapter 9) to the human experience of faith and the missionary imperative of proclamation. Paul's pastoral heart is again on display: his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is their salvation. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but a misdirection of it — a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, a pursuit of their own righteousness that refuses to submit to the righteousness of God.

The great passage of vv. 9–15 moves from confession and faith to calling on the name of the Lord to preachers sent with good news — a chain that runs from individual conversion back to the sovereign act of apostolic commissioning. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through preachers who are sent, who go, who speak. The chapter ends with the sobering testimony of Israel's own scriptures: they have heard, they have understood, and they have not believed. The tragedy of unbelief is complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's pastoral longing for Israel's salvation (v. 1) is the emotional key to the chapter. He is not writing as a detached analyst of Israel's religious failure; he is writing as a broken-hearted brother who knows exactly what his people are missing and cannot stop praying for them. The diagnosis is precise: "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Zeal without knowledge is not a small problem; it is perhaps the most dangerous religious condition possible, because it generates confident misdirection.

The contrast between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith (vv. 5–8) draws on Deuteronomy 30, where Moses speaks of God's word as near to the people — not beyond the sea, not in the heights of heaven, but in their mouths and in their hearts. Paul identifies this nearness with the gospel: "the word of faith that we proclaim." The righteousness of God is not a distant achievement to be scaled by heroic effort; it is a near word to be received by confession and faith.

Two verses stand between the diagnosis and that contrast, and they should not be passed over. They are the hinge of the chapter. Israel, Paul says, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, did not submit to God’s righteousness (v. 3).

Watch the sequence, because it is a clinical description of how a religious life goes wrong. First not knowing what God was offering; then setting about producing a version of it themselves; and finally — the word that makes it a moral matter rather than a misunderstanding — refusing to submit.

That verb is the surprise. One does not expect righteousness to be something a person submits to. But a righteousness that arrives as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is precisely what a competent, disciplined, self-respecting person finds hardest. The offence of the gospel is not that it asks too much. It is that it will not let you contribute.

Then v. 4, which the chapter cannot do without: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The word is telos, and it carries both senses at once — the terminus and the goal, where a road stops and what it was built to reach.

Both are true here and neither should be dropped. As a route to righteousness the law has come to its end, because the destination has arrived. And it was always heading there; Christ is not an alternative to the law but the thing it was pointing at, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that he does not overthrow the law but upholds it (3:31).

Note also the last clause, because it is the one that opens the door: to everyone who believes. The universal that will ring three times in vv. 11-13 has already sounded here, before the famous verses begin.

Verses 9–13 are among the most frequently memorised in Paul's letters — "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." The simplicity is staggering. Two things: confession of lordship, belief in resurrection. Both are the expression of the same faith. And the word "all" rings three times: everyone who believes (v. 11), everyone who calls (v. 13), for he is Lord of all and bestows riches on all who call (v. 12). The gospel has no ethnic or social exclusion clause.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Confession of Lordship
