Romans 10:9 makes the confession "Jesus is Lord" (Kyrios Iēsous) the central act of Christian profession. In the first-century Roman world, "Kyrios" was the title of Caesar — the one to whom ultimate allegiance was owed. To confess "Jesus is Lord" was therefore not merely a theological statement but a political one: Jesus, not Caesar, holds ultimate authority over my life. The early church was often persecuted for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord" — because they had already given that title to another. Every true Christian confession has this political dimension: it declares a transfer of ultimate allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses's vision of the nearness of God's word (Deuteronomy 30) had originally been given to Israel on the plains of Moab, just before they entered the land — as a word of covenant accessibility. God was not hiding himself; he had given his word and it was near. Paul's application to the gospel makes the same point: the righteousness of God is not a distant achievement but a near word, proclaimed by apostles, received by faith. Now: The simplicity of Romans 10:9 is the permanent rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. Salvation does not require a theology degree, a track record of spiritual achievement, or a passage through elaborate ritual. It requires the honest confession of a changed allegiance and the genuine belief in a historical resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Meaning first. Romans 10 continues the explanation of Israel’s unbelief that began in 9:30, now from the human side. Chapter 9 showed God’s sovereign choice; chapter 10 shows Israel’s responsibility. Israel was zealous, but sought to establish its own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s righteousness, which comes in Christ, the end of the law (vv. 1–4). The righteousness of faith is not a hard climb to heaven or a deep dive into the grave: Christ has already come down and risen up. It is near, in the gospel word: confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him, and you will be saved, whether Jew or Greek, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (vv. 5–13). But calling requires believing, believing requires hearing, and hearing requires preachers who are sent (vv. 14–17). Israel has heard, and has understood enough to be guilty, while Gentiles who were not looking have found God, who still stretches out his hands all day long to his stubborn people (vv. 18–21). Election never makes preaching unnecessary; it makes it hopeful.

Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. Right after the strongest teaching on election in the Bible, Paul prays for the salvation of unbelieving Jews. Chapter 9 ended on a stone laid in Zion and a nation tripping over it, and the very next thing Paul does is pray for them. He does not finish the argument and move to another subject; he finishes the argument and goes to his knees about it. That pays off what he began at 9:2–3. There it was grief. Through 9:6–29 it was doctrine, the hardest in the letter. Here it is prayer, and by 11:23 it will be hope. Four movements, one man, no contradiction between any of them. Election does not make prayer pointless. God ordains the means as well as the end, and prayer is one of his means.

Heart’s desire. The phrase is stronger than English usually carries. It is eudokia: good pleasure, delight, the thing you would choose if you could have whatever you wanted. It is the word used elsewhere of God’s own good pleasure (Ephesians 1:5, 9). Paul’s delight, the outcome he would pick above every other, is that these people should be saved. Not that they should be answered, or proved wrong, which was well within his powers and would have been satisfying. Saved. And notice whom he is talking to. Brothers, and the church in Rome was by now largely Gentile. Paul is asking a mostly non-Jewish congregation to care about Israel’s salvation, and he does it by opening his own heart rather than by issuing an instruction. In one chapter he will warn these same readers not to be arrogant toward the branches that were broken off (11:18). The work of that warning starts here.

For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God. Courtroom language: Paul appears for the defence. He is not conceding a point about opponents; he is testifying to something he knows at first hand. This is the man who advanced in Judaism beyond many of his own age, being extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Galatians 1:14), and who listed among his credentials, as to zeal, a persecutor of the church (Philippians 3:6; Acts 22:3–4). When Paul writes of zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, he is not describing a category of person. He is describing himself at thirty. That is what keeps the verse from contempt. He is not a man who never had the disease diagnosing people who do. He is a survivor of it, and he remembers exactly how right it felt.

But not according to knowledge. Knowledge here is epignōsis, true, full understanding. Sincerity is not enough. Zeal without truth can drive people hard in the wrong direction. And this is genuinely frightening: it is possible to be sincere, disciplined, costly, lifelong and wrong. Israel’s zeal was not a pose; it produced martyrs. Paul’s zeal was not a pose; it produced arrest warrants and a coat held at a stoning. Sincerity is real, and sincerity is not a saving category, and the two sentences must be held together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is wrong, or that sincere people are saved because they are sincere. Paul’s point is that sincere, zealous people can be lost if they reject God’s way of righteousness. Nor does it license contempt for people of other convictions, as though they were simply stupid. Paul credits their zeal, bears witness to it, and wants them saved rather than defeated. A Christian who uses verse 2 to feel superior has managed to extract contempt from a verse written in tears. And the cure is not cool accuracy instead of hot error. The man who diagnoses misdirected passion puts his heart’s desire at the front of the sentence. The remedy for zeal without knowledge has never been knowledge without zeal.

If God has already chosen, why should I pray for someone’s salvation? Because God has chosen to work through prayer, and he commands it (1 Timothy 2:1–4). Election is God’s purpose; prayer is one of the means by which he carries it out, just as preaching is. You do not know whom God has chosen, so you pray for everyone you love, as Paul did for a people who had rejected the gospel. And election is what makes such prayer hopeful. If salvation depended on the sinner’s own will, praying for a hardened heart would be useless. Because it depends on God, who can open any heart, no one is beyond his reach.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul’s deepest longing and prayer to God for the Jews is that they be saved, for he can testify that they are zealous for God, but their zeal is not based on true knowledge.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the salvation of those you know, even when you believe God is sovereign. Especially then: he is able to answer. And here is a test more useful than asking whether you are sincere, since you already know you are. When did you last change your mind about something in your faith because Scripture required it and not because it suited you? Zeal that is according to knowledge can be corrected, because it answers to something outside itself. Zeal without knowledge has no way of revising itself; it can only grow warmer. If nothing in your convictions has moved in twenty years, that is not necessarily faithfulness. It may only mean nothing has been allowed to speak.

For worship. Remember how Paul’s own case was resolved. Nobody argued him out of it. He was not shown a better system or told he was over-committed. He was stopped on a road and shown, in person, the one he had been so zealous against, and the first thing he asked was who it was he had been fighting. Zeal without knowledge is not cured by having less zeal. It is cured by meeting the one you were serving so badly. Blessed be the risen Lord, who stops persecutors on the road, turns their fury into love, and fills their hearts with desire for the salvation of the very people they once were.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God. Not ignorant that God is righteous, but of the righteousness that God gives, the gift of right standing revealed in the gospel (1:17; 3:21–22). They did not understand that God himself provides the righteousness he demands. Take the three verbs of verse 3 in order, because Paul has built a diagnosis and the sequence is the point: they were ignorant, they sought to establish, they did not submit. Ignorant is the mildest and the most surprising, because these were not people who had neglected the subject. They were the most literate religious community in the ancient world, entrusted with the oracles of God (3:2). The word is not about stupidity. It is about failing to recognise something that was in front of them.

And seeking to establish their own. “Establish” (histēmi) means set up, make stand, like building a monument. Their own righteousness: a record of law-keeping that they hoped would stand before God (Philippians 3:9). Hold that verb against the one at the end of the sentence: submit, to place yourself underneath. They are two entirely different physical actions. One is a man putting up a structure with his own name on it. The other is a man getting under something somebody else built. You cannot do both at once, and it is not chiefly a failure of understanding that stops a man doing the second. It is that he has spent thirty years on the first and it is nearly finished.

What it looks like from inside. The verse describes something more ordinary than villainy. Picture the man Paul has in mind. He tithes. He has never been unfaithful to his wife. He looks after his mother, keeps his word, gives to people in need, and has not missed a service in eleven years, and every bit of that is genuinely good. Ask him what stands between him and God and he will not sneer at grace or deny that he needs mercy. He will simply begin, somewhere in his answer, to describe himself. That is what establishing your own righteousness looks like from the inside. It does not feel like arrogance. It feels like diligence.

They did not submit to God’s righteousness. Receiving a gift requires humility. To accept God’s righteousness, you must admit you have none of your own. Pride refuses.

For Christ is the end of the law. “End” is telos, which can mean the termination, or the goal and fulfilment. The ESV note mentions that it can mean the goal. English forces a choice the Greek does not. The picture that holds both is a finishing tape. It ends the race, so that nobody runs on past it, and it is also the whole reason the race was run. It is not the opposite of the track. It is what the track was for.

For righteousness to everyone who believes. The law as a way of earning righteousness ends at Christ. Everyone who believes receives righteousness in him. Notice the qualifier that keeps this from becoming lawlessness: the end of the law for righteousness. It is the law’s role as the route to a right standing that has ended, not the law as God’s word, nor its power to show you what you are. Nobody is being told to stop reading Leviticus. They are being told to stop trying to climb it. Paul has already ruled out the other reading: do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law (3:31).

Where Christians differ: end or goal. Some take telos to mean that the law is entirely finished for Christians, with no ongoing role. Others take it to mean only that the law pointed to Christ. Verdict: Both senses are present, and they belong together. Christ is the goal the law aimed at: its sacrifices, promises and demands all pointed to him (3:21; Galatians 3:24). And so he is the end of the law as a way to gain righteousness: for everyone who believes, the attempt to be justified by law-keeping is over. But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains the rule of life for the believer, fulfilled by those who walk by the Spirit (8:4; 13:8–10; Westminster 19.5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may live lawlessly (6:15). The law no longer condemns believers, but it still shows them how to love. Nor does it make your week irrelevant; Paul is about to spend chapters 12 to 15 on how to live. What has changed is what the week is for. It is no longer material for a structure. It is the response of someone who has been given a home.

If I am not saved by keeping the law, why should I try to obey? Because obedience is now the fruit of salvation, not its price. You do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because you have been accepted, out of love for the one who saved you (John 14:15). The law shows a believer what love looks like, and the Spirit gives the desire and power to walk in it (8:4). And obedience is good for you: God’s commands are the instructions of a wise Father, not the hoops of a suspicious examiner. A justified person who does not care to obey has not understood what he has been given (6:1–2).

In a sentence. Because they did not know the righteousness that comes from God and tried to set up their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the culmination of the law, so that there is righteousness for everyone who believes.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test quicker than an examination of your motives. Finish this sentence without thinking too hard: I would say I have had a good week with God if I had ______. Most of us can complete it instantly, and the answer is almost always a list of activities: prayed more, read more, been more patient, not lost my temper on Wednesday. Notice what that list is. It is a set of scaffolding poles, the honest shape of a man still building, and it survives in people whose doctrine of grace is entirely correct. Give up building your own monument. Christ is your righteousness. Rest in him, and let this week’s obedience be thanks, not construction.

For worship. If Christ is the end, then the project is not merely unnecessary. It is over. There is nothing left to establish, and the only thing you can do with a finished building is put down the tools. The exhaustion of religious people is very rarely caused by their sins. It is caused by a construction project that God ended long ago. The tragedy of verse 3 is not that Israel wanted righteousness too little. It is that they wanted it enough to spend a nation’s history building one, while God held out a finished one the whole time. Blessed be Christ, who kept the law to the end and became the righteousness of everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law. Paul contrasts two ways of righteousness, both described by Moses. And notice whom Paul sets against Moses: not himself. Both quotations in this paragraph come from Moses. The contrast is not apostle against lawgiver; it is the lawgiver stating the terms, and the same lawgiver describing a word that comes near without anyone having to go and fetch it.

That the person who does the commandments shall live by them. From Leviticus 18:5. Paul quotes it also in Galatians 3:12. The principle of law: do, and live. Take it straight, because Paul is not accusing Moses of a trick. It is a genuine offer, and the terms are honourable. The law is not a trap laid to make people fail. The difficulty was never the offer. It was the doer. If you kept the law perfectly, you would live. But no sinner can (3:20; Galatians 3:10). So as a way to life, the law brings only death to sinners.

But the righteousness based on faith says. Paul personifies the righteousness of faith, letting it speak. It speaks words from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, where Moses told Israel that God’s word was not far off or too hard: it was near, in their mouth and heart. And Paul is not raiding Deuteronomy out of context, which is the usual charge. Look at where chapter 30 stands. It comes after the covenant curses of chapter 28, after the exile has been described in advance, and straight after God promises to circumcise the hearts of his people so that they will love him and live (Deuteronomy 30:6). The nearness Moses speaks of belongs to a passage about restoration after failure and about surgery performed by God on the human heart. Paul is reading Deuteronomy 30 where it actually sits.

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down). “Do not say in your heart” echoes Deuteronomy 9:4, where Moses warned Israel not to think God gave them the land because of their righteousness, and 8:17, where he forbade them to say, my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth. It is a formula aimed at private thoughts, the sentence nobody speaks aloud. So it is worth asking what that sentence sounds like now. Almost nobody says who will ascend into heaven? in those words. Its modern form is short, and most Christians have said it this month: there must be something more I have to do. That is the ascent: hearing the gospel, believing it in principle, and then quietly assembling a ladder, more discipline, more feeling, a better run of weeks, as though Christ needed fetching down and the fetching were your job. No one needs to climb to heaven to fetch Christ. He has already come down, in the incarnation. You do not have to make salvation happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses contradicted himself, or that the law was a mistake. Leviticus 18:5 states what the law demands; Deuteronomy 30 speaks of the grace that would circumcise hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6). Both were in Moses, and both point to Christ.

Was anyone in the Old Testament saved by keeping the law? No. The law’s promise of life for perfect obedience was real, but no sinner ever met it. Old Testament believers were saved the same way we are: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer he would send. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (4:6–8). The sacrifices pointed them to the coming Lamb. Only one man ever did the commandments perfectly and lived by them: Jesus Christ, and he did it for us.

In a sentence. Moses describes the righteousness of the law this way: the one who does these things will live by them. But the righteousness of faith says, do not ask in your heart who will go up into heaven (that is, to bring Christ down).

On a Tuesday. You cannot climb up to God. Christ has come down to you. Catch the sentence in your head the next time it surfaces, the one that says there must be something more you have to do before God will accept you. Answer it with Paul’s answer: not that the climb is difficult, but that it is unnecessary, because the journey has already been made in the opposite direction.

For worship. The ladder is not too short. There is nothing at the top of it that is not already standing beside you. The Son of God came down from heaven of his own accord, without being fetched, into a stable and onto a cross, so that sinners who could never ascend could be lifted up with him. Blessed be the Lord who came down, and who has done for us what the law demanded and we could not do.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
“or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);

“Or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). In Deuteronomy, the image was crossing the sea; Paul uses the abyss (abyssos, the deep, the realm of the dead), a related Old Testament idea (Psalm 107:26; Jonah 2). It is better to name what Paul has done than to gloss it. Deuteronomy 30:13 says beyond the sea. Paul has changed it, deliberately, to the realm of the dead, and he signals each application with that is. This is interpretation, of the kind Jewish teachers of his day practised openly; he is telling you he is applying the passage, not reciting it. And the change does real work. Over the sea is merely far. The abyss is the place from which nobody returns, and it is the second of the only two directions a human being could travel to reach God: up, and down. Paul closes both, because Christ has been to both and come back from both. No one needs to go down to the grave to bring Christ up. He has already risen. The great work is done.

The sentence from below. If the ascent says there must be something more I have to do, the descent is its opposite, and it is spoken by a different kind of reader: what he did cannot reach as far down as I have gone. That sentence has kept more people from Christ than atheism ever has. It does not deny the gospel. It simply holds that this particular case is beneath its reach: the thing done at nineteen, the years nobody knows about, the marriage wrecked on purpose. And Paul answers it by pointing to where Christ has been. He went down into death itself, and came up again.

But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” From Deuteronomy 30:14. Salvation is not far away. It is as close as the word you hear and speak. Measure that against where people instinctively put it. Nearer than the church building. Nearer than the minister. Nearer than the next conference, the next book, the next season when things have calmed down enough to think properly. The gospel is not somewhere you must get to. On Paul’s account it is already in the room, closer than the furniture.

(That is, the word of faith that we proclaim). Paul explains: the near word is the gospel message, the word that calls for faith. Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the gospel, because the gospel is what the law always pointed to. And this last clause stops nearness from becoming mysticism. The word did not become near by drifting. It got near because somebody said it out loud. Paul is about to build six verses on that: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (v. 14). The nearness of verse 8 and the preacher of verse 15 are the same fact seen from the two ends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation requires no response. The near word must be believed and confessed, as Paul says next. A thing can be in your mouth because you were taught it as a child and never once believed it. And in your heart does not mean the word is your own inner voice, or that you should look inside yourself to find it. It is near because it was brought and spoken, from outside, by someone sent. What is inside you is where it has landed, not where it came from.

What if I feel that God is far away? Feelings of distance are real, and many believers have known them (Psalm 13:1; 42:9). But the nearness of verse 8 is not a feeling; it is a fact about the word. Christ has come down and risen, and the gospel that offers him is as near as your Bible and your mouth. So when God feels far, do not try to climb up or dig down to find him. Go to the near word: read it, hear it preached, say it back to him in prayer. Feelings follow slowly. The promise does not wait for them.

In a sentence. Or do not ask who will go down into the deep (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart, that is, the message about faith that we preach.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test the passage hands you ready-made. Name the thing you privately believe still has to happen before you are right with God. Everyone has one, and most people can produce it in under ten seconds. Now notice which direction it points. Either it is something more you must achieve, which is the ascent, or it is something too far gone to be reached, which is the descent. There is no third option, and Paul has named and closed both before he gets to verse 9. Then take the near word at its word today: speak it and believe it.

For worship. The two questions of verses 6 and 7 are the only two a person can ask, and both are questions about travel. Who will go up? Who will go down? Paul’s answer is that the travelling is finished. Christ came down from heaven and went down into death, and rose from both to stand beside us in the word. The whole distance a sinner now stands from God is the width of an open mouth. Blessed be the God who has brought his salvation so near.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.

Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord. “Confess” (homologeō) means to say the same thing, to agree, to declare openly: to agree with God about his Son, where it can be heard. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name, the LORD. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God and to bow to his rule. In Rome, where people were expected to say Caesar is Lord, it was costly.

What two words cost. In Greek the whole confession was two words: Kyrios Iēsous. Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the Emperor Trajan around AD 112 to ask what should be done with Christians, and described the test he had settled on. They were brought in, told to offer incense and wine before the emperor’s image, and to curse Christ. Those who did were released. A capital examination came down to one sentence, said where witnesses could hear. That is why the mouth is named. Not because God needs to hear syllables, since he has already read the heart, but because the mouth is the organ that costs. Kyrios was Caesar’s own title, the word for the one who held the final right over your life. To give it to a crucified Galilean was to take it from somebody else. The empire was largely indifferent to private opinion; the early Christians were killed for what they would not say. Confession is a transfer of allegiance.

And believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead. Believing the resurrection is not just accepting a historical fact. It is trusting in the living Christ whom God vindicated (4:24–25). The heart in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will and affections. Saving faith is not a thought held at arm’s length; it is a conviction lodged in the deepest part of a person that reorients everything else. Calvin called it a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness toward us, founded on the promise freely given in Christ, revealed to our minds and sealed on our hearts by the Holy Spirit. And why the resurrection, of everything that might have been named? Because you cannot call a dead man Lord. Kyrios is a title for someone currently in office. The raising is God’s own verdict on the crucifixion: the Son declared to be the Son of God in power (1:4), and raised for our justification (4:25). The event you are asked to believe and the ground on which you are declared right are the same event.

You will be saved. A promise, firm and simple. It is a future tense and should be left future; there is a day it points to. But the verdict is not deferred with it. That has already been given.

For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. Paul reverses the order: heart first, then mouth. He is not careless. In verse 9 he is still walking through Moses’ sentence in Moses’ order, in your mouth and in your heart (v. 8). By verse 10 the quotation is behind him, and he sets the two in the order in which they actually happen. Faith in the heart is what receives righteousness; confession with the mouth is its outward expression. They are not two separate conditions but one response, inside and outside: one faith described twice, once from within, where it is trust, and once from without, where it is audible. Nor are justified and saved two prizes, a smaller one for believing and a better one for speaking. They are one rescue named twice: once by what it does to your standing before the Judge, once by what it does to your future. True faith does not stay silent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that saying the words is a magic formula, or that someone who cannot speak cannot be saved. It does not mean faith is a work that earns salvation. Faith receives; Christ saves. Jesus blocked the magical reading before Paul wrote the sentence: not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 7:21), the very words of the confession, on lips he does not know. Nothing is saved by the sound. No one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession is not what causes the new life. It is the first sound the new life makes.

I cannot remember a moment when I confessed Christ. Am I saved? Look at the verb. With the mouth one confesses is a present tense and a description, not a ceremony: not an event you may have failed to perform, but what a believer’s mouth goes on doing. Someone converted alone in a hospital bed, someone who came to faith so gradually there is no date to write down, someone who cannot speak at all: none is shut out. You have confessed every time you prayed to him, every time you called him Lord in a room where that was awkward, every time you told the truth about whose you are when a shorter answer was available. The question is not whether there was a moment, but whether your mouth now agrees with your heart.

Should I be baptised as part of confessing Christ? Yes. In the New Testament, baptism is the first public confession a believer makes, the moment he says with his whole body that Jesus is Lord (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:36–38). It does not save; faith in Christ saves. But it is Christ’s command to all who believe, and it marks you out before the church and the world as his. If you trust Christ and have not yet been baptised as a believer, speak to your church about it. Many faithful brothers baptise infants, and we honour them, but the pattern of Scripture is confession first, then the water.

In a sentence. If you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved.

On a Tuesday. Say it out loud, at work, at home, among friends: Jesus is Lord. Believe it in your heart, and live as one who belongs to him. And here is a test that does not require auditing your past. Think of the last time you had a plain opportunity to say whose you are and let it pass, and notice what you were actually afraid of. Not hell, not the loss of your soul. Something far smaller: a change in somebody’s expression, a conversation turning heavy, a reputation for being that sort of person. That fear is a small piece of what made this sentence dangerous in Rome, and the verse names the mouth on purpose, because that is the fear it is answering.

For worship. The argument of this letter reached its lowest point in chapter 3, in a silent courtroom: the law speaks so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God (3:19). That is where Romans left the human mouth: shut, with nothing to plead. Seven chapters later, the first thing the gospel does with a stopped mouth is give it something to say. And what it is given to say is not a defence. It is a name. Blessed be Jesus, the Lord, whom God raised from the dead, who opens the mouths of the condemned to confess him and fills their hearts with the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.

For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” Isaiah 28:16 again (9:33), now with “everyone” added to stress its universal reach. The Greek Old Testament says “whoever believes,” which implies everyone. And the point can be shown, not merely asserted. Paul quoted this sentence only a few verses ago, at the close of chapter 9, without the word everyone. Isaiah does not have it. Paul put it there. The one word he adds to the prophet is the word this whole paragraph is built on, and he says it twice more before the paragraph ends.

Everyone, in particular. Everyone is an easy word to believe in general and an almost impossible one to believe in particular. Nobody disputes it as a doctrine. Almost everybody keeps a private exceptions clause. Sometimes the exception is another person, a case so long-running and so obviously closed that hoping has begun to feel like poor judgment. Sometimes, more quietly, the exception is oneself. But everyone has no exceptions clause.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. In 3:22–23 there was no distinction in sin; here there is no distinction in salvation. Same need, same remedy. In chapter 3 those words introduced the worst news in the letter: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. The phrase was a leveller. It swept away every advantage anyone had counted on and left the whole world standing on one floor. Here Paul picks up the same phrase and turns it round. The words that closed every door now open one. Nobody is far enough in to be exempt from needing this, and nobody is far enough out to be barred from having it. The gospel can be for everybody only because the ruin was.

For the same Lord is Lord of all. One Lord, Jesus, over Jews and Gentiles alike (3:29–30; Acts 10:36). The ground Paul gives is not sentiment about inclusion; it is monotheism. If there were two Lords there could be two ways. There are not. One Lord means one door, and it also means that a Gentile calling on Jesus is not being admitted as a guest to somebody else’s God. He is calling on his own Maker.

Bestowing his riches on all who call on him. “Riches”: the riches of his grace and glory (2:4; 9:23; 11:33). To call on him is to pray to him for salvation, trusting him. The verb is a present participle, being rich toward all who call, and it does not describe a fixed sum divided among claimants. That matters to the reader who came late, or came out of wasted years, and carries the settled impression that what is left for him will be the reduced portion. There is no reduced portion. Nobody arriving now is served what earlier arrivals did not finish.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone will in fact be saved. The riches are for all who call on him. That leaves exactly one distinction standing in the paragraph, and it is not the one anybody was arguing about. Not Jew and Greek, not early and late, not the respectable and the wreckage. Only this: those who call on him, and those who do not. And that is not a line anyone is born on the wrong side of.

Does “no distinction” mean the Jewish people no longer matter? No. There is no distinction in the way of salvation: Jew and Gentile alike are justified by faith in the one Lord. But Paul still speaks of Israel’s special history and future (3:1–2; 11:28–29), and he began the letter with the gospel going to the Jew first (1:16). No distinction means no one has a separate road to God and no one is excluded from the one road. It does not erase God’s faithfulness to Israel, and it gives Gentile Christians no ground for looking down on Jewish people.

In a sentence. As Scripture says, anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame. For there is no difference between Jew and Gentile: the same Lord is Lord of all and richly blesses all who call on him.

On a Tuesday. Here is how to find out which exception you are holding, and it can be done tonight. Do not ask yourself whether you believe the word everyone; you will say yes. Listen instead to how you pray for the person whose case you have privately filed as hopeless. Are you praying as though the promise covers him, or as though you were applying for an exception to be made? The two prayers sound quite different, and you can hear which one is yours. Paul modelled the first sort at the top of this chapter, for people who had rejected the gospel.

For worship. The Lord is rich, and generous to all who call. His riches are not rationed or used up, and the last to arrive is served from the same full table as the first. Blessed be the one Lord of Jew and Gentile, whose grace levels every pride and lifts every outcast, and who has never once put to shame anyone who trusted him.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Paul quotes Joel 2:32, which Peter also quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). In Joel, the Lord is the LORD, Yahweh. Paul applies it to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (v. 9). This is a strong testimony that Jesus is God: to call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh. And this is the largest thing in the verse, though it does not stop to explain itself. In the Hebrew, the name of the LORD is the name given at the burning bush, four consonants that a synagogue reader would not pronounce, saying Adonai instead so that the name itself never crossed his lips. Paul takes that sentence, about that name, and applies it without a word of justification to Jesus of Nazareth.

Reasoning from it, not to it. Consider what has just happened. A man trained as a Pharisee, who had handled the sacred name with that much care all his life, hands it to a Galilean executed outside Jerusalem within his own adult lifetime, and does it in a subordinate clause, introduced by for, as proof of something else. He is not arguing that Jesus is divine. He is reasoning from it. He has laid the ground for four verses: confess that Jesus is Lord (v. 9); the same Lord is Lord of all (v. 12); and now the Scripture about the name of the Lord. The title moves from a confession, to a claim about scope, to the covenant name of God, without ever changing hands. The highest claim in the chapter is made in its quietest sentence.

Saved from what? Joel is worth reading for what saved means, because the promise is not floating. It stands at the end of a passage about the day of the LORD, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before that great and awesome day comes. Then the promise. That is rescue with a date and a named danger. Romans has named the same danger already: the wrath revealed from heaven (1:18), and the day of wrath a hard heart is storing up for itself (2:5). This verse is the exit from that day, and it has one moving part.

To call on the name of the Lord. To pray to him, appeal to him, trust in him, worship him (Genesis 4:26; 12:8; 1 Corinthians 1:2). It is faith speaking. “Calls” (epikaleō) is not a word for eloquence or correctness. It is what a person does who has no other options left and one name to say. It became, almost at once, a description of Christians: Paul writes to all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:2), and in Damascus the disciples knew Saul was coming to bind all who call on your name (Acts 9:14). The church’s first name for itself was a verb.

Everyone. The door is open to all without exception. No sinner who calls will be turned away. This free offer of the gospel is real, and it fits with God’s sovereign election: the elect are those who are brought to call, and none who call are turned away (John 6:37). The clearest case in the Gospels is a man with nothing else to bring. He is being executed. He has no time to make amends, no restitution to offer, no changed life to point to, and he cannot even free his hands. What he has is a mouth and a name, and he uses them: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42). He is told today. Everything this verse promises was shown once in public on the worst possible candidate, and Paul’s everyone has to be at least that wide.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people can call on him without believing, as Paul says next. It is not a formula, for the same reason verse 9 was not: the calling is the sound faith makes, not a lever that operates on God.

I called on him, but I felt nothing. Did it count? Read the promise again. It says will be saved, not will feel saved. What God attaches himself to here is the calling, not the sensation that may or may not come with it. Many of the calls he has answered were made by people who were sure at the time that they had spoken into an empty room. If you called on Christ in faith, he heard you, and his word stands whether your feelings agree today or not. Keep calling on him; that is what believers do all their lives. And let the promise, not your pulse, tell you where you stand.

In a sentence. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

On a Tuesday. Tell people plainly: anyone who calls on the Lord Jesus will be saved. Then call on him yourself. Try to remember, not the best prayer you ever prayed, but the shortest one you ever meant: two or three words, probably, at an hour you would rather not describe. That is the verb in this verse, and it is the whole of what is asked. Pray it again today, and pray it for someone else by name.

For worship. In Joel the name was too holy to be pronounced. In Paul it is the one thing a dying man can still get out. Everyone who calls: not Israel only, not the worthy, not those who have made enough progress. The name too holy to be said aloud in the temple has been put within reach of any mouth on earth, in any language, at any hour, without an appointment and without anyone standing in the way. The door was made that wide on purpose, and it cost the one who widened it everything he had. Blessed be Jesus, the LORD, who hears the shortest prayer and saves to the uttermost.

parallels.desc: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The logic of the gospel creates a missionary chain that runs backwards from salvation to sending: how can anyone call on one in whom they have not believed? How can they believe in one they have not heard? How can they hear without someone preaching? How can anyone preach unless they are sent? Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 — "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!" — and the beauty he celebrates is not aesthetic but teleological: the feet that carry the gospel are beautiful because of what they carry and what their arrival means for those who hear.

The rhetorical questions tighten the logic inexorably: sending → preaching → hearing → believing → calling → saved. Remove any link and the chain breaks. This is Paul's theological argument for the absolute necessity of gospel proclamation. The sovereignty of God in election does not make preaching unnecessary; it makes preaching the instrument through which God calls his elect. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (v. 17). The word is the means; the Spirit works through the means; the elect hear and believe. Preach.

The chain does not then run smoothly to its conclusion, and v. 16 is where Paul says so: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. Every link held. They were sent, they preached, Israel heard — and it was not believed. Paul reaches for Isaiah again, and the line he takes is the first verse of Isaiah 53, in the middle of the fourth Servant Song: Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? (Isaiah 53:1). It stands immediately before the description of the man despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions. So the unbelief being grieved here is not a late development. It was written into the prophecy of the cross itself: the servant was foretold as one who would not be believed.

The chapter ends with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures against Israel's unbelief. Have they not heard? Yes — all the earth has heard (v. 18). Did they not understand? Yes — Moses had already anticipated a day when Israel would be provoked to jealousy by a foolish nation (v. 19; Deuteronomy 32:21).

And then Isaiah, whom Paul says is so bold as to put it like this: I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me (v. 20; Isaiah 65:1). That is the hardest sentence in the chapter for anyone who assumes that finding God is the reward for looking for him. God turns up among people who were not enquiring, while the people who held the oracles do not come. Israel's rejection is not ignorance; it is disobedience (v. 21) — the stretching out of God's hands to a disobedient and contrary people. The love of God remains; the response of Israel does not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Necessity of Preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is the most important New Testament text on the theology of preaching. Preaching is not one option among many for communicating the gospel; it is the divinely appointed means by which faith comes. The Spirit of God works through the proclaimed word — the word heard, the word believed — to create the faith that saves. This is why the Reformed tradition has always given preaching the central place in worship: not as a performance or an educational exercise but as the means of grace through which God speaks and through which his people hear. "Faith comes from hearing" — and hearing requires a preacher, and a preacher requires a sending. The missionary imperative is embedded in the very logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The "beautiful feet" of Isaiah 52:7 originally referred to the herald who would bring to Jerusalem the news that the exile was over — Babylon had fallen, and God's people were coming home. Paul applies this image to the heralds of the new exodus: those who proclaim that sin, death, and the wrath of God have been overcome in Christ. The gospel is the announcement that the exile from God is over; the journey home has begun. Now: In an age that has substituted social media presence, personal authenticity, and lifestyle witness for the proclamation of the gospel, Romans 10:14–17 is a direct challenge: people are not saved by our online presence or our admirable lives. They are saved by hearing the word of Christ. We must preach — in whatever form that takes in our cultural moment — because faith comes by hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”

How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? A chain of questions, working backwards. Calling requires believing. Notice which way the chain runs, because that is the point of it. Paul has just said that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. So he asks what must already have happened for anybody to be in a position to call, and works upstream one link at a time, until he arrives somewhere surprising.

And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? Believing requires hearing. Some read it “him whom they have never heard”: in the preaching, Christ himself speaks (Ephesians 2:17).

And how are they to hear without someone preaching? Hearing requires a preacher (kēryssō, to herald, announce publicly). And this is where the promise of verse 8 is paid. The word is near you, Paul said, in your mouth and in your heart. But it did not become near by drifting there. Ask how it got into your mouth, and the answer is that it was in somebody else’s first.

And how are they to preach unless they are sent? Preaching requires sending (apostellō, the root of apostle). God sends preachers, and the church sends missionaries (Acts 13:2–3). The chain does not stop at the preacher. It stops at a passive verb: unless they are sent. Somebody else has to act first. Nobody in this sequence appoints himself, and the sending does not finally begin with a committee. It is God’s own initiative arriving in ordinary shoe leather. And that settles the objection often raised here, that if God has chosen his people, preaching is a formality. Paul argues the reverse. The God who appointed the harvest appointed the plough, and no farmer certain of a crop leaves the seed in the barn. Election does not make proclamation optional; it makes it worth doing, because God’s word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” From Isaiah 52:7, describing the messengers who ran across the mountains with news of Israel’s return from exile. Stage the scene rather than merely quoting it. A city waits for news it has no way of getting. Word travelled at the speed of a man’s legs; there were watchmen on the wall because there was no other way to learn how the war had gone. And what a watchman sees first, as a runner comes over the ridge, is feet: they crest the skyline before the man does. Nobody in that world thought feet were beautiful. They were the filthiest part of a person, the part a household slave was given to wash. Isaiah calls them lovely anyway, because of what they carry. And look at what the herald shouts: peace, good news, salvation, and then the line the whole scene is built for, your God reigns. The exile is over. There has been a change of government, and you can go home. It is the same announcement Paul has been unpacking since verse 9. The herald on the ridge cries your God reigns; the believer at the foot of the hill says Jesus is Lord. The gospel is the greater good news of deliverance from sin.

Where Christians differ: those who never hear. Some say people who never hear the gospel can be saved by following their conscience or other religions; this is called inclusivism. Others hold a wider hope, that God may save people who respond to the light of creation or conscience, pointing to Cornelius (Acts 10), to 2:14–16, and to Psalm 19, which Paul quotes in verse 18. Verdict: Paul’s chain says otherwise: calling requires believing, and believing requires hearing of Christ. There is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This is why missions matter so much. Cornelius is in fact the strongest case against the wider hope: devout as he was, an angel told him to send for Peter, who would declare a message by which he would be saved (Acts 11:14). Creation is enough light to leave a man without excuse (1:20) and not enough to save him. God may use many means to bring the word, but salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Westminster 10.4). Infants dying in infancy, and those incapable of being outwardly called, are in God’s hands and saved by Christ through the Spirit as he pleases (Westminster 10.3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only ordained preachers can share the gospel. Every Christian can speak of Christ. But God appoints preaching as the main means of salvation (1 Corinthians 1:21). And this passage is not a lever for pressure. The verb is passive, unless they are sent, so the chain never asks anyone to manufacture a calling he has not been given, and it plainly needs senders as well as goers. Nor does it make you responsible for the result; the very next verse says that faithful preaching and widespread believing are two different things.

Who are the sent, and must I go? Paul has in mind heralds sent to proclaim publicly, and the church still recognises and sends such people, as the church at Antioch sent Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1–3). Not every Christian is called to be a preacher or missionary. But ordinary Christians need no commission to speak of Christ. When persecution scattered the Jerusalem church, those who were scattered went about preaching the word (Acts 8:4), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). So everyone has a part: some go, many send by prayer and giving, and all speak of Christ to the people around them.

In a sentence. How can people call on someone they have not believed in? How can they believe in someone they have not heard of? How can they hear without someone preaching? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? As Scripture says, how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!

On a Tuesday. Here is a question that is not rhetorical, and almost everybody can answer it. Who told you? Not who taught you afterwards: who first put it into words in your hearing? A parent, a friend at work, a teacher, someone at a door, someone who said it badly and said it anyway. You are standing at the end of a long line of feet, and you can usually name the last pair. Then ask the second half: who told them? And then ask who is waiting to hear it from you. Pray for preachers and missionaries. Give to send them. And open your own mouth: your feet can be beautiful too.

For worship. There was almost certainly nothing striking about the person who told you: no eloquence you can remember, possibly an awkward conversation you would not want repeated. That is not where the beauty was. It was in what they carried, and it made them lovely all the way down to the dust on their shoes. Blessed be the God who sends, who reigns, and who puts the news of his Son’s victory into ordinary mouths and sends it running over the mountains to the ends of the earth.

parallels.desc: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”

But they have not all obeyed the gospel. The problem is not that Israel lacked preachers. They heard, but did not obey. Weigh the words, because Paul is exact. He does not write that Israel has not obeyed. He writes not all. That qualification carries weight: it leaves the remnant standing, it is why chapter 11 can ask whether God has rejected his people and answer with a flat no, and it stops this verse becoming a verdict on a whole nation. And notice the word itself. Three times in the last six verses the drumbeat has been everyone: everyone who believes, all who call on him, everyone who calls on the name of the Lord. It is the same Greek word here, turned over. The word that was a promise has become a measurement, and the measurement comes back short. That is the sound of the chapter’s hope meeting its grief in one syllable.

Obeyed. The gospel is a command as well as an offer: repent and believe (1:5; Acts 17:30). “Obeyed” (hypakouō) is related to “hear” (akouō): to hear under, hearing that submits. News is not normally something you obey. You believe a report or disbelieve it; nobody obeys a weather forecast. Paul says obeyed because of what this news announces. The herald on Isaiah’s ridge was shouting that there had been a change of government. An announcement like that does not merely inform you; it puts you under someone. That is why unbelief in this chapter is described in the language of refusal rather than mere error: they did not submit (v. 3), they have not obeyed (v. 16), they are disobedient and contrary (v. 21).

For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?” Isaiah 53:1, opening the great passage on the suffering servant. Even the prophet lamented that few believed his message about the servant who would be wounded for our transgressions. John quotes it too, of the Jews who saw Jesus’ signs and did not believe (John 12:38). And the location sharpens the grief. The very next lines speak of a man with no form or majesty that we should look at him, despised and rejected. So the question is not a general complaint about a hard audience. It is the preface to the report itself, and the report is about a crucified man. The difficulty was never that the message was badly delivered. It is what the message says, the same thing chapter 9 called a stone people trip over.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel has failed when people reject it. Isaiah foresaw it. Nor does it mean results do not matter to God’s servants. Results belong to God is true, and it is also the standard alibi of the lazy and the cold. Look at how Isaiah phrases his despair: Lord, who has believed? It is not a shrug delivered to an audience. It is grief handed upward. And Paul showed the same reflex at the top of this chapter, where his response to his people’s unbelief was to pray for them.

I have shared the gospel for years and no one has believed. Have I failed? Not if you have been faithful. Look at what Isaiah was sent to do. When God commissioned him, the commission itself described the outcome: keep on hearing, but do not understand (Isaiah 6:9). Isaiah asked how long, and was told, until cities lie waste. If faithfulness were measured by response, Isaiah failed for a lifetime, and so did Paul with his own people. Your task is to speak truly, live consistently, and pray persistently. The opening of hearts is God’s work. Many who seemed deaf for years have believed in the end, sometimes after the one who prayed had gone to glory.

In a sentence. But not all the Israelites accepted the good news. For Isaiah says, Lord, who has believed our message?

On a Tuesday. Hearing is not enough. Respond to the gospel with obedient faith. And here is a test about your own voice. When the person who will not believe comes up, listen to what you say about him when he is not in the room. Is it Isaiah’s sentence, with the word Lord at the front of it and a real ache behind it? Or is it a verdict, delivered to somebody else, about a case you have privately closed? The two can use almost identical words about the same person. Only one of them is still praying.

For worship. The servant whose report was not believed is the same servant who was wounded for the transgressions of those who did not believe, and who will yet see his offspring and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:10–11). His word is not defeated by unbelief; he bore the very rejection the prophet grieved. Blessed be the despised and rejected Lord, who was not believed and still loved, and who makes his report fruitful in his own time.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.

So faith comes from hearing. The summary. Faith (pistis) is born when the message is heard. “Hearing” (akoē) can mean the act of hearing or the message heard. God creates faith through his word. And the little word so draws a conclusion from the sentence just quoted. Isaiah asked who had believed what he had heard from us, and the noun there is the same akoē, the report. Paul takes the prophet’s own noun and draws the doctrine from it. If faith is what Isaiah found missing when the report went out, then faith is the thing that comes by the report. This sentence is the theology of preaching in a single verse. Faith is not finally produced by argument, emotional experience or social influence, though God may use all of these. It is produced by the word, which the Holy Spirit uses as his instrument.

And hearing through the word of Christ. The word (rhēma) of Christ is the message about Christ, and also Christ’s own word, for he speaks through his messengers. Some manuscripts read “word of God,” as the ESV note says, but “word of Christ” is the better reading. So the verse cannot be flattened into a general recommendation of listening. Faith comes through a specific message with a specific content: not a word about God in general, not encouragement, not religious atmosphere. The report is about him, and no other report does this. That is why the faithful exposition of what Scripture actually says has always stood at the centre of Reformed worship. Not because Reformed people love lectures, but because it is the word of Christ that creates faith, and the preacher’s task is to get out of the way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is our own achievement after hearing. The Spirit uses the word to give new birth and faith (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). It does not mean reading is excluded. Reading the Scriptures is also a way the word reaches us. Akoē is about a message reaching a person, not a statement about ears: the housebound believer with an open Bible, the deaf believer watching an interpreter, the prisoner reading a page in his cell all receive the word of Christ, and it does there exactly what it does in a crowded church. And it does not mean hearing is automatic. The verse just before exists to say that not all who heard obeyed. Sitting under preaching is not the same as receiving it, and a person can do the first for forty years.

How can I get more faith? Not by squeezing harder inside. People who long for more faith almost always try to solve it inwardly, by concentrating, resolving, trying to feel more certain. It does not work, because faith is not a substance you can press on; it is a response, and a response needs something to respond to. Faith grows as it feeds on Christ in his word. Sit under faithful preaching. Read the Gospels and let Christ speak. Memorise promises and pray them back to God. Take the Lord’s Supper, where the word is made visible. And ask God for faith; he gives it (Mark 9:24; Ephesians 2:8).

In a sentence. So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.

On a Tuesday. This verse hands you a lever that is not your own willpower, and you can test it backwards. Think of the season when your faith was thickest, not happiest but thickest, when God was most plainly real to you, and ask what you were doing in the weeks before. Then do the same with the thinnest stretch you remember, and ask what had quietly stopped. The answers are rarely mysterious. What is under the word grows thicker; what is away from it grows thinner, and so gradually that the person it is happening to is usually the last to notice. So go to the word: sit under preaching, read Scripture, listen.

For worship. Paul says elsewhere that Christ came and preached peace to you who were far off (Ephesians 2:17), written to people in Asia Minor who had never seen him. He preached to them through messengers. So the sermon you will hear next Sunday, imperfectly delivered by a tired man with a cold, is not merely a report about a distant event. It is the risen Christ still speaking to people who were not born when he was crucified. Somebody else is talking. Blessed be the living Word, who still speaks, and who creates faith by his voice.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the word of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”

But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have. Israel cannot excuse itself by saying it never heard. Take care over who they are, because this verse is sometimes made to say something Paul spent his life denying. He is not claiming that every human being has now heard the gospel. He tells the same church that his ambition is to preach where Christ has not been named (15:20–21). The question belongs to the argument he is running: it is Israel who cannot plead that the message never reached them. It had been announced in their own synagogues, in their own language, by their own countrymen, for some twenty-five years.

For “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” From Psalm 19:4, about the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows the words to describe how widely the gospel had spread: through synagogues across the Roman world, the message had reached Jews everywhere (Colossians 1:6, 23). As creation’s witness goes everywhere, so has the gospel to Israel. Psalm 19 is about the sky: day pours out speech to day, a testimony with no translator and no border, arriving everywhere at once simply because it is overhead. Paul is not proving from a psalm about stars that the gospel has been preached in every village. He is borrowing the psalm’s picture of reach. The announcement has gone out the way daylight goes out. And that closes a circle from the opening of the letter, where the sky was enough to leave a man without excuse (1:20); now the message that can actually save him has travelled the same roads.

But I ask, did Israel not understand? Maybe they did not grasp it? But Scripture itself had told them that God would turn to the Gentiles. Paul calls his witnesses in order: first Moses, then Isaiah.

First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation.” From Deuteronomy 32:21, in the Song of Moses. Israel made God jealous with idols, no-gods; so God would make them jealous with a no-people, the Gentiles. It is measure for measure. Israel provoked God by giving his love to a no-god; God answers by giving his love to a no-people. And the detail that makes the question unanswerable: Moses was told to teach this song to Israel by heart before they ever entered the land, so that it would stand as a witness against them in a future they had not yet lived (Deuteronomy 31:19–21). Israel had sung it for centuries. The prophecy of their own refusal, and of the outsiders brought in over it, was in their hymnbook. Did Israel not understand? They had it memorised.

Jealousy meant to win them back. This theme of jealousy returns in 11:11–14: the salvation of Gentiles is meant to provoke Israel to seek Christ. It is easy to hear it as spite, and it is the opposite. God does not say he will replace them. He says he will make them jealous, which is only worth doing if you intend to get somebody back. Paul describes his own Gentile ministry as a way of making his fellow Jews jealous in order to save some of them (11:14). The instrument is not a punishment. It is a rescue conducted in public.

With a foolish nation I will make you angry. A nation without understanding, without the law. That Gentiles like this should be welcomed would anger proud Israel. And here is a guard for the Gentile reader, who is flattered by nobody: the terms are no people and a foolish nation. The Gentiles are not chosen as the better party; they are chosen precisely because they are the ones nobody counted. The branch grafted in has no grounds for looking down the trunk at the branch broken off, which is the warning Paul is about to spend a chapter delivering.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every single Israelite had personally heard the gospel. Paul is speaking broadly: the message had reached the nation.

What about people today who have heard the gospel many times? They are in Israel’s position, and it is serious. Having heard is not a safe place to stay; it is greater light and greater responsibility (Luke 12:48; Hebrews 2:1–3). But it is also a mercy, because the word is still near. If that is you, do not tell yourself you will understand it better later. You have heard enough to come now. And if you are a believer with friends or family who have heard it all before, do not stop: keep praying, keep loving, and let your life make them jealous for what you have in Christ.

In a sentence. But have they not heard? Of course they have: their message has gone out into all the earth, to the ends of the world. Did Israel not understand? Moses was the first to say that God would make them envious by those who are not a nation, and angry by a nation that has no understanding.

On a Tuesday. Let your life as a Christian be so full of joy in God that it makes others jealous for what you have. Jealousy only works on something that looks worth having. Nobody has ever envied a life that appeared joyless, anxious and duty-bound. So ask whether anyone who sees you at close range, the unedited version, at home, when things go wrong, would want what you have. That is not a call to perform contentment; performed contentment provokes only suspicion. It is a call to go and get some, from the word that verse 17 just named, so that there is something there to envy.

For worship. Read the two verses together and the shape is remarkable. Refused by the people he had carried for fifteen hundred years, God did not withdraw. He went and was visibly loved somewhere else, in front of them, among the no-people and the foolish nation. That is a strange thing to do unless you mean to be missed. Blessed be the God whose jealousy is love, who gathers the outsiders and through them goes on seeking his own.

parallels.desc: their voice goes out through all the earth
I will make them jealous with those who are no people

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.” But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

Then Isaiah is so bold as to say. Isaiah dared to say something shocking. Paul quotes Isaiah 65:1–2. The verb means to throw caution aside, to dare. Paul is telling you that the prophet knew he was saying an outrageous thing. The outrage was not that God saves Gentiles; Isaiah says that many times. It was the manner of it.

“I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.” The Gentiles. They were not seeking God, but God sought them. This is grace: God takes the initiative. Compare 9:30. God let himself be found by people who were not looking for him. For a certain reader this is the best sentence in the chapter. There are people who read chapter 9 and came away frightened, quietly sure they are not among the chosen, and the evidence they bring against themselves is nearly always the same: I did not really want this. I came to it late, or badly, or for the wrong reasons. I was not seeking. Verse 20 takes that evidence off the table. Not seeking is the very description of the people God says he was found by.

But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.” A moving picture: God, like a parent, standing with hands stretched out all day, pleading with his children to come home. “Disobedient” (apeitheō, refusing to be persuaded) and “contrary” (antilegō, speaking against). Israel’s unbelief is not because God did not care. He held out his hands, and they refused. The second word means answering back, contradicting: the very posture chapter 9 said the clay had no standing for (9:20), now shown to be exactly what the clay did. Take the picture literally for a moment. Hold your own arms straight out and see how long before the shoulders burn. Two minutes is hard. All day long, says God. It is the posture of appeal and welcome, and no one holds it casually. Picture a parent in a doorway with arms open from morning until dark while a child walks past, again and again, and does not stop.

Side by side in Isaiah. Verse 20 is Isaiah 65:1 and verse 21 is Isaiah 65:2. They are consecutive. Paul did not hunt through the Scriptures for a counterweight; he simply kept reading, and sovereign grace and human refusal were already lying side by side in one paragraph. That answers a reading of chapter 9 that has done real damage. Close the book at the potter and the clay, and you end with a God who settles everything over people’s heads. A chapter later the same apostle ends his argument with God standing in a doorway with his arms out, and puts the loss down to a people who would not come. Both stand. Paul softens neither, and neither should anyone using him. The Lord Jesus said the same about the same city, in the street: how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Luke 13:34). The word he ends on is not could not but would not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has given up on Israel. The very next chapter begins: has God rejected his people? By no means. His hands are still held out. Nor does it mean his patience is endless indifference. A day has an evening. Paul has already warned against reading God’s patience as indifference (2:4–5). All day long is a measure of extraordinary endurance, not a promise that the arms will never come down.

Where Christians differ: the sincerity of the offer. Some argue that if God has elected only some, his offer of salvation to the non-elect cannot be sincere. Verdict: God’s outstretched hands are real. He truly calls all who hear the gospel to come, and he is grieved by their refusal (Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 23:37). His secret purpose in election and his revealed will in the gospel do not cancel each other. We do not fully understand how they fit together, but Scripture teaches both, and we must preach freely to all (Canons of Dort 2.5; 3/4.8).

I have drifted from God for years. Will he take me back? Yes. Look at the posture this verse describes: hands held out all day, to people who were refusing him at the very time. When you think of coming back after a long stretch of neglect, most people picture folded arms, a turned back, or at best a cool, formal patience. The text has already described God’s posture, and it is not the one you are bracing for. Think of the father in Jesus’ parable, who saw his son a long way off and ran (Luke 15:20). Come today. Confess plainly, return to his word and his people, and do not wait until you feel worthy.

In a sentence. And Isaiah boldly says that God was found by those who did not seek him and revealed himself to those who did not ask for him. But concerning Israel he says, all day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and stubborn people.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray tonight, take ten seconds to notice what you are unconsciously picturing God’s posture to be. Then replace it with this verse: arms out. If you have been resisting him, come home. And if you know someone who has, hold out your own hands too: keep the door open, keep the invitation warm, and do not let your face say what God’s does not.

For worship. Notice how the chapter is allowed to end. Not with a door closed and bolted, but with a posture being held. Paul’s very next sentence asks whether God has rejected his people, and answers no as forcefully as anything in the letter. The hands are still out at the end of chapter 10, because the argument is not finished. Isaiah was not writing about the cross, and it would be dishonest to pretend the verse means that. But a Christian cannot read it without seeing where those hands went in the end. Held out, all day, outside the walls of the city they were held out to. What God says he had been doing for centuries in figure, he did at last with nails through them, in public, for six hours. God sought you when you were not looking for him. The last picture chapter 10 leaves is not of a fist. It is of hands, still out on a Friday afternoon, on a hill outside the city, nailed open.

parallels.desc: I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me
I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people
