10.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.<sup>2</sup>For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness.<sup>4</sup>For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.<sup>5</sup>For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.<sup>6</sup>But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ’Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)<sup>7</sup>“or ’Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).<sup>8</sup>But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);<sup>9</sup>because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.<sup>10</sup>For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.<sup>11</sup>For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”<sup>12</sup>For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.<sup>13</sup>For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”<sup>14</sup>How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?<sup>15</sup>And how are they to preach unless they are sent? 11.title: The Mystery of Israel and the Doxology of Grace
11.overview:
Romans 11 completes the great argument about Israel that began in chapter 9. Paul has shown that God's word has not failed (chapter 9) and that Israel has heard and not believed (chapter 10). Now he asks: has God rejected his people? The answer is again the most emphatic negative in the letter: By no means! God has not cast away the people he foreknew. The evidence: Paul himself is a Jew, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin — and he has believed. The remnant is real.

But the chapter moves beyond the remnant to the mystery: Israel's hardening has served the purpose of Gentile inclusion, and Gentile inclusion is the means by which Israel will eventually be provoked to jealousy and saved. The olive tree image (vv. 17–24) holds the whole argument together: natural branches were broken off; wild branches were grafted in; the natural branches can and will be grafted back in. The God of the olive tree is the God of Israel's future. And that future ends not in permanent rejection but in the breathtaking statement: "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Remnant: God Has Not Rejected His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Has God rejected his people? By no means!" The vehemence of Paul's denial is significant — the same mē genoito he has used throughout the letter for the most outrageous misunderstandings of the gospel. The question of Israel's rejection is in the same category as the question of whether God is unjust (9:14) or whether we should sin that grace may abound (6:1). The answer is the same: unthinkable.

Paul's primary evidence is himself. He is a Jew. He has believed in Jesus as Messiah. Therefore God has not totally rejected Israel, because here is at least one Israelite who has been saved — and not the most promising one, either. The former persecutor of the church, the man who breathed threats and murder against the disciples of Jesus, stands as Exhibit A for the continued saving purposes of God toward Israel.

The parallel with Elijah (vv. 2–4) is instructive: when Elijah was convinced he was the only faithful Israelite left, God corrected him — seven thousand had not bowed to Baal. The prophet's perception of total abandonment was wrong. Paul draws the application: there is a remnant chosen by grace. Not by works, not by ancestry — by grace. And where grace operates, it is no longer works; the two principles are mutually exclusive. The remnant is real, small though it appears.

Then comes the harder half of the section, and it is not an appendix to the remnant — it is the same breath. What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened (v. 7). Three parties in one line: Israel as a whole, the elect within it, and the rest. Paul has just insisted that God has not rejected his people; he now says that most of them are hardened. The chapter is written by a man who saw no contradiction between those two sentences, and it cannot be read by anyone who holds only one of them.

The hardening is given scriptural warrant from two places welded together (v. 8) — God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, Isaiah 29:10 joined to Deuteronomy 29:4. The Deuteronomy setting repays knowing. Moses stands at the end of the wilderness years reciting what the people have watched with their own eyes: the plagues, the sea, forty years of bread out of the sky. His verdict on all of it is that to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand. Evidence was never the missing ingredient.

Then David (vv. 9–10), and the psalm is not chosen at random. Psalm 69 is the psalm of the righteous sufferer, the one the evangelists reach for to describe the cross — zeal for your house has consumed me; for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. Paul turns its imprecation on those who rejected the very sufferer it was describing. And notice what is asked to become a snare: their table. Not their enemies, not their circumstances. Their provision. The privileges listed back in 9:4–5 are the things they trip over.

None of which is the section’s last word, and it would misrepresent Paul to stop here. His very next sentence asks whether they stumbled in order that they might fall, and answers it with the same violent negative this section opened with.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remnant Principle in Scripture

The remnant theology of Romans 11:1–10 runs through the entire Old Testament: Isaiah's "remnant of Israel" (Isaiah 10:20–22), Micah's "remnant of Jacob," the faithful seven thousand in Elijah's day. God has never saved the entire nation of Israel simply by virtue of their physical membership in the covenant people; he has always worked through a called, believing remnant within the larger community. This remnant is not self-selecting; it is chosen by grace. Paul's point is that this has always been God's method — the new covenant does not represent a change in approach but a clarification and fulfilment of the approach God has always taken.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were invisible to Elijah — unknown to him, underground, silent. The remnant of God is often invisible to human perception. The prophet who declares the cause lost may be wrong; God's remnant is not necessarily visible or audible. Now: In seasons when the church appears to be in irreversible decline — when the statistics are grim and the cultural momentum runs entirely against Christian faith — the Elijah phenomenon is a perpetual danger: "I alone am left." The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears. God preserves what he has promised to preserve.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.

Meaning first. Romans 11 finishes Paul’s answer about Israel with hope. God has not rejected his people. First, there is a remnant now, chosen by grace, just as in Elijah’s day; the rest have been hardened, as Scripture foretold (vv. 1–10). Second, Israel’s stumble is not final. Through it salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous; and if their failure has brought riches to the world, their full inclusion will bring far more (vv. 11–16). Third, Paul warns Gentile believers with the picture of an olive tree. Some natural branches were broken off for unbelief, and wild branches grafted in by faith. So Gentiles must not be proud, but fear, for God can graft the natural branches back in (vv. 17–24). Fourth, Paul reveals a mystery: Israel’s hardening is partial and temporary, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved, for God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable (vv. 25–32). Finally, the whole argument of chapters 1–11 bursts into praise: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! (vv. 33–36).

I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Key words. The question raised by 10:21. “Rejected” (apōtheomai, thrust away). Paul’s wording echoes the promise that the LORD will not forsake his people (1 Samuel 12:22; Psalm 94:14). The form of the question in Greek expects the answer no.

By no means! Key words. Mē genoito: absolutely not.

For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. Key words. Paul is living proof. He is a Jew by birth, of a known tribe (Philippians 3:5), and once an enemy of Christ, yet God saved him. If God had rejected Israel, he would not have saved Paul.

God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Key words. “Foreknew” (proginōskō), as in 8:29: God set his love on them beforehand. His people here are the nation he chose in love; within it, as the next verses show, is the elect remnant. God’s foreknowing love cannot be cancelled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every Jew is saved, or that God has two ways of salvation, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. There is one way, faith in Christ, for all (10:12).

In a sentence. Paul asks, then: did God reject his people? Not at all! He himself is an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God did not reject his people, whom he foreknew.

On a Tuesday. If God has not given up on Israel after centuries of unbelief, he has not given up on you, or on the people you pray for.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah. Key words. Paul turns to 1 Kings 19, after Elijah’s victory on Mount Carmel, when Jezebel threatened his life and he fled to the wilderness in despair.

How he appeals to God against Israel. Key words. “Appeals” (entynchanō) is the word used of the Spirit’s intercession (8:27), but here Elijah pleads against Israel, not for it.

“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” Key words. From 1 Kings 19:10, 14. Elijah thought he was the only faithful one left.

But what is God’s reply to him? Key words. “Reply” is chrēmatismos, a divine answer, an oracle.

“I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” Key words. From 1 Kings 19:18. Notice “I have kept for myself.” The faithfulness of the seven thousand was God’s doing. He preserved them. The remnant exists because of God, not because of their strength.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the seven thousand were the only ones God cared about. The point is that God always keeps a people, even when it looks as if faith has died out.

In a sentence. Don’t you know what Scripture says about Elijah, how he complained to God about Israel: “Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I am the only one left, and they are trying to kill me”? And what was God’s answer? “I have kept for myself seven thousand who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

For worship. When you feel alone in your faith, remember Elijah. God has kept for himself many more than you can see.

parallels.desc: I, even I only, am left
seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. Key words. Paul applies Elijah’s situation to his own day. “Remnant” (leimma, a leftover). “Chosen by grace” is literally according to the election (eklogē) of grace: God chose them freely, not for merit. The thousands of Jews who believed in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41; 21:20) were this remnant.

But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works. Key words. Grace and works are opposites as the basis of God’s choice. If God chose because of works, it would be wages (4:4).

Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Key words. Grace (charis) is free, undeserved favour. Mix in merit and it stops being grace. Some later manuscripts add a further sentence about works no longer being works; the ESV rightly follows the shorter, earlier reading.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the remnant are passive. They believe and obey. But their faith is the fruit of grace, not its cause.

In a sentence. So in the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, it is not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

On a Tuesday. Grace is free or it is not grace. Stop trying to earn what God gives. And stop measuring others by what they have earned.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”

What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. Key words. Israel was seeking righteousness before God (9:31; 10:3), but did not get it, because it sought it by works.

The elect obtained it. Key words. The elect (literally “the election”) are the remnant chosen by grace. They obtained righteousness, through faith in Christ.

But the rest were hardened. Key words. “Hardened” (pōroō, to make callous, like hard skin over a wound) is passive, implying God did it, as he hardened Pharaoh (9:18). It is a judicial act: God gives over to blindness those who refuse the light.

As it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.” Key words. A blend of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. A “spirit of stupor” (katanyxis, numbness, deep sleep): spiritual insensibility. Jesus quoted similar words from Isaiah 6 about those who would not understand his parables (Matthew 13:14–15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God hardens innocent people who want to see. The hardening is a judgement on persistent unbelief. And it does not mean the hardening is total or final, as verse 25 will show.

In a sentence. What then? What Israel sought so earnestly it did not obtain. The elect among them did, but the others were hardened, as Scripture says: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see and ears that could not hear, to this very day.”

For worship. If you see Christ, it is because God opened your eyes. Thank him, and pray for those who are still blind.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”

And David says. Key words. Paul quotes Psalm 69:22–23, a psalm of the suffering righteous man. The New Testament applies this psalm to Christ often: zeal for your house (John 2:17), they gave me vinegar to drink (Matthew 27:34, 48).

“Let their table become a snare and a trap.” Key words. The table: their feasts, their comforts, perhaps their religious privileges and the law in which they trusted. What should have been blessing becomes a trap.

A stumbling block and a retribution for them. Key words. “Retribution” (antapodoma, payback): a just recompense for rejecting God’s anointed.

Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever. Key words. Blindness and bondage. “Forever” (dia pantos) here means continually, constantly, not necessarily eternally, as the following verses show that Israel’s hardening is not final.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse Jews or anyone else. David’s prayer is a cry for God’s justice against those who persecuted his anointed king, fulfilled in God’s judgement on those who rejected Christ. Christians are told to bless those who persecute them (12:14). And it does not justify the shameful history of Christian hatred of Jews.

In a sentence. David says, “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a payback for them. May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent continually.”

On a Tuesday. The good things God gives can become a trap if they replace him. Do not let your comforts or religious habits blind you to Christ.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section does not begin at the tree. It begins with a question about the difference between two ways of going down: did they stumble in order that they might fall? (v. 11). The distinction is the whole argument. A stumble is what happens on the way somewhere — you go down, and you get up. A fall, in the sense Paul is denying, is terminal. His answer is the same violent negative that opened the chapter.

What follows is the mechanism, and it is stranger than a consolation. Their trespass has meant salvation for the Gentiles, and that Gentile salvation is aimed back at Israel — so as to make Israel jealous, which is Moses’ own word from Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted a chapter earlier (10:19). Then the arithmetic of v. 12: if their failure has meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion. Paul is reasoning from the lesser to the greater, and the reasoning only works if there is a fullness still to come.

Verses 13–14 are more startling than they look, and they are addressed to Gentiles explicitly. Paul says he makes much of his Gentile ministry precisely in order to provoke his own people and save some of them. The apostle to the Gentiles is running a strategy whose second target is Israel; the two ministries are not in competition, and the Gentile church is, without knowing it, part of how God intends to reach the synagogue.

Then two images before the tree. If their rejection meant reconciliation for the world, their acceptance will mean life from the dead (v. 15) — a phrase Paul does not explain, and which readers have taken either as the general resurrection at the end or as a quickening of such magnitude that no smaller word would do. And v. 16: if the firstfruits of the dough are holy, so is the whole lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches. That is the offering of Numbers 15:20–21, where a consecrated portion makes the batch consecrated — a part standing for a whole, which is exactly what a remnant is and exactly what the tree is about to illustrate.

The olive tree is one of the most evocative images in the letter. The cultivated olive tree is Israel — the covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs, sustained by the promises of God. Natural branches (unbelieving Jews) have been broken off — not because God has given up on the tree, but because of unbelief. Wild branches (believing Gentiles) have been grafted in — not because of their natural superiority but purely by grace, "grafted in contrary to nature" (v. 24). The tree itself, its root and its sap, remains unchanged; what changes is which branches are bearing fruit on it.

Paul's warning to the Gentile believers is sharp and pointed: "Do not be arrogant toward the branches" (v. 18). The Gentile who imagines that the Jewish people have been permanently and finally replaced, that God has transferred his covenant purposes entirely and irreversibly to the Gentile church, has not been paying attention to chapters 9–11. God is able to graft the natural branches back in (v. 23). Indeed, he has said he will. The mercy shown to Gentiles is not a reversal of God's purposes for Israel; it is part of the very mechanism by which those purposes will ultimately be fulfilled.

The warning against Gentile pride is not merely a pastoral nicety; it is a theological corrective to supersessionism — the view that God has permanently replaced Israel with the church, that the covenant promises to Abraham and his physical descendants are entirely and exhaustively fulfilled in the Gentile church. Romans 11 will not allow this. The natural branches can be grafted back in; the God of the olive tree has not changed his mind about the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and the Question of Supersessionism

Romans 11:17–24 is the central text in the debate between supersessionism (the church has entirely replaced Israel as the covenant people) and its alternatives. The text resists the supersessionist reading: unbelieving Jews are broken off branches — not dead stumps — and can be grafted back in. The root and richness of the olive tree (the Abrahamic covenant and its promises) remain; what changes is which branches are currently bearing fruit. The Reformed tradition has generally held to a form of "fulfilment theology" — the church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel — while resisting the conclusion that God's purposes for ethnic Israel are entirely exhausted. Romans 11:25–29 will make this explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gentile believers in Rome were apparently in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief with a degree of spiritual smugness. Paul's corrective is immediate: you stand only by faith; the one who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. The Gentile's security in the olive tree rests on the same grace that brought him in — and that grace is not a possession he holds, but a gift he receives. Now: Two thousand years of church history have produced exactly the Gentile arrogance Paul warned against — anti-Semitism often wrapped in theological language, the assumption that God has finished with the Jewish people. Romans 11 stands against this permanently. God has not and will not abandon the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!

So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? Key words. To stumble is to trip; to fall is to go down and not get up. Is Israel’s stumbling over Christ (9:32) a permanent fall? Was that God’s purpose?

By no means! Key words. No. The stumble is not the end of the story.

Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles. Key words. God brought good from Israel’s sin. When the Jews rejected the gospel, the apostles turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46; 18:6; 28:28). Israel’s no became the world’s opportunity.

So as to make Israel jealous. Key words. The purpose, from Deuteronomy 32:21 (10:19). When Israel sees Gentiles enjoying the blessings promised to Israel, God means it to stir them to come back.

Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles. Key words. “Failure” (hēttēma, defeat, loss, diminishing). Their loss has become the Gentiles’ gain.

How much more will their full inclusion mean! Key words. “Full inclusion” (plērōma, fullness). If their loss brought such blessing, their fullness, a great turning of Israel to Christ, will bring far more. Paul looks forward to this in verses 25–26.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God caused their sin as a mere tool. Israel’s rejection was truly their trespass. But God overruled it for good, as he did with Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20) and with the cross itself (Acts 2:23).

In a sentence. So Paul asks: did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Not at all! Rather, because of their transgression, salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel envious. And if their transgression means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches will their full inclusion bring!

For worship. God turns his people’s failures into blessings for the world. Praise him for his wisdom, which no sin can defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.

Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Key words. Paul addresses the Gentile believers in Rome directly. They needed to understand that Israel’s story is their story too, and not to despise the Jews.

Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles. Key words. Paul’s special calling (1:5; 15:16; Galatians 2:7–8; Acts 9:15).

I magnify my ministry. Key words. “Magnify” (doxazō, glorify): he honours and gives himself fully to his work among the Gentiles.

In order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them. Key words. “My fellow Jews” is literally “my flesh.” Paul’s Gentile ministry had a Jewish goal. As Gentiles came to faith, he hoped some Jews would be stirred to seek the Messiah. “Save” here means be God’s instrument in saving them (1 Corinthians 9:22). “Some”: Paul is realistic. Not all, but some.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul neglected the Gentiles or saw them as mere bait. He loved them. But his love for Israel ran through all he did.

In a sentence. Paul is talking to you Gentiles. Since he is the apostle to the Gentiles, he takes pride in his ministry, in the hope that he may somehow stir his own people to envy and save some of them.

On a Tuesday. Do your work in such a way that it draws others to Christ. A faithful Christian in an ordinary job can make others hungry for God.

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world. Key words. Their rejection (apobolē, casting away): God’s setting aside of Israel for unbelief. Through it the gospel went to the nations, and the world was reconciled (5:10; 2 Corinthians 5:19).

What will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? Key words. Their acceptance (proslēmpsis, being received back) will mean life from the dead. Some take this as the final resurrection, which the conversion of Israel will come just before. Others take it as a figure for a great spiritual revival in the world, an outpouring of new life. Either way, Israel’s return will be wonderful.

If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump. Key words. From Numbers 15:17–21. The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy, set apart to him. The firstfruits are probably the patriarchs, or the believing remnant. Because God consecrated them, Israel as a whole remains set apart in his purpose.

And if the root is holy, so are the branches. Key words. The root is the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom the promises were made (v. 28). The image prepares for the olive tree.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Jew is personally holy or saved. “Holy” here means set apart by God’s covenant purpose, as the children of a believer are called holy in 1 Corinthians 7:14.

In a sentence. For if their rejection brought reconciliation to the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead? If the part of the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

For worship. God’s purposes for his people are not finished. Look forward with joy to what he will yet do.
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.

The olive tree. Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree (Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 14:6). There is one tree: the one people of God, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. It is not that Israel is one tree and the church another.

But if some of the branches were broken off. Key words. Unbelieving Jews. Note “some,” not all.

And you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others. Key words. Gentile believers, wild by nature, outside the covenant (Ephesians 2:11–12), now grafted in by faith, among the believing Jews.

And now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree. Key words. Literally the root of fatness, the rich sap of the tree. Gentiles share in the blessings promised to Abraham (Galatians 3:14, 29).

Do not be arrogant toward the branches. Key words. “Arrogant” (katakauchaomai, boast against). Some Gentile believers in Rome were looking down on Jews.

If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. Key words. The church owes its life to Israel’s root. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22). Our Bible, our Saviour, our promises all came through Israel.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists teach that God has two distinct peoples with two programs, Israel and the church. Others teach that the church has simply replaced Israel, so ethnic Israel has no further place. Verdict: The olive tree shows one people of God across both testaments, rooted in the promises to the patriarchs. Gentiles do not form a new tree; they are grafted into the old one. So there are not two peoples. But neither has God finished with ethnic Israel: the natural branches can be, and will be, grafted back into their own tree (vv. 23–26). The church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, not a separate plan.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Gentiles must become Jews or keep the ceremonial law. They are grafted in by faith alone.

In a sentence. If some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others and now share in the rich root of the olive tree, do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember: you do not support the root; the root supports you.

On a Tuesday. Never speak of the Jewish people with contempt. Your faith grows from their root. Pray for them, and love them.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.

Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.” Key words. The proud Gentile says: they were removed to make room for me. I must be special.

That is true. Key words. Paul agrees with the fact, but not with the pride.

They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. Key words. The real reason: unbelief, not ethnicity. And you stand only by faith, not by merit. Faith is the empty hand that receives; it gives no ground for boasting (3:27).

So do not become proud, but fear. Key words. Literally, do not think high thoughts. Fear here is reverent awe and humble watchfulness (Philippians 2:12; Proverbs 3:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in terror of God. It means a humble, reverent dependence that never takes grace for granted.

In a sentence. You will say then, “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” Granted. But they were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand by faith. So do not be arrogant, but tremble.

For worship. You stand only by faith, and faith is a gift. Bow low, and stand in awe.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.

For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Key words. If God did not spare Israel, with all its privileges, when it fell into unbelief, he will not spare Gentile churches that do the same. Many once-flourishing churches have been cut off: think of the churches of North Africa and Asia Minor (Revelation 2:5).

Note then the kindness and the severity of God. Key words. Two sides of God’s character, held together. Kindness (chrēstotēs, goodness, generosity, as in 2:4) and severity (apotomia, literally cutting off, sharpness). Both are real.

Severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you. Key words. Israel’s unbelief brought severity; the Gentiles’ faith received kindness.

Provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off. Key words. A conditional warning. Continuing (epimenō, remain, persevere) in God’s kindness means continuing to trust it, not trusting yourself.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Some take this verse to show that a truly saved person can lose salvation. Verdict: Paul speaks here mainly of Gentiles as a group, a branch of the tree, not of each individual’s election. And the warning is one of God’s means of keeping his elect. Those who are truly in Christ will continue, because God keeps them (8:30, 38–39; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). Those who fall away show that they were not truly of us (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and true believers heed it. This is the perseverance of the saints (Westminster 17.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our own effort to keep ourselves. It depends on God’s kindness, which keeps us continuing in it.

In a sentence. For if God did not spare the natural branches, he will not spare you either. Consider therefore the kindness and sternness of God: sternness to those who fell, but kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off.

On a Tuesday. Take God’s warnings seriously. They are not threats against his children but loving fences that keep them safe.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.

And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in. Key words. The way back is open. Their unbelief, not their ancestry, cut them off. Faith will graft them back in.

For God has the power to graft them in again. Key words. Humanly, a broken branch cannot be put back. But God can do it. Israel’s salvation depends on his power, as everyone’s does.

For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree. Key words. Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock, not a wild branch onto a cultivated tree. Paul knows this. “Contrary to nature”: God did something unnatural, a miracle of grace, in bringing Gentiles in.

How much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree. Key words. If God did the unnatural thing, how much easier the natural one. It is their own tree. Paul’s “will be” looks forward with confidence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews can be saved apart from faith in Christ. Grafting in happens when they do not continue in unbelief.

In a sentence. And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. After all, if you were cut out of an olive tree that is wild by nature and, contrary to nature, grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into their own tree!

For worship. No one is too far gone for God. Pray with confidence for Jewish friends and for all who seem cut off.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reveals a mystery so that the Gentile believers will not become proud: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved, as the prophets foretold of a Deliverer from Zion who will remove ungodliness from Jacob. As regards the gospel, Israel is at present opposed to it for the Gentiles’ sake; as regards God’s choice, they are loved because of the patriarchs, for God does not take back his gifts and call. Just as Gentiles once disobeyed and now have received mercy, so Israel has disobeyed so that they too may receive mercy; God has shut everyone up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all. Paul ends in wonder at the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, whose ways no one can trace or advise: all things are from him, through him and to him, and to him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God's Covenant Purposes

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" — is the theological capstone of chapters 9–11 and one of the most important statements about God's faithfulness in Scripture. The word translated "irrevocable" (ametamelēta) means without repentance — God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. Applied to Israel: whatever the full meaning of "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26), it means at minimum that God has not and will not permanently and finally abandon the people he chose. Applied to the individual Christian: the calling and justification God has effected in her life will not be revoked. The golden chain of 8:29–30 and the irrevocability of 11:29 are two sides of the same coin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of vv. 33–36 was Paul's own response to the argument he had just made. Having argued through three chapters about divine sovereignty, human responsibility, the mystery of Israel, and the purposes of God — he does not end with a systematic summary. He ends with worship. This is the correct response to the depth of God: not the mastery of a doctrine but the surrender of a doxology. Now: In an age that demands that every theological mystery be resolved into a satisfying rational system, the doxology of Romans 11:33–36 is the necessary reminder: we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge exceed our categories. The only posture that is finally appropriate before the mystery of divine election and human salvation is the posture Paul strikes: "From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever."

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;

Lest you be wise in your own sight. Key words. From Proverbs 3:7. Paul tells this mystery to keep Gentile believers humble.

I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers. Key words. A “mystery” (mystērion) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God (16:25; Ephesians 3:3–6). Not a puzzle, but a revealed secret.

A partial hardening has come upon Israel. Key words. Partial: not every Jew is hardened (the remnant believes). It is also limited in time.

Until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. Key words. The fullness (plērōma) of the Gentiles is the full number of elect Gentiles that God intends to save. “Come in”: into the kingdom, the people of God. The hardening lasts until then.

And in this way all Israel will be saved. Key words. “In this way” (houtōs): in this manner, by this process. Through the hardening of part of Israel, the coming in of the Gentiles, and the jealousy that provokes Israel to faith.

As it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob.” Key words. From Isaiah 59:20–21, with words from Isaiah 27:9. The Deliverer is Christ. Israel’s salvation, like everyone’s, comes through him, by turning ungodliness away from Jacob: forgiveness and new hearts.

Where Christians differ: who is all Israel? Three main views are held among Reformed Christians. First, all Israel is the whole church, Jew and Gentile, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16); this was Calvin’s view. Second, all Israel is the total of elect Jews saved throughout history, the remnant in every generation. Third, all Israel is the Jewish people as a whole, who will turn to Christ in large numbers in the future, before his return. Dispensationalists add a separate future plan for national Israel in a thousand-year kingdom. Verdict: The third view fits the passage best. In verse 25, Israel means ethnic Israel, distinguished from the Gentiles; it would be strange for the word to change meaning in the next sentence. The contrast of now and then (vv. 12, 15, 23–24, 30–31) points to a future turning. So Paul expects a great conversion of the Jewish people to Christ. But this happens through the gospel, by faith in Christ, into the one olive tree, the church. It is not a separate plan of salvation, and it does not require a rebuilt temple or a thousand-year earthly kingdom. It fits the amillennial view: the church age ends with the return of Christ, the resurrection and the judgement, and no secret rapture. All Israel need not mean every individual Jew; in Scripture it often means Israel as a whole (1 Samuel 7:5; 2 Chronicles 12:1). The Westminster Larger Catechism teaches us to pray for the calling of the Jews (Q. 191).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews can be saved without Christ, and it does not give any ground for anti-Jewish hatred. Nor does it mean any modern political state fulfils this prophecy; Paul speaks of conversion to Christ.

In a sentence. Paul does not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be conceited: Israel has experienced a hardening in part until the full number of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved. As it is written: “The deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn godlessness away from Jacob.”

On a Tuesday. God is working out a plan that spans the whole of history. Your part in it is to pray, to witness, and to stay humble.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.” As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.

“And this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.” Key words. Isaiah 59:21 joined with Isaiah 27:9, echoing the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33–34. Israel’s salvation will be by forgiveness of sins in Christ, the heart of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:8–12).

As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. Key words. In relation to the gospel, unbelieving Israel stands as God’s enemy, opposed to the message and under his displeasure. Their rejection opened the door for the Gentiles: for your sake.

But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers. Key words. Yet in relation to God’s choice, Israel as a people is still loved, because of his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. God loved the fathers and chose their offspring (Deuteronomy 4:37; 7:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean they are saved because of their ancestors. No one is saved by family merit. It means God’s love for the patriarchs guarantees his continued purpose for their descendants, which will be fulfilled when they turn to Christ.

In a sentence. “And this is my covenant with them when I take away their sins.” As far as the gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake; but as far as election is concerned, they are loved on account of the patriarchs.

For worship. God remembers his promises across thousands of years. He will remember his promises to you.

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,

For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. Key words. “Irrevocable” (ametamelētos, without regret, never taken back). God does not change his mind about what he has given and to whom he has called. The gifts are the privileges of 9:4–5; the calling is God’s choosing of Israel as his people. This is also a great comfort for every believer: God never revokes his saving call (8:30).

For just as you were at one time disobedient to God. Key words. The Gentiles, before conversion, were disobedient (1:18–32; Ephesians 2:1–3).

But now have received mercy because of their disobedience. Key words. Israel’s disobedience opened the door of mercy to the Gentiles.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God’s calling of Israel guarantees salvation without faith. It means God’s purpose for Israel stands and will be fulfilled.

In a sentence. For God’s gifts and his call can never be revoked. Just as you who were at one time disobedient to God have now received mercy as a result of their disobedience,

On a Tuesday. When you doubt whether God still wants you, remember: his calling is irrevocable. He does not regret calling you.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.

So they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. Key words. The pattern reverses. Jewish disobedience brought mercy to Gentiles; mercy to Gentiles will bring mercy to Jews. Some manuscripts omit the second “now,” as the ESV notes. If it stands, it means that the time of mercy for Israel is the present gospel age, and it can come at any time.

For God has consigned all to disobedience. Key words. “Consigned” (synkleiō, shut up together, imprison). God has shut up everyone, Jew and Gentile, in the prison of their disobedience, so that no one can escape by their own merit (Galatians 3:22).

That he may have mercy on all. Key words. The purpose: so that all who are saved are saved by mercy alone. “All” here means all kinds, Jew and Gentile alike, both groups. No one gets in except by mercy.

Where Christians differ: universal salvation. Some read “mercy on all” as meaning that every human being will finally be saved. Verdict: The context is about two groups, Jews and Gentiles, not every individual. Paul has just spoken of branches cut off and of God’s severity (v. 22), and elsewhere of eternal destruction (2 Thessalonians 1:9). God shows mercy on both groups without distinction, but not all individuals are saved. Hell is real and conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46).

In a sentence. So they too have now become disobedient, in order that they too may now receive mercy as a result of God’s mercy to you. For God has bound everyone over to disobedience so that he may have mercy on them all.

For worship. No one is saved except by mercy. Neither are you. Let mercy make you humble, grateful and merciful.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!

The doxology. After eleven chapters of the deepest theology in Scripture, on sin, justification, union with Christ, the Spirit, election and Israel, Paul does not end with a conclusion but with worship. Doctrine is meant to lead to doxology (from doxa, glory).

Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! Key words. Three depths. The riches of his grace and mercy (2:4; 9:23; 10:12). The wisdom of his plan, which uses even sin and hardening to bring salvation to the world (1 Corinthians 1:24). The knowledge by which he foreknew his people and sees all things.

How unsearchable are his judgments. Key words. “Unsearchable” (anexeraunētos, cannot be fully investigated). His decisions and decrees go beyond our understanding.

And how inscrutable his ways! Key words. “Inscrutable” (anexichniastos, cannot be tracked, like footprints that cannot be followed; also in Ephesians 3:8). We cannot trace the paths of his working.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is irrational or that we can know nothing about him. He has revealed much, as Romans shows. But what he has revealed opens onto a depth no creature can fathom. Mystery is not an excuse to stop thinking, but the place where thinking turns to worship.

In a sentence. Oh, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable his judgements, and his paths beyond tracing out!

For worship. When you reach the end of what you can understand about God, do not complain. Worship.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”

“For who has known the mind of the Lord.” Key words. From Isaiah 40:13, in the great chapter on God’s incomparable greatness. No creature fully knows God’s thoughts. God knows himself fully; we know only what he reveals (1 Corinthians 2:11, 16).

“Or who has been his counselor?” Key words. No one advised God when he planned salvation. He did not need help or input. His plan comes from his own wisdom alone (Job 15:8; Jeremiah 23:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should not pray or bring our requests to God. He invites prayer. But we do not instruct him; we trust him.

In a sentence. Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his adviser?

On a Tuesday. You do not need to understand everything God is doing in your life. He needs no adviser. Trust his wisdom.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”

“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” Key words. From Job 41:11 (see also Job 35:7). No one has ever put God in debt. No one can claim that God owes them salvation. Everything we have, including the faith we give him, he first gave us (1 Corinthians 4:7). This sums up the message of Romans: salvation is by grace, not earned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God does not reward his people. He does, but all his rewards are grace, crowning his own gifts.

In a sentence. Who has ever given to God, that God should repay them?

For worship. You have never given God anything that was not first his. Give him everything, and thank him for everything.

parallels.desc: who has first given to me, that I should repay him?

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

For from him and through him and to him are all things. Key words. The whole of reality in one sentence. From him: he is the source of all things (Creator). Through him: all things exist and are carried out by his power (Sustainer, Ruler). To him: all things exist for his glory (Goal). This includes salvation: planned by him, carried out through him, and ending in his praise (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16).

To him be glory forever. Amen. Key words. The right response to all of this. Glory (doxa): honour, praise, weight. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: our chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever (Q. 1). Amen: so be it, truly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needs our glory to be complete. It means he deserves it, and our joy is found in giving it.

In a sentence. For from him and through him and for him are all things. To him be the glory forever! Amen.

For worship. Everything is from him, through him and to him, including you. Live today to his glory. Amen.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.<sup>19</sup>Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”<sup>20</sup>That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.<sup>21</sup>For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.<sup>22</sup>Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.<sup>23</sup>And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again.<sup>24</sup>For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.<sup>25</sup>Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.<sup>26</sup>And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;<sup>27</sup>“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.”<sup>28</sup>As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.<sup>29</sup>For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.<sup>30</sup>For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,<sup>31</sup>so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy.<sup>32</sup>For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.<sup>33</sup>Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!<sup>34</sup>“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”<sup>35</sup>“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”<sup>36</sup>For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

12.title: The Transformed Life
12.overview:
"Therefore" — with this word, chapters 12–16 are connected to everything that has gone before. The mercies of God described in chapters 1–11 are the foundation; the transformed life of chapters 12–16 is the superstructure. Paul does not move from theology to ethics because theology is the theoretical part and ethics is the practical part; he moves from theology to ethics because the ethics are the fruit of the theology. The mercies of God are not merely things to be believed; they are the motive force of a whole new way of living.

Chapter 12 opens with one of the most celebrated calls to consecration in the entire New Testament: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (v. 1). The language is deliberately sacrificial — the life of the justified Christian is offered to God in its entirety, not merely its "spiritual" dimension. And then the renewal of the mind (v. 2), which makes possible the discernment of God's will — the good, acceptable, and perfect. The rest of the chapter is the practical outworking of these two verses across the life of the Christian community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God" — the ethical appeal is grounded entirely in the indicative of grace. Paul does not say "in view of your obligations" or "in view of the moral law." He says: in view of the mercies of God — the whole sweep of justification, adoption, the Spirit, the love that cannot be separated from, the glory that is coming. It is the mercies that create the motivation; the obligation flows from the gift, not from duty alone.

"Present your bodies" — not just your souls or your religious activities, but your bodies: the physical, concrete, embodied reality of your daily existence. The body that gets up in the morning and goes to work. The hands that type the email. The mouth that speaks in the meeting. The feet that walk into the neighbour's house. Paul insists on the bodily nature of Christian worship because God insists on it: the gospel is not a recipe for spiritual escapism but for the consecration of the whole life — body and soul, private and public, sacred and secular — to God.

"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (v. 2) — the passive voice is significant: be transformed, not transform yourself. The transformation is something that happens to you, from the inside, through the renewal of your mind by the Spirit and the Word. The Christian does not achieve transformation by heroic effort; she submits to it by attending to the means through which God renews the mind — Scripture, prayer, worship, community, suffering. And the evidence of transformation is discernment: the ability to prove what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 demolishes the sacred-secular distinction that has plagued Christian thinking since the patristic era. The body — presented to God as a living sacrifice — is itself the site of worship. This means that the Christian's daily work, physical rest, sexual life, eating and drinking, financial decisions, and embodied relationships are all, in principle, acts of worship when offered to God in faith and obedience. The Reformers' insistence on the holiness of ordinary life is grounded here. John Calvin saw the entire creation as the theatre of God's glory; Paul grounds that vision in the consecrated body of the believer. Your body is not a vehicle for your soul; it is the instrument of your worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of sacrifice was immediately understood by both Jewish and Gentile readers. In the Jewish tradition, sacrifice was the central act of worship — the presentation of an offering to God. Paul is saying that the entire life of the Christian is now the sacrifice: not an animal brought to an altar, but a person brought to God in the totality of their daily existence. The temple has been interiorised; the altar is everywhere; the offering is ongoing. Now: The call to "not be conformed to this world" is perpetually urgent because the world perpetually presses in. Every culture — including Christian subculture — has its conforming pressures, its assumed values, its default ways of measuring worth, success, and meaning. The renewal of the mind is the counter-pressure: learning to see all of life through the lens of Scripture, of the gospel, of the mercies of God, until the world's categories no longer have automatic authority over us.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.

Meaning first. Romans 12 begins the practical part of the letter (chapters 12–16): how people who have received God’s mercy should live. Paul does not leave doctrine and then turn to ethics as a separate subject; the “therefore” of verse 1 ties the whole Christian life to the mercies of chapters 1–11. First, the foundation: give your whole self to God as a living sacrifice, and be transformed by a renewed mind, not squeezed into the world’s shape (vv. 1–2). Second, life in the church: think of yourself soberly, for we are one body with many members, and each must use the gift God’s grace has given (vv. 3–8). Third, a string of short commands describing genuine love: love within the church, love toward outsiders, and love toward enemies, ending with the call to overcome evil with good (vv. 9–21). Gospel grace produces a new kind of person and a new kind of community.

I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God. Key words. “Appeal” (parakaleō, urge, exhort, encourage) is a pastor’s pleading, not a cold order. “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, and obedience follows as a response, never as a way to earn them. “Mercies” (oiktirmoi, compassions): all that God has done in Christ: justification, adoption, the Spirit, election, his faithfulness to Israel.

To present your bodies as a living sacrifice. Key words. “Present” (paristēmi), the word used in 6:13, 19 for offering your members to God. “Bodies”: not just your soul, but your whole self as you live in the world, with your eyes, hands, tongue and time. In the Old Testament, sacrifices were killed. Christ made the one atoning sacrifice for sin (Hebrews 10:10–14). Now believers offer themselves as living sacrifices, not to atone, but in thanksgiving.

Holy and acceptable to God. Key words. Holy: set apart for God, like an offering without blemish. Acceptable: well-pleasing to him. Through Christ, our imperfect offerings please God (1 Peter 2:5).

Which is your spiritual worship. Key words. “Spiritual” is logikos, which can mean rational, reasonable, fitting; the ESV note mentions the rendering rational. “Worship” is latreia, the priestly service of the temple (9:4). In view of God’s mercies, this is the only reasonable response. Worship is not just what we do on Sunday; it is the whole of life given to God.

Do not be conformed to this world. Key words. “Conformed” (syschēmatizō, pressed into the shape of). “This world” is literally this age (aiōn), the present evil age with its values, opposed to God (Galatians 1:4). Do not let it mould you.

But be transformed by the renewal of your mind. Key words. “Transformed” (metamorphoō, the word used of Jesus’ transfiguration, Matthew 17:2, and of believers being changed into Christ’s image, 2 Corinthians 3:18). Both verbs are present tense and passive: keep on being transformed, by God’s work in you. The means is the renewing of the mind, a new way of thinking shaped by God’s word.

That by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. Key words. “Testing” (dokimazō, to prove, approve after testing). A renewed mind learns to recognise God’s will in daily decisions. The will of God here is his moral will, revealed in Scripture, not secret guidance. It is good (morally right), acceptable (pleasing to God) and perfect (complete, lacking nothing).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must withdraw from the world (John 17:15). It does not mean the body is bad. It means the believer’s whole life belongs to God and is being changed from the inside.

In a sentence. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in view of God’s mercy, Paul urges you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; this is your true and fitting worship. Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is: his good, pleasing and perfect will.

On a Tuesday. Start the day by offering yourself to God: your body, your work, your words. Then feed your mind on his word, so that the world does not shape your thinking more than Scripture does.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The renewed mind produces, first, a sober assessment of oneself — neither inflated pride nor false modesty, but honest recognition of the measure of faith God has given and the gifts he has distributed. The image Paul uses is the body: one body, many members, each with a different function. No member of the body of Christ is the whole body; no gift given to one member is given to all; the diversity is not a deficiency but the design.

Paul's list of gifts in vv. 6–8 — prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, showing mercy — is not exhaustive but representative. Each gift comes with a manner: prophesy in proportion to your faith, serve in your serving, teach in your teaching, exhort in your exhorting, give with generosity, lead with zeal, show mercy with cheerfulness. The gifts are not to be displayed but exercised — put to work in the service of the body for the benefit of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts listed in Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata — graces, gifts of the Spirit. The Reformed tradition has emphasised that every gift is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not for the personal spiritual enhancement of the recipient. The gift of teaching is not given so that the teacher can be admired; it is given so that the body can be built up. The gift of mercy is not given as an ornament of personal piety; it is given to be exercised toward those in need. Gift and function are inseparable; the gift that is not exercised in service is a lamp hidden under a bowl.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church was a remarkable mixture of social classes, ethnic backgrounds, and educational levels. The gifts distributed by the Spirit crossed every human boundary: the slave might have the gift of teaching; the educated Greek might have the gift of service. The body-of-Christ framework was the theological revolution that made sense of this diversity. Now: The contemporary church regularly struggles with two opposite errors in the theology of gifts: the inflation of spectacular gifts (leading to unhealthy spiritual hierarchy and competition) and the dismissal of ordinary gifts (leading to the impression that only the "up-front" gifts matter). Romans 12:6–8 keeps the balance: every gift, faithfully exercised in its proper sphere, is a grace from God and a service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.

For by the grace given to me. Key words. Paul speaks with apostolic authority, which itself was a gift of grace (1:5; 15:15). He speaks humbly as he calls them to humility.

I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think. Key words. A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphroneō), but to think soberly (sōphroneō). The first fruit of a renewed mind is a right view of yourself. Pride divides the body; humility builds it.

But to think with sober judgment. Key words. Sober: sensible, realistic, neither inflated nor falsely humble. Humility is not pretending you have no gifts; it is seeing your gifts as God’s gifts.

Each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. Key words. “Measure” (metron): portion, allotment. God gives each believer faith and gifts in varying measure. Some take the measure of faith as the standard of faith, the same for all: the gospel itself. Others take it as the amount of faith or gifting given to each. Either way, what you have was given, so there is no room for boasting (1 Corinthians 4:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean self-hatred or refusing to serve. Sober thinking includes recognising your gifts so that you can use them.

In a sentence. For by the grace given to Paul, he says to every one of you: do not think of yourself more highly than you ought, but rather think of yourself with sober judgement, in keeping with the faith God has distributed to each of you.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself by what God has given you, not by comparison with others. That cures both pride and envy.
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.

For as in one body we have many members. Key words. Paul’s favourite picture of the church (1 Corinthians 12:12–27; Ephesians 4:15–16). A human body is one, yet has many parts.

And the members do not all have the same function. Key words. “Function” (praxis, activity, work). An eye sees; a hand works. Difference is not a problem but the design.

So we, though many, are one body in Christ. Key words. Our unity is “in Christ”: we are joined to him, and so to one another. The church is not a club of individuals but an organism.

And individually members one of another. Key words. Each believer belongs to every other believer. You need them, and they need you. A Christian without a local church is like a hand cut off from the body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone must be the same. Nor does it mean that differences in gifts mean differences in worth.

In a sentence. Just as each of us has one body with many members, and these members do not all have the same function, so in Christ we, though many, form one body, and each member belongs to all the others.

For worship. Thank God for the other members of your church, even the ones very different from you. You belong to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
